You can easily taste the hints of onion and a touch of cumin. I cannot make out the other flavors, and to my palate there are no jalapenos or other piquant ingredients.

The consistency is like a dense brown paste. I like mine a little less dense so I mix in a half teaspoon of olive oil per half cup serving. You can adorn this with any additional ingredients like queso fresco or caramelized onions and jalapenos, of mix it with fresh salsa as a dip.

I mentioned that this is healthy. This particular brand is on par with most home made refried black beans at 200 calories per serving and 8 grams of far with 23 grams of carbs. Those numbers are, give or take, the average for most recipes. Where this one shines if the sodium level - still high at 490mg per half cup - is significantly less than the 1050-1100mg per serving for most other recipes. While the sodium content would upset my cardiologist, it's better than home made (or other canned variants of this dish.)

Note that if you have issues with soy the packaging warns that it may contain traces of it. Be forewarned. However, if you have mininal dietary restrictions and love the taste of authentic refried black beans this is pretty close to the real thing and is the equal of any restaurant version I've enjoyed on either side of the border.

title: A delicious and guilty pleasure
text:
Note: I purchase these locally so this review will only discuss the product and not factors such as price and shipping costs.

I've become addicted to this slightly bitter mixture of the sparkling mineral water from Northern Italy's Lombardy region and the blood orange (aranciata rossa) from Sicily.

The problem is, at 140 calories per 11.15 ounce can (and a whopping 32 grams of sugar), I have to watch my intake. If you are watching either calorie and/or sugar values of what you consume this is one to occasionally enjoy. The real irony is I am attracted by the bitterness which is predominate despite the high sugar content.

I will admit that this is refreshing, and especially so on a humid Florida day. However, since it is a guilty pleasure I have a ritual in which I serve mine in a fancy glass to remind myself that enjoying one is a special occasion to be savored.

In a perfect world I could drink as many as I wanted with no adverse affects. Alas, I do not live in such a world - but mine is made a little brighter when I have one of these.

title: Quick, authentic and will make a great paella with a few tweaks
text:
I am impressed by how close a packet of this seasoning will come to making a great paella. The ingredients are somewhat simple: garlic, salt, paprika, cornmeal, pepper, cloves and saffron. There is also added coloring. The salt is a full quarter of the mix, and the less than three percent saffron content can be boosted with a high quality saffron added. I use [[ASIN:B007P51VHO Persian Saffron]] and steep it in hot (but not boiling) water before adding it to the paella as a stock.

There are a few things that will make this the perfect spice blend. First is to use a true paella rice from Spain's Calasparra region. Second, use a proper liquid-to-rice ratio. My favorite brand of Calasparra rice (called bomba) is [[ASIN:B0050ILG4Q this one]], and the ratio I have come to use is 3.5 parts water to one part rice. Finally, use a proper paella pan and place all of the ingredients in it and cook at low heat. No stirring is required. If you are used to making risotto these directions sound counter-intuitive, but I assure you that they will work. In fact, you will be treated to a crispy bottom, called socarrat, that is much like the 'tahdig' that is so prized in Persian rice and highly prized in paella as well.

Although the high sodium content may give you pause, when mixed with the other ingredients the actual sodium per serving of paella is relatively low. Also, if you opt to use just the packet without adding more saffron you will still get an authentic tasting paella. The only shortcut I recommend against is using a rice other than one from Calasparra. To me that will make all of the difference.

title: The ONLY rice from the ONLY region
text:
This is the 'bomba' rice that only comes from the Calasparra region and is the only rice you should be using if you are making paella. I discovered this brand locally and my point of comparison is another brand from the same region: [[ASIN:B00EYBZ8OO Zoe Brand Diva Select Bomba Rice]]. Like that one, this has perfectly dry grains that are aromatic. Those factors indicate that this rice has been properly stored and handled.

Note that if you are only now discovering rice from the Calasparra region this rice has a high absorption rate of liquid. In fact, I have found that 3.5 cups of water to a cup of this rice is the ideal ratio. More importantly, this rice needs to be cooked in an open pan (preferably a paella pan like a [[ASIN:B000QYM2OC Carbon Steel Paella Pan]]) and left to cook without stirring. Unlike the labor-intensive risotto, you put everything in the pan, set to low heat and let cook.

Regardless of cooking method, this or any other brand from the region is a necessary ingredient for authentic paella. This particular brand stands out because it is first quality and, frankly, the price is below any other geniume Calasparra bomba rice I have found. If you are not fortunate enough to find this locally this brand is one that I personally trust and one I would order online of I could not obtain it any other way. Trust me, this rice makes a big difference in how a paella turns out.

title: Flavorful and respectable nutritional values
text:
Note: I purchase these locally so this review will focus on the actual product and not address variable factors such as price and shipping costs, which can change with both sellers and time.

These beans are not only flavorful, but plump, firm and with an excellent texture. I typically have them as a side dish with rice, but I have also used them in soups. In the latter they maintain their firmness as long as you add them in at the last stage and do not heat any higher than simmer.

Among the reasons I love these is the nutritional values. Each serving is a half cup (there are three in this can). Each is 80 calories with zero fat or cholesterol. Sodium is 380mg per serving, which may be high for folks who have restrictions, but that can be reduced to a nominal amount if you drain and rinse the beans before preparing them.

Ingredients are simple: water, beans, salt and a relatively safe and benign additive called calcium disodium EDTA that is for color retention.

One final thing that I love about the ones I get locally: Goya is now shipping these with an easy open, pull tab top that makes it a snap to open. In that respect these beans are flavorful, nutritious and convenient.

title: Absolutely delicious and healthy
text:
I consume a lot of grains and this is one of my favorite blends. When I saw this at my local Publix I was a little put off by the price, but grabbed one of each blend from their display. This is my favorite for a few reasons.

First, I love the convenience of preparing brown rice and quinoa in a mere 90 seconds. Making brown rice in my pressure cooker is a 45 minute process and quinoa - prepared properly - takes at least 25 minutes. So for convenience alone this won me over.

The flavor is superb. I have used this as both a side dish and the foundation of main dishes when I add fish or vegetables. I also love the texture. Getting brown rice to the correct texture that is not chewy or mushy is a near art, but the grains in this blend are perfect. Same with the quinoa.

I mentioned that this is healthy. Here are the stats: Each serving is one cup (compare to the half cup servings for Uncle Ben's ready rice blends).

There are 240 calories per serving, approximately 35 of which are from fat. Total fat is 3.5 grams per serving (a half gram of which is saturated fat), with 47 grams of carbs and 400mg of sodium. If the sodium looks high remember that the serving size is a full cup, which makes the content less than half of some of Uncle Ben's blends to which I am comparing this.

The ingredients are also healthy. In fact, with the exception of the sea salt everything else is certified organic. Of the ingredients the only red flag is the soy lecithin, which some folks find to be an allergen. Otherwise, it's simple and natural: whole grain brown rice and whole grain quinoa with sunflower oil, sea salt, garlic powder, tapioca starch, onion powder, dried garlic, parsley and black pepper.

This goes perfectly with a little olive oil or butter, and a squeeze of lemon works wonders too.

title: A wonderful break from the mundane
text:
Two things: (1) I purchase this locally, so am reviewing the product and not pricing or shipping, and (2), I agree that to my palate this is not the most flavorful of the Seeds of Change blends. It is, however, a healthy side that has multiple textures and flavors, and a touch of the ancient. The blend is based on grains grown in the 'Fertile Crescent'

What I particularly love is the convenience of having this precooked. If you were to make this yourself it would involve individually cooking each type of grain because each has a different cooking time. Moreover, this has dietary fiber and protein that should be a part of any balanced diet. The grains in this blend are long grain brown rice, barley, rye, bulgur, red winter wheat, quinoa and wild rice. You can use this blend as a hot side or as a cold salad - Middle Eastern style - depending on the main course and your mood.

The seasonings and flavors, with the exception of the salt, are all certified organic. They give a subtle, but not overwhelming, flavor to keep the grains interesting instead of bland. I sometimes just squeeze a little fresh lemon juice or dribble olive oil over the mix. The spices and herbs used are: evaporated cane juice (essentially sugar), dried onion and red bell pepper, garlic powder, parsley, chili pepper, black pepper and cumin. There are also a few ingredients that you need to know about in case you have allergies, which are: tapioca starch, high oleic sunflower oil and tamari powder. The latter contains soybeans, salt and rice flour.

Nutritionally, this blend is Calories: 240 calories per one cup serving (about 30 of which are from fat), 47 grams of carbs, three grams of fat and 340mg of sodium. The sodium may be a red flag if you have restrictions, but remember that the serving size if a full cup versus the half cup size of competing products that actually contain more sodium per serving.

I love the convenience of being able to prepare this blend in a quick 90 seconds instead of spending literally hours making it from dry grains. It's convenient and one of the ready grain blends that I frequently enjoy as a side dish.

title: Positively delicious and convenient
text:
I discovered this and a few other blends at my local Publix and gave them a try. They are delicious. Exotic actually, and have reasonable nutritional values. I will say that they are a little pricier than the Uncle Ben's Ready Rice blends that compete for shelf space, but these are much lower in sodium than that brand.

What I love about this blend is the mix of spices and herbs that flavor the grains. With the exception of the sea salt in the ingredients everything is certified organic - another factor in my decision to willingly pay a premium price (locally, at the time of this review, it's about the same as online, with no shipping charges.)

Contents are white basmati rice, garbanzos, potatoes, carrots, mung beans, lentils and onions. These are seasoned with an exotic blend of spices that include sea salt, coriander, cayenne pepper, cumin, cinnamon and clove. Note: this blend does contain high oleic sunflower oil and soy lecithin, so if you have issues with those then you may want to avoid this product.

Nutritionally there is a single one cup serving (as opposed to half cup servings in the Uncle Ben's blends) that come in at 230 calories of which approximately 35 are from fat. Actual fat content is 3.5 grams and 41 grams of carbs. Sodium is 480mg - not horrible but a red flag if you have restrictions.

Bottom line: this is a wonderful and reasonably healthy rice blend that has a touch of the exotic from a Tibetan recipe. It goes with practically any main dish and at 90 seconds in a microwave is fast to prepare.

title: Exceptional quality
text:
There are three things that I look for in polenta meal: Aroma, texture and color. The first hits you as soon as you open the bag and it's heavenly. Evidence of the second comes when you roll a pinch through your fingers to feel the dry, coarse grind. The final one is color and this one has uniform coloration.

I will say that this grind takes a little more water than most, but that is easily compensated for by increasing the water to meal ratio from the normal 3:1 to 3.5:1. One note: although I use a special pan designed for cooking polenta (a [[ASIN:B000V5YP7I Old Dutch Solid Copper Polenta Pan with Wooden Handle]]) that is not truly necessary. What is necessary is using good water and minding the polenta until it is fully cooked.

If you are new to cooking polenta here is how I make mine. This method includes how I compensate for this particular grind of meal. I put a few drops of olive oil in the water as well. I also start mine cold by adding it to water before turning up the heat, then bringing it up to medium and stirring the whole time. It's time consuming and labor intensive, but it's a tried and true method for me. Using this meal it takes from 35 to 45 minutes on medium heat and constant stirring to fully cook it to my preferred consistency. Since I often make polenta as a step in making crostini this one is perfect. It cooks up slightly dry and firm. Part of that is a function of my longer cooking time, but part is the great grind of this particular meal because it has sufficient surface to absorb water.

The bottom line is this is a premium grade of corn meal that is ground perfectly for traditional polenta. Moretti makes other grades of meal, but this one if the most common and this brand is one of the best in my opinion.

title: Kick-start your own Ethiopian (or Eritrean) cooking
text:
The recipe on this package was almost worth the price of the spices themselves. I purchased this locally on a whim and the results from following the recipe (and using this mix) were spectacular.

This is not my first time using a Pursuit of Spice product. I also have used their [[ASIN:B005OSZLZW Pursuit of Spice Moroccan Tagine]] with the same great results. While I am adept at North African cooking I wanted to learn how to make some of the dishes from the Horn of Africa and this is a wonderful way to quickly get into it.

One modification I made to this blend was to add a little [[ASIN:B004C9PTCE Bhut Jolokia Powder]] to the blend because I wanted something more spicy than normal bereberé. However, I did use the dry cooking onion approach that the recipe called for for making the bereberé part of the dish and it made a big difference in the flavor - for the better.

In addition to a delicious meal that was flavored perfectly for my palate, this set of spices and the recipe gave me the confidence to start cooking other East African cuisine. This one is convenient and a great way to experiment. If you decide to continue cooking Ethiopian or Eritrean dishes you will probably outgrow this kit and start mixing your own spices. However, this will start you on your journey.

title: Perfect for new tagine owners
text:
I purchase my own spices, but this package is a convenient way to get the right proportions of essential spices for tagine cooking. I've given tagines as gifts and always include one of these packets so the recipient can immediately use it.

Aside from the high quality of the spices that are both fresh and aromatic, the value of this pack for someone new to North African cooking is the blend. It's been skillfully done with just the right amounts of each spice. Equally important to the new comer to this style of cooking is the recipe on the packaging itself. Granted this is a fairly generic dish, but if the instructions are followed to the letter this will allow anyone with a modicum of cooking skills to create an exotic dish using easy to find ingredients.

Although I mentioned a tagine, you definitely do not need one to cook the dish per the included recipe. Cooking with one will intensify the flavors (especially from the spices in this pack), and will make the serving experience authentic. If you do not own a tagine, but are considering purchasing one I recommend the [[ASIN:B0060M6EJ8 Moroccan Large Simple Cooking Tagine By Treasures of Morocco]]. It's family sized, reasonably priced and it's the real thing.

Bottom line: this will allow you to experiment with North African cooking without spending a fortune on the individual spices. If you do decide to add that cuisine to your menus you can then purchases the necessary spices for your pantry. I personally use this blend for my North African cooking, but I make that cuisine weekly: [[ASIN:B008437X78 Mediterranean Gourmet Ras El Hanout]].

title: Not bad for a California arborio rice
text:
I normally use a different brand of arborio rice, but was introduced to this one when my brother gave me a few bags. I was initially skeptical because I had never heard of the brand and was put off by it being domestic. My concerns were unfounded.

This rice is as consistent as the one I normally use. What I mean is after two bags spread over six months each time I prepared risotto the grains toasted in the butter correctly and absorbed stock at the same rate and ratio. More importantly, the grains were fresh and after cooking were flavorful with the authentic arborio texture.

I do have to forewarn that the 'stovetop cooking instructions' on the bag should be completely ignored. Their instructions bear no relation to how to prepare this particular grain for making risotto. It's more slanted towards making steamed rice - something risotto is not. However, that does not detract from the product, which is a surprisingly high quality arborio rice. I am not sure I will continue purchasing this brand since I am more than happy with the one I normally use, but I would not hesitate to make risotto with it for discerning guests either.

title: Delicious and convenient, but with caveats
text:
Make no mistake - this rice is convenient and packed with flavor. If you have no dietary restrictions and are physically active then you will probably love this for a number of reasons.

Foremost is convenience. In 90 short seconds you can have perfectly prepared grains that are plump and steamed to perfection. That alone makes this wonderful because properly steaming wild rice requires a pressure cooker and about forty minutes. Adding in the faster cooking long grain rice would entail steaming them separately and mixing them.

Second is the flavor. Undeniably delicious and can stand by itself as a side dish or combined with meat, fish or vegetables to be en entree.

Where the problems surface is if you are on a restricted diet, especially for sodium. This package contains a stratospheric sodium level and more than nominal fat content. Sodium is over the top at 690mg per serving. Fat is 2.5 grams a serving and account for 25 of the 210 calories. Those undo the health benefits of wild and long grain rice as a part of a balanced diet for those of us who have to count sodium and fat intake. Moreover, while the fat in this product is not particularly bad for folks who are young and active, the sodium is at levels that I consider to be too high for any diet.

I get around the sodium and fat problems by 'cutting' this with steamed jasmine or basmati rice I prepare then mixing this into the plain steamed rice. It works out well when I am cooking for company. A final note; follow the directions and this will cook perfectly. Especially Step 2 listed on the back of the package that requires you to tear back two inches at the notch on the top left side of the package. Failure to do that (or cooking longer than 90 seconds in a microwave) can get messy.

title: Excellent quality
text:
Disclaimer: I purchased this locally so my review is confined to the product and not pricing or shipping costs.

While shopping at my local Walmart this caught my eye and I decided to purchase a can and compare it to my normal brand (Goya). This one is easily the equal in my opinion. It passed my test of how quickly it will flash into oil when you boil it. That indicates that this coconut milk is pure and has not been altered or the oil removed or reduced. Note that the can does list water and a preservative called potassium meta bisulfide as ingredients.

The taste and viscosity are what I would expect from premium coconut milk - or even milk fresh from a ripe coconut. Indeed, this is the perfect liquid to steam jasmine rice for either savory or sweet dishes, and when flashed into oil is ideal for a number of Southeast Asian dishes. I use this for making a dish called ginataan that is favorite dish from the Bikol region in the Philippines. It's also perfect for many Thai dishes. In fact this is a product of Thailand.

Going forward I intend to make this my preferred brand since it's half the price (locally) of the Goya brand I had been using, with the same quality and cooking characteristics.

title: Fast, convenient and mostly healthy
text:
This is one of the better ready rice packs that Uncle Ben's offers. Some of their ready rice packs come with unhealthy additives and high sodium, but this one and a few others in this series are actually healthy.

What I love is the convenience of making the rice quickly and easily. There is a notch on the left side of the bag that allows you to pull a small (approximately two inch slit) before microwaving. Make sure you use it or the bag will literally explode. Also I recommend not exceeding the 90 second cook time. If you follow the instructions to the letter you will e rewarded with rice that is plump, full of flavor and has that perfect grain separation that we all strive for when steaming rice.

I am less enamored of the ingredients. This package contains canola or sunflower oil (the contents claim 'and/or'), which bring the fat content to each of the two servings in the pouch to 2.5 grams. This equals twenty-five of the 200 calories for each serving. Not terrible, mind you, but if you are on a strict diet this will cut into your daily limit of fats. Sodium is a manageable 10mg per serving, which is a vast difference from some of Uncle Ben's ready rice dishes that contain well over 650mg per serving. Carbs are 40mg, which is on par with most long grain rices.

Overall, this is one of the rare, healthy convenience foods. It cuts over fifteen minutes out of the time it takes to steam rice yourself, and aside from my minor complaints is both delicious and healthy - a combination you do not often find.

title: Not as healthy as it implies
text:
Many of us associate wild rice with healthy eating. Unfortunately this rice is anything but if you have sodium restrictions. However, I will start with the positive things and save the caveats for last.

On the plus side this is a convenient way to quickly prepare and serve wild and long grain rice. Wild rice normally requires a pressure cooker and a lot of time to get grains that are not mushy or chewy, and are plump and flavorful. Adding in long grain rice to the equation and you would have to steam the two separately and mix them afterwards because they have different cooking times. This package solves that problems and does so in a mere ninety seconds. The rice is delicious and perfectly cooked, although it's too salty for my taste. More about that below.

On the negative side this package contains a whopping 650mg of sodium per serving. Also, unlike other Ready Rice dishes from Uncle Ben's this one claims three servings per package instead of two, so the sodium level of over the top to say the least. Even if you are not on a sodium-restricted diet this is plain unhealthy. I get around this by only using this rice when I have a larger number of guests over and mix it in with normally steamed basmati or jasmine rich. I use a 2:1ratio or my own steamed rice to this and the sodium level and saltiness are at more acceptable levels.

I will give this one credit for having significantly less fat than [[ASIN:B0025UNWWQ Uncle Ben's Ready Rice Whole Grain Medley]], but neither is what I would call healthy.

One final note: follow the directions on the bag regarding making a two inch slit in the bag (there is a notch that allows you to simply accomplish this). Failure will inevitably result in an exploded bag inside your microwave. I learned that the hard way.

title: Delicious, but there are problems
text:
I've purchased a number of Uncle Ben's ready Rice products and most have ingredients that slightly raise fat or sodium, but not to levels that are a red flag. This one, unfortunately, does. Worse, the main ingredients - brown, red and wild rice - are the basis of a healthy diet.

Before going into the problems I did find the rices to be cooked to perfection. If you ever steamed brown, red or especially wild rice you know that it's time consuming and requires a pressure cooker to get right. Steaming all three grains and getting it right is a spectacular feat, and these are cooked right. each grain retains its own characteristic with the brown rice coming out plump and the red and wild grains less plump, but not mushy or chewy.

What ruins what should be a perfectly healthy side are the high sodium level and the fat content. Sodium is over the top at 690mg per serving. Fat is 2.5 grams a serving and account for 25 of the 210 calories.

One other thing I have found - and this is my personal taste - is the rice is too salty. i manage to get around that by steaming an equal amount of basmati rice and mixing this into the plain steamed rice. That cuts the saltiness and distributed the fat and sodium to manageable levels.

Also be aware that the picture on the package depicts a lighter color rice dish. I have uploaded a customer-supplied image that shows how dark this truly is. That is not necessarily a bad thing, but presentation is a part of serving and you should know what the cooked product will look like.

A final note; follow the directions and this will cook perfectly. Especially Step 2 listed on the back of the package that requires you to tear back two inches at the notch on the top left side of the package. Failure to do that (or cooking longer than 90 seconds in a microwave) can get messy.

title: An authentic taste of Mesoamerica
text:
This sauce has both heat (a respectable 11,600 Scoville units) and an interesting flavor that is supposed to be based on ancient recipes. Before proceeding I want to disclose that I purchase this locally (indeed, it's actually served in one Mexican restaurant I patronize in Daytona Beach), so my review is going to focus on the product and not address price or shipping.

Habanero peppers dominate the flavor profile. Interestingly, this sauce does not have the strong bite one associates with habaneros. Instead it has a slower spread and burn like Scotch bonnets from the Caribbean. But that is where the similarity to Caribbean sauces ends. Although vinegar is second only to the peppers as an ingredient the flavor profile has a minimum of sourness. I am guessing that it's the acidity from the tomatoes that mask it, or the spices which are so skillfully blended into this sauce.

Its earthy brown color matches the earthy flavor that augments the habaneroa. It has a moderate viscosity that easily pours, but does not run off like the more watery Tabasco-style sauces. Saltiness is yet another dominating component of the flavor profile. If you have sodium restrictions do be aware that this sauce contains 105mg of sodium per serving (about 4 grams).

If you love hot sauces and put flavor equal to heat you will probably love this one. For me there is an added pleasure in believing that this is based on a Mesoamerican recipe, but it's the flavor that won me over.

title: The best I have tried - and no hidden surprises in the ingredients
text:
Prior to discovering this ready-serve style brown rice I had been purchasing [[ASIN:B0074EE6RI Uncle Ben's Ready Rice Whole Grain Brown Rice]]. There were some minor issues with that one, but the convenience and quality of the grains won out. When I discovered this rice I immediately made it my preferred brand and choice.

The grains cook up plump and flavorful, with a perfect texture. Brown rice is notoriously difficult to cook properly without a pressure cooker, so finding one that is essentially pure and cooks in 90 seconds versus around 45 minutes is a boon. In fact if you cook it using a microwave per directions on the lid you will be treated to rice that is neither too chewy nor mushy - perfectly steamed.

I mentioned that this is essentially pure. What I mean by that is this is basically rice that has been parboiled so the main ingredients are rice and water. The label on the lid claims only those, but the product description on this page at the time of the review also claims calcium carbonate. Basically that is what you get if you are taking calcium supplements. However, when comparing this to the Uncle Ben's brown rice at the top of the page this one has 155 calories per serving and a very nominal 5mg of sodium. The Uncle Ben's contains an additional ingredient - either canola or sunflower oil (or both) - which accounts for 30 of the 190 calories per serving. It also has triple the sodium.

Bottom line: this is a fast and convenient way to enjoy perfectly steamed brown rice. If you are particular about additives this is also one of the purest brands I have tried (I have tried many more than the Uncle Ben's to which I am comparing this and that is the second purest!) Going forward this is the one I will purchase and recommend.

title: Fast, delicious, but a small gotcha if you are on a strict diet
text:
I was tempted to subtract a star because this rice has a more than a nominal amount of fat from added oil. However, it's so delicious and perfect if you follow the directions and microwave it for a mere minute and a half that I gave it my highest mark.

The rice is fragrant as only a properly steamed brown rice can, and it is cooked to perfection. The plumb, flavorful grains make this one worth the trade-off for me because it would take forty-five minutes in a pressure cooker for me to achieve the same results. If you've ever steamed brown rice you will know that I mean.

What irks me, though, is this has - according to the box - either canola or sunflower oil (or both), which accounts for 30 of the 190 calories per serving (there are two servings per package.) That comes in at three grams of fat per serving, which is why I added a caveat in the title. However, sodium is a scant 15mg per serving.

For me the convenience and the perfect brown rice grains outweigh the minor nutritional factors. I do wish this rice was unadulterated with oil, but on the other hand I can live with it. It is truly a heart-healthy convenience food and that has to count for something.

title: Creamier than yellow and a different flavor
text:
Since purchasing my [[ASIN:B000V5YP7I Old Dutch Solid Copper Polenta Pan with Wooden Handle, 5 Quart]] I've been experimenting with different types of polenta meal. I've come to love the Moretti brand because of the variety and quality of the ground meal that they offer.

This one is a typical bramata grind. It's coarse, but a little finer than other brands of bramata style polenta, and this one is white instead of yellow. Like all of the Moretti products I have tried this one has a wonderful aroma of ground corn meal as soon as you open the bag. That aroma is an in indication of quality. Also like other polentas from this brand they cook slightly faster than some other brands. That is because Moretti grinds them slightly finer.

Because I wanted to make a creamier polenta I used a 4:1 ratio of water to meal. I normally use a 3.5:1, which is still wetter than most ratios, but this meal absorbs quickly and I did not want it to be too firm or dry. I add a few drops of olive oil and a pinch of baking soda to cold water, then the polenta meal. I then bring up the heat while stirring. I do this to keep it from getting lumpy. Cooking takes from 35 to 45 minutes on medium heat and constant stirring to fully cook it to my preferred consistency.

I tasted the finished polenta and was surprised by the difference in flavor between this and the more traditional yellow. This has a less pronounced corn flavor. For the dish I used a lot of butter and crumpled gorgonzola cheese. For a second batch I used less butter and brie cheese, which turned out to be my favorite recipe (although I had to add some sea salt to that version.)

Overall this white polenta has both a different flavor and slightly different texture than the yellow type. I am sold on the Moretti brand, which I purchase locally. Each bag has been fresh, and each type cooks perfectly.

title: Brings boring eggs to life
text:
I tend to eat my eggs poached or boiled to cut down on fats and honestly was getting bored with the taste. I found this in a local Indian/Middle Eastern store and had to try it - and eggs have never been the same.

This is much more than salt and pepper with a few spices thrown in. To my palate it's a skillful blend of complementary flavors with a few surprises. The garlic and cumin are what I expected. Even the cinnamon since I love both Sicilian and North African cooking that includes it in savory dishes. There is just enough sugar and nutmeg to add an interesting contrast between sweet and slightly bitter in the flavor profile. The ginger added to the piquant character of the pepper. In fact the only way know the flavor is to try it, and it's simply perfect on eggs. Also use it as a garnish on egg salads or deviled eggs.

There is 380mg per 2 gram serving, but frankly I could not imagine using two whole grams of this seasoning on an egg or even three. I use the slightest pinch, which is enough to make a poached egg interesting without overwhelming it. In fact I recommend that you start with less and add more if needed if you have never used this blend.

title: Near perfect and salt free
text:
I rarely eat meat, but when I do it's lamb. This rub is very close to the blend I mix myself, but I like this one more. For one thing the quality of the herbs and spices in this one is top notch. The aroma is simply amazing. More importantly, the lavender is not overwhelmed by the garlic or rosemary in the blend - mixing those properly takes a lot of skill and this one is perfect.

Do note that the tin contains about three tablespoons of mix. That may seem shockingly small, but a very little of this goes a long way. The key is to actually rub the blend into the meat and let it set and marry before cooking. A tablespoon will easily flavor two pounds of lamb - and possibly more if you are adept at applying rubs to meats.

The flavors are truly Mediterranean. I add come crushed mint, cumin and a little lemon zest to the mix before rubbing it into the meat. That is for my personal taste. The point is while this works beautifully out of the tin you can add your own touch. I usually rub in a little olive oil just before cooking to seal in the juices and flavor.

What I love is the fact that this contains no salt or any other ingredient that is not a natural spice or herb. No preservatives or flavor enhancers. You can control how much salt goes into a dish by adding it yourself. For folks like me who have sodium restrictions this is a major feature. As an aside, adding salt to a rub before cooking inhibits the cooking time, so from a culinary perspective the lack of it in this mix is a plus.

This is a pricey mix, but when you consider how much lamb it can flavor (and the price of the lamb itself) it's a bargain.

title: Exceptional as a rub or seasoning
text:
I've used this as a rub on both red and white fish before broiling or grilling and it imparts an exotic flavor. The packaging implies Chinese cuisine, but there are so many vastly different regional ones that it's too broad of a generalization. I will say that this has a vague flavor of Southeast Asia and is a fusion of Vietnamese, Laotian, Cambodian and Thai flavors. Sort of. But that is that makes it special. It will transform common American fare into something both exotic and familiar.

In addition to using this as a rub I've used it as a dip and condiment, as well as a spice mix. For a dip or condiment I typically mix a pinch with fish sauce, add a squeeze of lime and some chopped bird's eye peppers. It's perfect for grilled or broiled vegetables like eggplant, zucchini, as well as some meats. I do not eat meat these days, but when I lived in the Philippines I would use a similar concoction, minus these spices, for port and other types of meat and it was delicious. I can imagine how much better they would have been had I had this blend on hand.

As a seasoning a pinch in a stir fry or even a soup or stew will enhance it and all that exotic touch. Something less is more, so if you want to subtly alter the basic flavor profile of a dish use this instead of your normal seasonings.

For me the best thing about this spice blend (and the others made by this brand) is the absolute absence of salt or additives. You get just the herbs and spices and they are fresh and aromatic. If you need salt you can control the amount. Some other brands include not only salt, but preservatives in their blends. Also note that these tins are small, but a little does go a long way. Each one contains about four tablespoons, and most meals use about a single tablespoon. The tins are perfect for keeping the ingredients fresh, but after you open one I recommend using it up in two to three weeks to ensure that you are using the herbs and spices at their peak potency.

title: One of the best herb and spice blends for fish
text:
First I want to address some complaints about the quantity of these tins: they are small, but a little of this rub goes a long way. You do have to rub it into the fish - not merely sprinkle it - to get the full flavor from the smallest amount of mix. A tablespoon will more than adequately cover a one pound piece of salmon and there are three tablespoons per tin.

The herbs and spices are fresh and highly aromatic. The tin helps keep them that way, although I would recommend using up a tin within a few weeks of opening it. What I love is there is no salt. Period. Most blends include it and for those of us who have sodium restrictions this is a major plus. If you must have salt you can add it yourself. The ingredients are simple: garlic, onion, dill, tarragon, pink peppercorns, lemon peel, paprika, black pepper and fennel. It's the quality of the ingredients that I mentioned above and the skillful blend that make this a value. You could buy the herbs and spices yourself, but getting the proportions right is the hard part.

I've used this on various types of fish from salmon to flounder and it works on them all. It's my secret ingredient for most of the fish-based dishes that I serve.

Just be aware that each tin only contains three tablespoons of the mix and you will not be disappointed. Especially since you can easily flavor three pounds of fish per tin. It's the flavor that counts and this - to me - is worth every penny for how it transforms my fish into something special.

title: Perfect traditional blend
text:
This is one of the most balanced mulling spice blends I have found. In fact I cannot make my own blends any better, and the ingredients used in this brand are aromatic and fresh. In fact you could make an expensive potpourri with this stuff.

What I love about it besides the wonderful fragrance is there are no strange additives. Like the can promises this is all natural and contains only cinnamon chips, orange rind, whole allspice, whole cloves, cinnamon oil and orange oil.

These impart the traditional aroma and flavor in a winter cider or even tea. A tea infuser or a spice ball, depending on what you are making, and quality tea leaves or unfiltered cider are all you need. This quickly infuses any hot liquid and has the added benefit of filling your house with a near intoxicating fragrance. I can speak for unfiltered cider and various teas, but not wine. I have never mulled vino, but I am sure this would work as intended for that too. I do fear that the potent flavors would mask any nuances of the wine.

title: Not exactly blazing hot, but packed with flavor
text:
'Hot' is a subjective term, and blazing hot even more so. This sauce does pack some heat, but the main reason I love it (and awarded five stars) is the flavor. The ingredients are somewhat simple and straightforward: peppers, water, vinegar, salt and some spices.)

What sets this apart from other Scotch-Bonnet sauces is the peppers themselves impart a touch of sweetness. Also, instead of giving this sauce a sour quality the vinegar actually makes it tangy. It has the obligatory saltiness to round out the basic flavor profile for a hot sauce, but at a scant 39mg of sodium per serving this is practically guilt free for me. I have sodium restrictions and have to watch my intake.

The heat has almost no bite and is the typical slow build, spread and burn type that is characteristic of Scotch bonnet peppers. It's certainly much hotter than Tabasco sauce, but not as hot as, say, [[ASIN:B0000GHNTK El Yucateco Green Chile Habanero Sauce]]. Not very precise, but that is the best I can describe the piquant qualities of this sauce.

If you love maximum flavor with respectable heat you will probably enjoy this sauce. I'll confess that I do not purchase it often, but when I do a bottle does not last me long. So many hot sauces and so little time.

title: High quality meal
text:
You can tell as soon as you open the bag that the corn meal is of the highest quality. The first indication is the aroma. The second is as you roll a pinch through your fingers it's dry, has a coarse grind and has uniform coloration.

The proof, though, is in the cooking. There are a lot of variations on that so I am going to explain how I do it. I use a slightly wetter ratio for all styles of polenta: 3.5:1 instead of the normal 3:1. I put a few drops of olive oil in the water as well. I also start mine cold by adding it to water before turning up the heat, then bringing it up to medium and stirring the whole time. It's time consuming and labor intensive, but it's a tried and true method for me. Using this meal it takes from 35 to 45 minutes on medium heat and constant stirring to fully cook it to my preferred consistency. Since I often make polenta as a step in making crostini this one is perfect. It cooks up slightly dry and firm. Part of that is a function of my longer cooking time, but part is the great grind of this particular meal because it has sufficient surface to absorb water.

One other note: although I use a special pan designed for cooking polenta (a [[ASIN:B000V5YP7I Old Dutch Solid Copper Polenta Pan]]) that is not truly necessary. What is necessary is using good water and minding the polenta until it is fully cooked. This brand will ensure that you have the best ingredients.

title: Reminds me of Southeast Asian sauces
text:
This is one of the most interesting sauces I have tried because it bridges the chasm between two of my favorite regions: Asia and Caribbean. What makes this special is the flavor profile that is certainly piquant, but has a touch of tang with pronounced saltiness and garlic. To my palate it's perfect.

Do be aware that this is a relatively mild sauce that is more focused on flavor. It does have an initial bite and a nice heat build and spread, but it's not scorching. Part of the Asian flavor elements come from the fish sauce. In fact, I've long used a hot pepper and a lime-like fruit called a kalamansi in fish sauce as a condiment. This sauce has the same basic foundation with a nice mix of natural flavors from the peppers and a ton of garlic. I love garlic, but it did mask some of the peppers' natural nuances.

I did a little experimenting and found that freshly chopped cilantro is a perfect complement to the flavor of this sauce. I have been doctoring the sauce with cilantro for grilled fish, as well as broiled eggplant.

Note that the sodium in a serving is 125mg. That is not extraordinarily high given a serving is two tablespoons, but is still a number you need to watch if you have sodium restrictions.

Bottom line: this is a skillfully blended sauce that is packed with flavor and just enough heat to keep it interesting. I'll definitely be purchasing more in the future.

title: Bargain if you cannot get this locally
text:
I am not going to address the price and shipping costs because those are variable and can change in an instant. I will say that if you cannot purchase this locally this is a bargain. For one thing you are getting two 23.5 ounce bottles for close to the price of the same number of 4.5 ounce bottles. If you go through this sauce the way I do the savings add up.

If you are new to this sauce you are in for a treat. . In Costa Rica this is used as both a condiment and a cooking ingredient. I use it mainly as a condiment. What makes this special is the fairly complete and complex flavor profile, which is sweet and tangy, and has some relatively mild heat from the chiles. It is somewhat less hot than Tabasco sauce.

The rest of the flavor profile is savory from the vegetables used, including the expected onions, but the unexpected cucumbers and cauliflower, and a interesting addition of carrots. There is a hint of bitterness, probably from the turmeric, and an interesting blend of other spices that includes cumin for a taste of the exotic and black pepper. It's also salty with close to 20mg of sodium per gram of sauce. However, it's used in lieu of salt, not in addition to in much he same manner that Asian tables use fish or soy sauce instead of salt.

It's great on eggs and is a key ingredient in Costa Rica's national dish, gallo pinto, which is black beans, rice and some vegetables served mixed. It's also excellent on fish, especially salmon, but also even the more delicate white types like flounder.

title: Country-style (from Lombardi)
text:
I found this locally and decided to give it a try since I love polenta. This is quite different in both flavor and appearance from the more common bramata style. The grind is close to the same between the two, but this one has buckwheat that adds a complementary nutty aspect to the flavor. It also gives a speckled look to the meal and the finished polenta.

This particular brand has a wonderful aroma and a bag goes a long way. One thing I noticed is that it cooks to the same perfect consistency each time. In other words, if you follow your recipe using identical heat settings and proportions each time it will come out the same as the last. That is not always the case with other polenta meal I have used in the past that had wide variations even when using the same bag of meal.

Cooking is about the same. I use a [[ASIN:B000V5YP7I Old Dutch Solid Copper Polenta Pan]], but you can get by with any pot that is sufficiently large. I do deviate a bit from what most recipes recommend. For one thing I add a little olive oil to the water, and for another I add the meal to the water before bringing up the heat. That greatly aids in keeping the polenta lump-free. However, it's labor intensive because you have to start stirring as soon as the meal hits the water - and continue until it's ready to serve. The cooking process on medium heat takes somewhere between 35 and 45 minutes (I go by the way it looks and the consistency more than time.) I also add a teaspoon of baking soda to the water before adding the meal.

Even locally this is a premium priced polenta. However, the essence of Italian cooking is to always use the best ingredients and this brand is the best I have ever tried. This particular style - the corn and buckwheat blend - is definitely worth trying if you want an authentic country-style polenta.

title: A taste of Barbados
text:
I love Caribbean sauces, and particularly love the diversity among them - especially between the northern Caribbean and the southern islands. This one has all of the hallmarks of a great southern sauce: more fruity and sweet, but with a respectable amount of heat.

While not among the hottest sauces from the region the flavor profile is almost evenly split between sweet and pungent. There is a bit of tang, and very little saltiness. In many respects it is one of the most unique Caribbean sauces I have tried. Part of the reason for that is the choice of fruit - the star fruit - which is enigmatic in itself. It has a subtle hint of citrus, but also is similar to fleshy fruits like apples, although not quite that either.

The tang mainly comes from the citric acid and mustard, while the turmeric both colors the sauce and gives it a slightly bitter aftertaste. What I love is the Scotch bonnets which add both flavor and heat. The heat is the slow burn type typical of those peppers, without the bite of habaneros that are often used in the southern Caribbean sauces.

Since I am on a sodium-restricted diet I especially love the low sodium levels, which come in at 60mg per serving. That is less than many other Caribbean sauces and significantly less than Mexican and Mesoamerican ones.

The sauce is thick and can be spread almost like mayonnaise. I've used it on just about every conceivable dish, including fish, eggs and even as a condiment for soups and stews. Do note that you have to refrigerate this sauce after opening it.

title: For those who love the heat
text:
This is the sibling to a milder (but still respectably hot) sauce called [[ASIN:B0075ANC9Y Hot Caribbean Pepper Sauce by Tortuga]]. There are some major differences between the two sauces aside from the heat.

One of the major differences is this one has a much simpler flavor profile that is completely dominated by the pungent aspects. It's truly hot, but is a little sour with vinegar providing that flavor component. Another thing is this one has a strong, very pronounced bite unlike the normal slow burn and spread quality of Scotch bonnets. I am sure that is from the seeds that are suspended in this viscous sauce. There are spices that I cannot truly identify that do level out the flavor profile a bit. I am fairly sure that turmeric is in there because of the hint of bitterness. However, this is made to be hot, so do not expect any balance, nor completeness with respect to flavor.

Another key difference between this and the milder sibling is this is less salty. That's interesting because this brand seems to use as little sodium as possible. Since I am on strict restrictions that is a great thing for me. This sauce has less than half the sodium of the milder one (30mg vs. 65).

This sauce has a definite place in my kitchen. Indeed, both styles from this brand do. I love the heat from this when I am in the mood for something hot and biting, and the flavor from the other when I want food to be the center of my focus. Do note that this sauce must be refrigerated after you open it.

title: True flavor of Costa Rica - shoube be named 'Tico sauce'
text:
This sauce has one of the most complete and balanced flavor profiles of any I have tried from among a large number of regions and cuisines. In Costa Rica this is used as both a condiment and a cooking ingredient. I use it mainly as a condiment. More about that below.

The flavor profile is dominated by sweet and tangy, and has a definite piquant quality from the chiles. I would characterize the heat as mild, but that is subjective. It's certainly no hotter than Tabasco sauce and probably less hot to most folks' palates. The sweet is from sugar and molasses, and tangy from both mustard and vinegar.

The remaining components of the flavor profile are savory from the vegetables used, including the expected onions, but the unexpected cucumbers and cauliflower, and a interesting addition of carrots. There is a hint of bitterness, probably from the turmeric, and an interesting blend of other spices that includes cumin for a taste of the exotic and black pepper. Surprisingly there is no garlic (or any that I can taste, anyway). Then there is the saltiness. No surprise there since there are close to 20mg of sodium per gram of sauce. That is pretty high and should be noted if you have sodium restrictions. However, there are only 10 calories per thirty grams, so the sauce is relatively healthy in all other respects. One final nutrition note: this sauce may contain traces of soy and/or milk products.

I use this on broiled and grilled vegetables, especially eggplant and zucchini. It's great on eggs and is a key ingredient in Costa Rica's national dish, gallo pinto, which is black beans, rice and some vegetables served mixed. It's also excellent on fish, especially salmon, but also even the more delicate white types like flounder.

If you love sauces with a touch of the exotic, but will enhance just about any kind of cuisine give this one a try.

title: A true indulgence
text:
If you love a smoother, more balanced coffee with a taste of chocolate and a subtle hint of nuts this is worth trying.

Connoisseurs will probably opt for the beans over this ground coffee, but I assure you that it is fresh and so aromatic that you will think it's freshly ground. The grind itself is perfect for a Costa Rican coffee maker called a chorreador, but also works as perfectly in my [[ASIN:B000CNY6UK Bialetti 6800 Moka Express 6-Cup Stovetop Espresso Maker]]. The basic characteristics are deep and rich, with a touch of chocolate in the flavor that really comes through in the aftertaste. The acidity is unobtrusive, which enhances the smoothness and body. There is a slightly earthy quality as well, but it is low in the flavor. In fact, I would have to rate this as moderately complex because as I sit here writing about it (and enjoying a cup as I do so) there are nuances that I am just now paying attention to.

Although the price stretches my fixed income budget I indulge myself with this a few times a year. There is something about the way the aroma fills my house when this is brewing, and the rich, smooth flavor that this coffee has that makes it worth every penny to me.

title: In a word: exquisito
text:
A friend brought me back a bag of this from her visit to Costa Rica. From the second I opened the bag the amazing aroma overwhelmed me. It was when I brewed it that I was hooked.

The grind is fine and perfect for a moka pot like my [[ASIN:B000CNY6UK Bialetti 6800 Moka Express 6-Cup Stovetop Espresso Maker]]. Brewed in such a pot - correctly - guarantees a great cup of coffee. This one is strong, but with the characteristic richness and smoothness of a Cuban or other Latin style. It's significantly different from the slightly bitter European blends. In those coffees the slight bitter taste is prized and I, too, enjoy it. But I am particularly fond of the Cuban coffees because of their richness and this Costa Rican coffee is every bit the equal of the best Cuban grinds to my palate.

I mentioned that the grind is perfect for the moka-style pots. I suspect the key difference is in the beans and also in the roasting process. Of course the sugar content has something to do with it too. This coffee, ground, is a lighter brown - almost with a hint of red clay coloring - and the flavor has that caramel taste that comes from the ten percent sugar that is blended into the grounds.

According to my friend the folks with whom she stayed when visiting Costa Rica claims that this is the best selling brand in that country. It is also characteristic of the unique flavor of Costa Rican coffee. I have no reason to doubt either claim and every reason to continue buying this wonderful brew.

title: Top quality for Turkish, Arabic and Greek coffees
text:
I found this locally. Actually I found the companion product, [[ASIN:B002ABW7GW Cafe Najjar Classic with Cardamom Turkish-style ground coffee]], first and was so impressed that I immediately went back and purchased this one.

This is the real thing, from the fresh, aromatic coffee to the extra fine, powdery grind. It is ground especially for brewing in an ibrik (also called a cezve). I prefer to hand grind my cardamom with a mortar and pestle and do my own blending. To that end this is the perfect coffee for that. I will admit that the brand's pre-blended coffee is almost as good, but there is nothing like fresh ground cardamom in my opinion so I now have the best of both worlds. For the record I have found that [[ASIN:B002SWJQSK Rani Green Cardamom Pods]] are the best I have come across in the US, so if you use that spice in your coffee give that brand a try.

In order to obtain the best results from this coffee it must be brewed in an ibrik. Using one requires a very specific technique: First, use good water. Filtered or bottled. Most tap water will ruin the flavor of the brewed coffee. Second, DO NOT fill the maker more than half way. And when heating do not use any heat source or setting above medium low. As soon as it boils immediately remove it from the heat and let it settle down. Trust me, it can get quickly out of control, so pay close attention. You can do a second boil to increase the strength of the brew.

If properly brewed this coffee will win you over. It has already become my favorite brand and I am not likely to switch. I value both freshness and quality beans in my coffees, and this one has both.

title: Exquisite flavor for canned peppers!
text:
Note: I purchase these locally so my review will address the peppers and sidestep variable factors such as price and shipping costs.

What I love about these jalapenos is they have a flavor that is actually as good or better than when I fire-roast peppers I buy fresh. I always keep a dozen or so cans in my pantry for times when I do not have fresh jalapenos on hand and want a quick omelet or to spice up some beans or make a fresh salsa.

They are hot. Not terribly so, but they have a nice bite and will balance out the piquant part of a flavor profile for most dishes.

An advantage of these over fresh is the piquant quality is consistent. What I mean is I can sound on the peppers in one can being identical in heat to any other can. With fresh peppers it's hit or miss - sometimes they are milder than I want and others much hotter than I expected.

There is a disadvantage to these as well. They are very high in sodium at 150mg per serving (there are about four servings per can). For most uses I simply drain them and quickly rinse to remove most of the sodium without affecting the basic flavor.

These are convenient, relatively inexpensive when compared to other brands, and have a flavor that no other canned peppers I purchase come close to having. Plus, as I mentioned above, they are as good as my home made fire-roasted jalapenos (minus the sodium.)

title: Truly authentic flavor
text:
Although this is pre-made the initial impression is fresh and rich as though it just came from a molcajete. The flavor profile is probably why you get that impression. The japalenos are definitely at the top of the flavor, but the way that the garlic, onions and spices are blended into the tomatoes is what makes it so savory. The vinegar and the acidity from the tomatoes gives it a slightly sour flavor too. This salsa uses fresh tomatoes and a puree, so it's rich and somewhat thick. Not super thick like dips, but not thin and runny either.

The two tablespoon serving size is twice that of other salsas and sauces. The ten calories and two grams of carbs per serving are healthy numbers for folks who are on a diet. The 200mg of sodium, however, is pretty high. To be fair, if I compare that with the normal single tablespoon serving size of most other brands of salsa that number is not horrible. It still bears remembering if you are on a sodium-restricted diet.

A word about heat: that is a relative quality because we are all different. I would say that this sauce is about three times as hot as Tabasco sauce, but in a very different way. It has a stronger initial bite when you first taste it, but the savory components of this salsa's flavor profile will cause you to perceive the flavor differently than the sour, salty Tabasco, so it's difficult to compare.

I use this as both a condiment (usually on scrambled eggs or in some soups), as well as an ingredient when I am cooking pinto beans. Although it is a little thin in viscosity\, I have used this as a dip. The flavor is there, but it's a little too runny in my opinion. When I set this out as a condiment I warm it up first.

If you like a rich sauce with a little bite and heat, especially over eggs or in an omelet, this is a wonderful salsa.

title: My absolute favorite La Victoria sauce
text:
I always keep a few different sauces from La Victoria in my pantry and this is, hand's down, my favorite. For one thing, I love very hot sauces. This may not be able to compete with some of the other hot sauces on the market in that department, but it has a lot of heat and a very pronounced bite that is more like a habanero than a jalapeno.

What makes this my favorite, though, is the flavor. It is not only authentic Mexican, but is a perfect example of Mesoamerican flavors too. The flavor profile is certainly dominated by the pungent quality of the green jalapeno peppers (which are some of the hottest I have ever tasted), but also by the sour and tangy characteristics imparted by the vinegar and tomatillos. In fact, this also contains green tomatoes, which give a slightly bitter flavor that completes the flavor profile. The salt and savory components are definitely in the profile. In fact, at 260mg of sodium this is a sauce that I have to use in moderation because of dietary restrictions. The garlic, onions and bell peppers complete the savory aspect of the flavor profile, making this one of the most balanced hot sauces I have ever enjoyed.

I mentioned a high sodium level. That is assuaged in part by the fact that the serving size for this sauce is two tablespoons - twice the size of other sauces. Still, at 130mg per tablespoon the level is still a red flag if you have to watch your sodium intake. The rest of the nutritional values are excellent: only two grams of carbs and 10 calories.

If you love real heat with a bite and authentic Mexican (and Mesoamerican) flavors this is a sauce you will want to try. I always have a jar on hand to use in both cooking and as a condiment.

title: Rich with a lot of heat
text:
Up front I want to disclose that I purchase this locally and will not address variables like price and shipping costs. This review will focus strictly on the sauce.

This sauce has a wonderful flavor profile: it is piquant, but has a savory side that comes from the tomatoes, onions and the natural flavors of the peppers used (red jalapeno and red California chiles.)

There is a slight tang from the vinegar, but the peppers dominate the overall flavor. In fact, the bite from the peppers keeps this sauce interesting. It's hot, but certainly not the hottest sauce on the market. It is slightly salty, rounding out the flavor profile.

Nutritionally this sauce has respectable numbers: 10 calories per two tablespoon serving (most sauces have a one tablespoon serving size), with 170mg of sodium and 2 grams of carbs. If you halve those numbers that compare very favorably to a typical serving of just about any competing product.

It has a nice consistency and easily spreads over food or mixes into it. I sometimes use this when making guacamole and it adds a definite kick to it. It also works as an add on to sofritos when making beans, soups and stews. Of course it is perfect over eggs and similar dishes.

title: Addicting, but a little high in sodium
text:
Two disclaimers: (1) I purchase this locally, so am not going to make price or shipping an issue, and (2) take my complaints about sodium with a grain of salt if you are not on a restricted diet.

This is nearly identical to its sibling, [[ASIN:B0041KTBQE matouk soca hot sauce]]. They both share a basic flavor profile that is dominated by considerable heat and a wonderful tanginess. The key differences between the two are that this one is a little less sweet and slightly more tangy, and this one has a much higher sodium content that I will address below.

Like many sauces from Trinidad/Tobago this one is thick and can be spread over your food like mayonnaise or used as a rich dipping sauce. It tips in favor of heat versus flavor, but does have flavor as well. It's a simpler kind that is unlike the complex and balanced flavors of its northern cousins from Jamaica and that area of the Caribbean. The onion, celery seed and garlic in this sauce are responsible for the flavor. I am not quite sure what the 'West Indian herbs' listed in the ingredients are, but I can taste thyme.

With respect to heat it's a mellow heat that has almost no bite, but spreads and builds until you have a nice, hot glow.

I mentioned sodium in the title and in my disclaimers. That this sauce contains 115mg of sodium. Not a showstopper for folks who do not have dietary restrictions, but is a red flag for those of us who do. Sodium is almost a third more than the Soca product and close to three times the sodium of most Jamaican sauces. Needless to say, saltiness is prominent in the flavor profile.

Overall, this is a delicious sauce with respectable heat. It's not the hottest sauce on the market - it's not even the hottest sold by this brand - but is full of flavor. If you love the Jamaican sauces and wanted to explore the flavors of the southern Caribbean this is a good place to start.

title: Tangy, rich and full of flavor
text:
Note: I purchase this locally so this review will focus strictly on this sauce and not price, shipping or other factors.

This sauce has a fairly balanced flavor profile and a wonderful, peppery bite that is not particularly hot. It is just piquant enough to mask the sour component of the flavor profile from the vinegar and create a tangy taste. It's the tomato paste that gives this sauce the richness and thick viscosity. The acidity from it also levels out the sour aspect of the vinegar into more of a tangy taste. The savory flavors of the garlic, onions and natural flavors of the chili peppers and spices are why I love this sauce.

I use this on eggs, to flavor Caribbean style beans, and as a substitute for tomato in some sofritos when I am making lentils or stews. This also goes very well on traditional Mexican fare on which you would normally use a taco-style sauce.

The sodium is a tad high at 115mg per tablespoon, but that is not a showstopper unless you are on an ultra strict diet. The five calories per serving is low and the single gram of carbs is nominal.

If you want a hotter sauce this brand has an excellent salsa called [[ASIN:B00B1HE142 La Victoria Red Salsa Jalapea Extra Hot]]. It is much hotter and slightly different with respect to the basic flavor profile, but will go with just about any food that this one does.

title: Almost as good as homemade
text:
Note: I purchase this locally so this review will confine itself to the product and not address price, shipping or other factors not specifically related to the product.

This is a true sofrito with mainly the same ingredients I use when I make it from scratch (and some I would prefer to leave out.)

The flavor is a nice balance among the tomato paste, peppers, garlic and onion, and spices. In fact it's so perfectly balanced that I measure my homemade flavor against this one. However, there are a few things of which you should be aware. Foremost is that it contains MSG (monosodium glutamate). If you get a reaction from that then you may want to avoid this particular product.

Another red flag is that it contains 2565 mg of sodium per twelve ounce jar, which can be a problem for people on a low sodium diet. Finally it contains soy that can cause reactions in some people. These do not necessarily detract from the quality and flavor of this sofrito, but you should be aware of their presence if you or anyone in your family has issues with them.

As I mentioned I often make mine from scratch, but there are times when I need to whip up a dish quickly so I keep a few of these in my pantry for those occasions. It's perfect as a base for stews and soups, for basting fish before broiling or cooking it en papillote style, and even for adding to salsas and bruschetta to impart an ineffable flavor that never fails to please my guests.

title: Straightforward flavor profile and enough heat to keep you interested
text:
Note: I purchase this locally so my review is going to focus strictly on the product and not address variables such as price and shipping.

If you are just now trying the Trinidad/Tobago sauces the first thing you will notice is these are very different from the northern Caribbean sauces with their more complex flavor profiles and the Mesoamerican ones that are more earthy in flavor.

This sauce in particular is one of the hotter Trinidad sauces, so pungent is the dominate component of the flavor profile. The other two prominent components of the flavor profile are sour/tang and salt. The sour/tang comes from both the vinegar and mustard, which are high on the ingredient list, and the saltiness is 140mg of sodium per serving. That level is almost four times the salt in the Jamaican hot sauces and is a red flag if you have sodium restrictions.

What I love are the heat and flavor from the Congo peppers used in this sauce. They are a variant of habanero, so expect a strong bite as well as heat. They are unlike the Scotch bonnets used in Jamaican that have the slow burn and spread of that pepper. This one grabs you.

This is not the hottest sauce on the market, but is one of the hotter sauces that combines heat and flavor. For me personally flavor is as important as heat and that has earned this sauce a permanent place in my pantry.

title: Excellent quality
text:
I measure the quality of a good coconut milk by how quickly it will flash into oil when you boil it. This one passes that test, which indicates that the liquid has not been altered or the oil removed or reduced. This is important if you use this to cook some dishes that require coconut oil with the flavor that the boiling process imparts.

The milk seems to have a good balance of both flavor and viscosity. It is truly as if you had opened a ripe coconut and drained the liquid from it.

I use this for cooking some dishes like ginataan from the Bikol region in the Philippines, but also for flavoring jasmine rice when I am steaming it. In that case I use half coconut milk The results are simply delicious and can be a dessert dish if turned into a rice pudding, or a savory dish when served with someting spicy.

If you are counting calories you do need to know that a mere two ounces of this milk is 90 calories, of which 78 are from fat. Fat per serving is 8.7 grams, all of which is saturated and carbs are 1.9 grams. Sodium, though, is a low 9 grams and it contains 1.9 grams or protein. When you consider that this can contains 6.75 servings the nutrition figures indicate that you should use coconut milk sparingly. I do, but look forward to the times when I can treat myself to it.

Overall this is an excellent brand (I purchase a lot of Goya products), and this coconut milk passes all of the quality tests to which I put it. I do not think you can go wrong with this one.

title: Authentic and surprisingly good for pre-made
text:
I normally hand blend cardamom into a finely ground Turkish coffee I purchase pre-ground. I spotted this in a local international food store and gave it a try.

In a word: impressive. The extra fine, powdery grind is ideal for brewing in an ibrik (also called a cezve), and the aroma was fresh and wonderful. I have no doubt that the beans used were of the highest quality, as was the cardamom. I am somewhat ashamed to admit that this is 'almost' as good as my home blend in which I hand grind my beans and cardamom pods with a mortar and pestle. One reason why this is so good is the quality coffee and cardamom that I mentioned, but also the proportions.

The best coffee can be wrecked if not properly brewed. This find grind demands not only the ibrik I mentioned. They can be purchased in modern configurations like the [[ASIN:B004Z2OSO8 HIC Brands that Cook Stainless Steel Turkish Warmer]] or the more traditional ones like a [[ASIN:B005G74ARQ Turkish Coffee Pot (cezve/ibrik) with wooden handle]].

Regardless of which brewing vessel you choose the technique will also make or break the experience. This coffee requires a very specific technique: First, use good water. Filtered or bottled. Most tap water will ruin the flavor of the brewed coffee. Second, DO NOT fill the maker more than half way. And when heating do not use any heat source or setting above medium low. As soon as it boils immediately remove it from the heat and let it settle down. Trust me, it can get quickly out of control, so pay close attention. You can do a second boil to increase the strength of the brew.

Properly brewed this is a superb coffee blend that comes very close to hand ground and blended coffee and cardamom. It is also authentic.

title: High quality
text:
These pods are of the highest quality, due in no small part to the way they are stored and shipped.

The aroma as these are crushed and ground with a mortar and pestle is the first indication of quality. They have an intense fragrance and the flavor they impart to the coffee and tea I use them in exceeds my expectations.
If you have used pods that were shipped in sealed bags you are in for a pleasant surprise with these. You need less of these pods to produce the same results with most other pods.

One of the key reasons these are a notch higher than other greed cardamom pods I have purchased in the past is they are packed and stored in sealed jars. This keeps the minute amount of oils in the pods from drying, resulting in the fragrance and flavor I raved about above.

Another key reason these are my preferred brand is they seem to release their flavor better when ground with my mortar and pestle. Granted, that will bring out the flavor in any pods, but these seem to be the best.

My main use is to make coffee, a taste I acquired when I was living in the Middle East. For Turkish and Arabic coffee I purchase pre-ground [[ASIN:B003TNIDF4 Mehmet Efendi Turkish Coffee]], grind a pod of this cardamom in with my mortar and pestle, then brew in an ibrik.

I also make chai with this. The method I use is to once again pull out my trusty mortar and pestle and prepare the spices for it using a pod of this cardamom, a piece of a cinnamon stick, a clove and a single black peppercorn.

As far as I am concerned this is the best cardamom available outside of some exotic spice market in India or the Middle East. The quality is the absolute best I have come across and it's worth every penny.

title: When I don't have time to make it from scratch ...
text:
This is the key to making authentic Puertorriqueño dishes and is fairly easy to make from scratch. However, there are days when I am too busy or the local supermarket is out of culantro or the cilantro is looking lame. This is my fall back and I probably go through a jar of this a week. More if I am buying this instead of making it myself.

I love this brand because the flavor is fresh and intense - just like homemade - and even the aroma is delightful as soon as you open the jar.

Do note that this contains MSG, so if that ingredient causes any physical problems you should not purchase this product. It also contains some soy, another ingredient that causes problems with some people. Also, while the calorie count is nominal at about 5 serving, the sodium is 35mg per serving (and there are 16 servings in this jar.) While not unduly high you should be aware of the sodium level if you have dietary restrictions.

My main use is as a base for pinto beans, but it's a perfect base for just about any soup or stew recipe you can think of. You can also use it as a garnish over the top of lentils, meats and entrees. I use it on fish when I am cooking it 'en papillote' style, which has always been a big hit among my guests.

I keep a few jars in my pantry for last minute dishes and it is a base that I use more than a few times a feel. If you love Puertorriqueño, but cannot get the fresh ingredients to make fresh recaito, this one is a great choice.

title: Great flavor, but ...
text:
For folks who want a more flavorful, slightly hotter alternative to Tabasco this is a great sauce. However, this is not especially hot, and as another reviewer pointed out, the ingredients only list cayenne pepper with no mention of habaneros. That is not necessarily a problem, but it is misleading to consumers and I subtracted a star because of it.

The flavor profile is similar to Tabasco: it's sour from the vinegar, salty and only slightly piquant. The carrots do add a savory component that cuts down on the sourness and is why I think this is a perfect alternative to Tabasco - the flavor.

For me the showstopper is the high sodium content: a whopping 190mg per serving. That is over four times the sodium of some of the Jamaican hot sauces I enjoy. Take that level into account if you do have sodium restrictions.

Going back to the comparison to Tabasco, this sauce has the same thin viscosity and even has a cap that is designed to throttle the flow of the sauce from the bottle. Contrast that with some of the habanero sauces from Jamaica, Trinidad/Tobago and Mexico that are thick and rich.

This sauce will probably disappoint folks who love a lot of heat or are expecting the bite and flavor of habaneros. However, if you love Tabasco you may love this one even more.

title: Habanero heat and flavor
text:
Disclaimer: I purchase this sauce locally so I am confining this review to the sauce and not factors such as price and shipping.

At 11,600 Scoville units this sauce has respectable heat. In fact the pungent aspect and the natural taste of habanero peppers dominate the flavor profile. The interesting thing is that although vinegar is second only to the peppers as a major ingredient the flavor profile has a minimum of sourness. Perhaps it's the acidity from the tomatoes that mask it, or the spices which are so skillfully blended that I cannot pick out any individual ones.

Another thing that is interesting is this sauce does not have the strong bite one associates with habaneros. Instead it has a slower spread and burn like Scotch bonnets from the Caribbean. But that is where the similarity to Caribbean sauces ends.

Its earthy brown color seems to match the earthy flavor that surrounds the habanero flavor. The sauce itself has a moderate viscosity that easily pours, but does not run off like the more watery Tabasco-style sauces. Saltiness is yet another dominating component of the flavor profile. If you have sodium restrictions do be aware that this sauce contains 105mg of sodium per serving (about 4 grams).

This is definitely a Mesoamerican recipe that will please you if you love either the flavor of habaneros or the heat from that pepper.

title: Convenient size and wonderful flavor with respectable heat
text:
