I was going through the 10 ounce size bottles every three days, so this larger bottle is a convenience - and less expensive where I purchase mine locally.

This thick, rich sauce is second to Matouk's [[ASIN:B00025DKYG Matouk's Flambeau Sauce]] in heat so it tends toward heat versus flavor. However, it is flavorful too. It's a simpler kind of flavor that is unlike the complex and balanced flavors of its northern cousins from Jamaica and that area of the Caribbean. The vinegar and mustard give this sauce a lot of tang, and there is a little sweetness. For heat it is a mellow-but-intense kind of spiciness that spreads and builds in intensity. It doesn't immediately hit you like the bite of a habanero.

Do be aware that this sauce contains a whopping 115mg of sodium. That is almost a third more than other Trinidad/Tobago hot sauces that I have tried,, and close to three times the sodium of most Jamaican sauces. Needless to say, saltiness is prominent as are the onion, celery seed and garlic, which are the foundation of the savory aspect of the flavor. I am not quite sure what the 'West Indian herbs' listed in the ingredients are, but I can taste thyme.

If you love Caribbean hot sauces, but want a little more heat this is an excellent one. Just take into account the sodium levels.

title: Relatively mild, but delicious
text:
Folks who love truly hot sauces will find this to be too mild for their palates. However, if you want a little heat and a lot of flavor this is going to please.

A note about the peppers in this sauce and their characteristics: bird's eye peppers do not have the harsh bite of habanero peppers. This pepper has a subtle bite, but builds and spreads until you have a warm glow. This is very similar to the peppers used in North African harissa (and the slow spread and burn in that paste is an indication of quality), as well as in the Caribbean Scotch bonnet (a much hotter pepper).

What makes this sauce both interesting and one that I personally love is the flavor. In fact, the flavor profile is relatively two dimension, with two components dominating it: piquant from the peppers and sour from the vinegar, lemon and mustard. The sour is really a sour/tang, and that is why I personally love this sauce. It's almost like a balance of two opposing flavors competing for your palate. And since the peppers do not scorch your taste buds you can enjoy every nuance, including the herbs (oregano is easy to detect) and very faint hint of garlic.

For me this is the perfect hot sauce for fish - it does not overpower the flavor of a quality filet, and the tang and sour perfectly complement the flavor. Interestingly this is also great on broccoli and rapini (broccoli rabe).

One final aspect of this sauce that appeals to me is the sensible sodium level, which is a manageable 70mg per teaspoon serving. Many hot sauces have a third or more higher levels. Also, this sauce is a scant 5 calories per serving.

If you are looking for truly hot sauce, this is not it. It you want a wonderful blend of low key heat and tang, you will probably love this one.

title: Heat with a bite and flavor
text:
This hot sauce is for folks who love heat with good flavor. This one comes in at a respectable 9000 Scoville units, which places it between the milder [[ASIN:B0000GHNTA El Yucateco Red Chile Habanero Sauce]] that is 5790 units, and the brand's authentic Mesoamerican sauce, [[ASIN:B001EOMQ9E El Yucateco XXXtra Hot Kutbil-ik Sauce ]], that is 11600 units.

Each of the brand's sauces has a slightly different flavor profile. This one is unmistakably piquant, but also has a noticeable sour component and a salty one. It does have 100mg of sodium per 5ml serving, so if you have sodium restrictions take that into account.

What I particularly love about this sauce is that it's super thick. In fact, among the other sauces this brand sells, this one seems to have the highest viscosity. It pours slowly and will spread evenly. The heat has a sharp bite that is characterized by the habanero pepper, but it also tends to settle and then slowly build and spread in the same manner as a Scotch bonnet pepper.

While I love the Caribbean sauces for their more complex flavor profiles, there are times when I want a sauce with a real bite and a simpler flavor that goes with more complex dishes like mofongo. In those cases this is the one I invariably reach for. If you have not tried this sauce and you love heat and flavor you will be in for a treat.

title: Relatively mild with an interesting flavor
text:
As far as habanero-based hot sauces do this one is relatively mild at only 5400 Scoville units, but the flavor is interesting and makes this a worthwhile sauce even if you prefer much hotter ones.

The flavor profile itself is fairly simple: piquant (from the peppers) and salty (each four gram serving contains 75mg of sodium, which is less than the other El Yucateco sauces). The savory component and the interesting flavor comes from carrots, which I do not believe I have ever encountered in a hot sauce. In fact, the carrots, along with a light sour component from the acetic acid, give this sauce almost a fusion flavor. It's as though this mainly Mesoamerican sauce has taken on characteristics of the more flavorful Caribbean sauces. In that respect the sauce lives up to its name.

I mentioned that this is relatively mild. That is a subjective term, even when expressed as Scoville units that measure the heat. For one thing, the high water content in this sauce dilutes the potency of the habaneros and takes away the edge of the bite for which that pepper is known. It comes across as smoother like the Scotch bonnet. In that respect the sauce does, in fact, remind you of a Caribbean hot sauce. This is certainly much hotter than a Tabasco-style sauce, and is on par with [[ASIN:B0000GHNTA El Yucateco Red Chile Habanero Sauce]], which is slightly hotter at 5790 Scoville units. However this sauce is definitely mild compared to [[ASIN:B000ITT9D2 El Yucateco XXXtra Hot Sauce]], which is almost twice as hot at 11600 Scoville units. This sauce, though, has significantly more flavor (to my palate).

Overall, this is an interesting fusion of Mesoamerican and Caribbean hot sauces. If you love heat you probably will not like this one, but if you value flavor it's definitely worth trying.

title: Hot and sassy
text:
This is not Matouk's hottest sauce ([[ASIN:B00025DKYG Matouk's Flambeau Sauce]] has that honor), but it comes close. Where this one excels is the masterful blend of both heat and flavor.

Scotch bonnet peppers dominate the flavor profile with a piquant quality that is hot-but-mellow. That sounds like a contradiction, but means that is the hot build-and-spread glow that does not have a harsh bite like the habanero-based sauces.

The second dominating part of the flavor profile is sour. The vinegar and mustard impart that along with a pronounced tang that perfectly balances the piquancy. That is what separates the Trinidad sauces from the Jamaican ones. On the other hand, this lacks the complex nuances of a Jamaican sauce and is less sweet. You can also taste the onion, garlic and what I think if thyme in the underlying flavor. The sauce itself is thick and viscous, and the balance of flavor and heat makes this one of my favorites.

Like most hot sauces from Trinidad and Tobago this one is a little saltier than the ones from the northern Caribbean. Sodium is 90mg, which is twice that of most Jamaican sauces, but average for ones from Trinidad.

If you love heat and flavor, this is a wonderful sauce. It is one of my favorites and the one that showed me that not all Caribbean hot sauces are the same. This one from the southern end of the Caribbean is vastly different from its northern cousins - especially the more familiar Jamaican sauces. Not better necessarily, but different.

title: Low in heat and high in flavor
text:
This is about half as piquant as the other Matouk sauces, but has an interesting flavor that is dominated by tang. The papaya adds an interesting savory dimension to the flavor profile, while the vinegar and mustard are responsible for its tartness - an interesting contrast to the piquant elements of the flavor profile.

It is spicy, but in a more subdued way that is probably a result of the aging the bottle claims for the peppers. I love the characteristic Scotch bonnet slow build and spread type of burn with almost no bite, which separates the Trinidad/Tobago sauces from the Jamaican ones. Also, this is not as sweet as the Jamaican sauces.

Another reason why I love this sauce is because at only 40mg per serving it's low in sodium. This is half the sodium of many other hot sauces, so if you have sodium restrictions this is definitely a more guilt-free sauce. Do note that unlike most other hot sauces this one needs to be refrigerated after opening. It's a small price to pay for the flavor this sauce packs.

title: Nice heat and and delicious, tangy flavor
text:
This sauce is thick and has the kind of heat that spreads and builds in intensity. It doesn't immediately hit you like the bite of a habanero - it sneaks up on you. In that respect it is a mellow-but-intense kind of spiciness. The vinegar and mustard give this sauce a lot of tang, and there is a little sweetness (not as much as the Jamaican sauces, but it's there.)

It tips in favor of heat versus flavor, but does have flavor as well. It's a simpler kind that is unlike the complex and balanced flavors of its northern cousins from Jamaica and that area of the Caribbean.

Do be aware that this sauce contains a whopping 115mg of sodium. That is almost a third more than other Trinidad/Tobago hot sauces that I have tried,, and close to three times the sodium of most Jamaican sauces. Needless to say, saltiness is prominent as are the onion, celery seed and garlic, which are the foundation of the savory aspect of the flavor. I am not quite sure what the 'West Indian herbs' listed in the ingredients are, but I can taste thyme.

If you love Caribbean hot sauces, but want a little more heat this is an excellent one. Just take into account the sodium levels. If the sodium is an issue you may want to try [[ASIN:B000T4B6YQ Matouk's Soca Hot Sauce]], which is almost identical in flavor except it is a little sweeter and has just a touch less tang. It also has a third less sodium than this sauce.

title: High level of heat and wonderful flavor
text:
This is one of Matouk's hotter sauces with the heat spreading and building until there is a wonderful, endorphin-releasing glow. If you are more used to habaneros than Scotch bonnets this slow build will take you by surprise because there is no immediate bite like you experience with the habanero peppers.

What characterizes this sauce is it's thick and viscous like most Trinidad/Tobago sauces, but it has a fairly simple flavor profile: a lot of heat from the Scotch bonnet peppers and a lot of tang from the vinegar and mustard. There is a touch of sweet from the cane sugar, but nothing like the Jamaican hot sauces. It also has an easily detected saltiness that the other sauces from Trinidad and Tobago do not. The saltiness is due to the relatively high sodium content. At 90mg per five gram serving it's over double that of other Matouk sauces. Not terrible, but something to note if you do have restrictions in your diet.

I said that this sauce has a wonderful flavor: the onion, celery seed and garlic in this sauce combine to impart a savory taste. I am not quite sure what the 'West Indian herbs' listed in the ingredients are, but I can taste thyme.

If you like your sauces hot and flavorful this is a great one to try. If you want a sauce with the same basic flavor profile, but a little less sweet and with a little more tang also give [[ASIN:B0002DD7V4 Matouk's Calypso Hot Sauce]] a try - it's nearly identical to this sauce, but with those characteristics. I have a hard time deciding which of the two I love the most.

title: Domestic tomatoes with high sodium content
text:
Frankly there is nothing wrong with non D.O.P. tomatoes (San Marzano tomatoes that do not have the Denominazione d' Origine Protetta guarantee of coming from a specific region and grown in accordance with Italian law for that particular product). In fact I use a domestic brand ([[ASIN:B000R8YIH6 Carmelina 'e San Marzano Organic Italian Chopped Tomatoes in Puree]]) that to my palate is as good as the imported ones with the D.O.P. designation.

What I do not like about these tomatoes is they have well over ten times the sodium of the brand I mentioned. It's an even higher ratio for the D.O.P. brands I have used. For example, the 410mg of sodium per half cup serving compares poorly against the 25mg in the Carmelina or the 10mg in a D.O.P. brand I will mention below.

Also note that many Italian and some domestic brands are simple: tomatoes and tomato juices in which the sodium is a natural part of the tomato. This brand is a little less natural: in addition to the tomatoes it contains salt, calcium chloride and citric acid. None of the ingredients are harmful, but they do alter the natural flavor of the tomatoes. I have literally tried these side-by-side with the Carmelina brand and the differences are marked.

I will concede that these are sweet and the contents are thick and dense. Frankly I think this brand falls a little short on taste and texture when compared to true San Marzano tomatoes, and the same goes for some of the San Marzano style tomatoes like the ones I use.

Compared to popular domestic brands of crushed tomatoes like Progresso, Hunts and other tier one brands this is a cut above. No question about the quality of these tomatoes outside of the San Marzano niche. However, as long as you realize that this is not the real thing and not even the best of the domestically grown San Marzano variety of tomato, then it comes down to flavor and price. If you can get these at Whole Foods the value is reasonable. If you are ordering these and paying a shipping premium I suggest that you consider either one of the real D.O.P. brands like [[ASIN:B007NJZF9C Strianese Italian DOP San Marzano Tomatoes]] or my preferred domestic brand I cited above.

title: Superb in many ways
text:
The quality of this is easily determined as soon as you open the bag: it's highly aromatic with a fragrance that is both powerful and pleasant. A quick taste indicates the bitter, nutty flavor of perfectly roasted cumin. Even the grind is superb because it's powdery and will easily coat any food.

What I love is the bags are perfectly sized for those of us who use a lot of ground cumin. Larger bags will go stale too quickly. I have found that even in the tightly sealed jars in which I transfer this after opening the bag it looses the aroma and potency in about a month. At the rate I use this, one bag will last about two weeks. Sometimes less.

I mentioned storing this in a sealed jar after opening - also store it in a dark place. I do this for all of my spices and it extends their useful life considerably. This is especially important for cumin, and this one in particular because it has such wonderful nutty nuances that will quickly disappear if improperly stored.

I use this in the same way I do cumin in general, but also for some interesting vegetable recipes I found. One is to coat cauliflower with this and roast in an over. Another is for a dish called aloo gerra that uses this, turmeric, a touch of lemon and fresh cilantro as the savory components of a diced potato dish. It was do delicious that I used this geera in my aloo palak (curried potatoes and spinach) recipe in lieu of the ground cumin I normally use and it was greatly enhanced. That is one more indication that this is not just any roasted ground cumin.

If you are new to cooking with this spice know that you cannot just sprinkle it unless you are using it as a condiment. For cooking you should bring a little oil up to medium head and then add this. Stir for about two minutes and it will release even more flavor and aroma. Then use it in your recipe.

Bottom line: this is very high quality and you can easily tell the difference between this and the ground cumin you normally find in the spice section of a grocery store.

title: A good way to try most of the Matuok sauces
text:
This set makes an excellent gift. It is also a good way to try most of the Matouk sauces to discover which if the best for your palate. The only sauce that is missing from this set is the [[ASIN:B0041KTBQE matouk soca hot sauce]]. However, that one is very close in flavor and heat to one that's included in this pack so it's not a glaring omission.

Here is what you get in order of the hottest to the mildest:

[[ASIN:B00025DKYG Matouk's Flambeau Sauce]]: this is a fairly one dimensional sauce that is characterized by heat and tang. It is flavorful, but its main claim to fame is heat. If you love ultra hot sauces that have a taste of the southern Caribbean you will probably love this one. It's a favorite in my house.

[[ASIN:B0002DD7V4 Matouk's Calypso Hot Sauce]]: this hot sauce has the same pungent and tang dominated flavor profile as the Soca hot sauce that I mentioned is not included, but with a little more sour and tang than that one. In fact, the only main difference between the two is this one has a little less of the sweet component and slightly more tang.

[[ASIN:B0002DD6JC Matouks, Salsa Picante Hot Pepper Sauce]]: love the hot-but-mellow quality of the Scotch bonnet peppers. That sounds like a contradiction, but what I mean is there is no real bite. Just a wonderful build of heat until you are blissed out from the release of endorphins. Another thing that I love about this is it has a lot of tang from the vinegar and mustard. That aspect of the flavor profile is what separates the Trinidad sauces from the Jamaican ones. On the other hand, this lacks the complex nuances of a Jamaican sauce and is less sweet.

[[ASIN:B0002E4EQ0 Matouk's West Indian Hot Sauce]]: the mildest of the lot and half the heat of the last two I listed. Unlike other Caribbean sauces the ones from Trinidad where this is made have a slightly different flavor profile. The ones from Trinidad/Tobago tend to be less sweet, but retain the sour and tart components of the flavor profile. This one has a touch of tropical fruit from the papaya, and a definite sour counterbalance from the vinegar. It does not taste 'vinegary' - tart is a better description. The mustard combines with the vinegar to give this sauce a lot of tang. One final difference between this and other Caribbean sauces - especially Jamaican - is this is much lighter on onions.

I have only provided a brief sketch of the flavor characteristics - please see the other reviews for each product to which I have linked above. The bottom line is this is a great way to try these sauces if you cannot get them locally.

title: Nice heat and superb flavor
text:
This may not be the hottest sauce on the market, but it does have respectable heat. It's also packed with flavor and has a tang that lets you know it's from Trinidad/Tobago.

I love the hot-but-mellow quality of the Scotch bonnet peppers. That sounds like a contradiction, but what I mean is there is no real bite. Just a wonderful build of heat until you are blissed out from the release of endorphins. Another thing that I love about this is it has a lot of tang from the vinegar and mustard. That aspect of the flavor profile is what separates the Trinidad sauces from the Jamaican ones. On the other hand, this lacks the complex nuances of a Jamaican sauce and is less sweet.

Like most hot sauces from Trinidad and Tobago this one is a little saltier than the ones from the northern Caribbean. Sodium is 90mg, which is twice that of most Jamaican sauces, but average for ones from Trinidad.

You can taste the onion, garlic and what I think if thyme in the underlying flavor. The sauce itself is thick and viscous, and the balance of flavor and heat makes this one of my favorites.

title: Very hot with a simple flavor profile
text:
First, if you love heat this sauce has it. It's made with Congo peppers, which are a variant of habanero, so it has both heat and a strong bite. This is definitely a departure from other Caribbean sauces from the north - especially Jamaican - which have the slow burn and spread Scotch bonnets.

Aside from the heat - the pungent quality - the flavor profile is also heavy on sour and tang. This is in part from the vinegar and in part form the mustard. It's saltier than other Caribbean sauces, so that is also prominent in the flavor profile. In fact, at 140mg of sodium per serving it raises a red flag for those of us who have to watch out intake. Put another way, it has almost four times the sodium of most Jamaican sauces and twice the sodium of many other sauces from the Trinidad/Tobago sauces.

The spices blended into this sauce are difficult to detect because the other components of the flavor profile mask them. For lack of a better word I will call their contribution to the overall flavor ineffable because even if you cannot taste what they are I am sure you notice it if they were missing.

Bottom line: this is a fairly one dimensional sauce that is characterized by heat and tang. It is flavorful, but its main claim to fame is heat. If you love ultra hot sauces that have a taste of the southern Caribbean you will probably love this one. It's a favorite in my house.

title: Hot, tangy and mellow - does have high sodium though
text:
This hot sauce has the same pungent and tang dominated flavor profile as [[ASIN:B0041KTBQE matouk soca hot sauce]], but with a little more sour and tang than that one. In fact, the only main difference between the two is this one has a little less of the sweet component and slightly more tang.

Extending the comparison to the Soca sauce I would say that this one is identical in the heat. And, like that one, it's a mellow heat that has almost no bite, but spreads and builds until you have a nice, hot glow. Do be aware that this sauce contains a whopping 115mg of sodium. That is almost a third more than the Soca product and close to three times the sodium of most Jamaican sauces. Needless to say, saltiness is prominent in the flavor profile.

From a savory perspective, the onion, celery seed and garlic in this sauce are responsible for that flavor profile component. I am not quite sure what the 'West Indian herbs' listed in the ingredients are, but I can taste thyme.

Like many sauces from Trinidad/Tobago this one is thick and can be spread over your food like mayonnaise or used as a rich dipping sauce. It tips in favor of heat versus flavor, but does have flavor as well. It's a simpler kind that is unlike the complex and balanced flavors of its northern cousins from Jamaica and that area of the Caribbean.

If you love Caribbean hot sauces, but want a little more heat this is an excellent one. Just take into account the sodium levels.

title: Heat and tang - not as flavorful as other Matouk sauces, but hotter than most
text:
This sauce has a fairly simple flavor profile: a lot of heat from the Scotch bonnet peppers and a lot of tang from the vinegar and mustard. There is a touch of sweet from the cane sugar, but nothing like the Jamaican hot sauces. It also has an easily detected saltiness that the other sauces from Trinidad and Tobago do not.

I was surprised by the pungent characteristics. It is hotter than I expected, but still has the more mellow spreading and building heat than habaneros or their Trinidad cousin the Congo pepper. The onion, celery seed and garlic in this sauce combine to impart a savory taste. I am not quite sure what the 'West Indian herbs' listed in the ingredients are, but I can taste thyme.

There is a mellow quality to the sauce that balances the heat. I am sure that is from aging the Scotch bonnets in vinegar and salt. However, the sodium content is high at 90mg per five gram serving - over double that of [[ASIN:B0002E4EQ0 Matouk's West Indian Hot Sauce]]. Not terrible, but something to note if you do have restrictions in your diet.

The sauce itself is thick and has a relatively high viscosity. It's an orange color, probably due to the coloring agent called FD&C yellow #5. This is the only synthetic ingredient in the sauce and can pose a risk to folks who react to tartrazine. The other ingredients are natural, including modified corn starch and xantham gum used as thickening agents, and potassium sorbate, which is a natural preservative.

This sauce lacks some of the flavor that I have come to love in most sauces from Trinidad and Tobago, but makes up for it in heat. I reach for it when I want a little more kick than I usually enjoy.

title: Relatively mild, but packed with flavor
text:
As hot sauces go this one is relatively mild (especially when compared to its sibling, [[ASIN:B005CMA4OI Matouk's Flambeau Sauce]].) It's the flavor that makes this a favorite.

Unlike other Caribbean sauces the ones from Trinidad where this is made have a slightly different flavor profile. The ones from Trinidad/Tobago tend to be less sweet, but retain the sour and tart components of the flavor profile. This one has a touch of tropical fruit from the papaya, and a definite sour counterbalance from the vinegar. It does not taste 'vinegary' - tart is a better description. The mustard combines with the vinegar to give this sauce a lot of tang. One final difference between this and other Caribbean sauces - especially Jamaican - is this is much lighter on onions.

Heat is there, but more subdued. Perhaps that is a function of the aging the bottle claims for the peppers. It does have the characteristic Scotch bonnet slow build and spread type of burn with almost no bite.

Aside from the intense tropical flavor I love this sauce because at only 40mg per serving it's low in sodium. This is half the sodium of many other hot sauces, so if you have sodium restrictions this is definitely a more guilt-free sauce.

One final note: unlike most other hot sauces I use this one needs to be refrigerated after opening.

title: Incredible flavor
text:
I have been trying Caribbean hot sauces lately and have grown to love their flavor. This one is a little different from the rest. For one thing it's based on habanero peppers instead of the Scotch bonnet peppers common to other Caribbean sauces (and especially those from Jamaica.)

The spices are different as well. Most of the Jamaican sauces have sweet equally prominent with pungent in their flavor profiles. This one has a touch of sweet, but tends more towards savory. Also, while the Scotch bonnets are hot the habaneros in this sauce have a bite that the Jamaican peppers lack. Not a harsh bite, but a sharp one.

It's the flavor, though, that caused me to fall in love with this sauce. Among them are a few surprises because the other Caribbean sauces do not normally contain some such as the green peppers which levels out the habaneros and tames them, and the complementary thyme and basil. celery is another unique ingredient that one rarely finds in a hot sauce, and although some Caribbean sauces contain mustard the extra tang it adds to this one gives it a special flavor too. More importantly the vinegar in this sauce is also tangy. If there is one complaint I have it's the 70mg of sodium per five gram serving. That is nearly twice as much as the level in other hot sauces.

What I especially love, though, is how thick this sauce is. You do need to shake it well before each use because the ingredients settle between uses. It takes a while due to the viscosity of the sauce, but you will not get the fill flavor without a good shake first.

One note: while the bottle claims 'Extra Hot' it really isn't. Or to my palate, and I am not a hot fanatic - I go for flavor first. I would put this a little hotter than [[ASIN:B0000GHNTA El Yucateco Red Chile Habanero Sauce]], which I also enjoy. However, there are much hotter sauces on the market, so if you crave ultra hot you may be disappointed in this one. On the other hand, if you love maximum flavor and some heat you will probably love this.

title: Surprisingly mild and flavorful for a habanero sauce
text:
This sauce took me by surprise. The majority of habanero sauces I've tried are super hot with a piercing 'bite'. This one is much milder with a pleasant bite and an after glow that is more like that of a Scotch bonnet than a habanero. For folks who are focused on the heat this one comes in at 5790 Scoville units. In other words, pretty mild.

What surprised me most is the flavor. Most habanero sauces have an unpleasant taste to my palate that I will mask with garlic, onions and other pungent flavors when I cook with them. There is a hint of that taste in this sauce, but it's blended in with the rich tomato base with its slight acidity, and also masked with the vinegar in this sauce.

Be aware that the sodium content on a serving is 90mg. This is still manageable for folks who have to watch their intake, but is twice as high as Tabasco and most of the Jamaican hot sauces on the market.

I love this because sometimes I crave a sauce with a little more bite than I can get from the Scotch bonnet sauces I normally have on my table. In fact, I always keep a bottle of this around for that and the wonderful flavor it imparts to some dishes like scrambled eggs. If you love hot sauces, but are not ready to jump into the ultra hot ones this is a good level that is hotter than Tabasco and milder than most of the super hot ones.

title: More flavorful alternative to Tabasco and other hot sauces
text:
The most direct comparison I can make is that this one has more heat and flavor than Tabasco or any of the North American sauces I have tried. However, it does have a slightly sour taste from the cane vinegar - a flavor characteristic that it shares with Tabasco and its competitors. It is also much hotter than the Tabasco type sauces.

This one stands out in the flavor and the blend of peppers. Ingredients simply list unspecified spices, but I can detect what may be tamarind because there is a tang that you cannot get with just vinegar. There is also a little sweetness that I am guessing is cane sugar since nearly all Jamaican hot sauces contain it. It is salty with 80mg of sodium per serving, which is double that of Tabasco and also most Jamaican hot sauces.

I started this review by making a comparison to Tabasco, which shares many characteristics with this one. Since describing tastes is difficult I will also do a direct comparison to another Grace product, [[ASIN:B002LEKLJ8 Grace Scotch Bonnet]]. This one is thinner in viscosity, not as rich flavored, but with a more pronounced bite. The bite is probably from the habanero peppers that are blended with the Scotch bonnet ones in this sauce. Once the initial bite subsides the piquant component has the characteristic build and spread glow of the Scotch bonnet peppers.

Overall this is an excellent substitute for the Tabasco style sauces on the market. Indeed this seems to have been designed to sell in that market space since it appeals to folks who want a more exotic alternative to Tabasco, but who are not as fond of the Caribbean styles of hot sauces that are sweeter and hotter.

title: Interesting flavor - a different curry flavor
text:
Curry mixes vary from one cuisine to another. It's easy to tell an Indian style from Malaysian from South African (just to name a few). This Caribbean style has its own flavor profile that tends towards sweetness. Of course that is a characteristic of most Caribbean cuisines and especially Jamaican.

The vinegar counters the sweetness with a tart, slightly acidic component of the flavor profile. Also, this has enough salt to keep it interesting, although the actual sodium content per tablespoon is only 40mg. The turmeric - the essence of any curry - adds a touch of bitterness, rounding out the flavor profile. That is not to say that it's missing the piquant or savory components. The Scotch bonnets give it some heat. Not biting heat, but the slow spread and glow kind. For some reason all Grace products I have tried are milder than their well known competitor (Walkerswood). I am not comparing, but making an observation because it comes down to a matter of personal taste. I love both brands for different reasons.

This sauce is savory. I love the way it can be used for cooking or as a condiment. A dribble over fish will greatly enhance it. It also goes beautifully with pressure cooked greens like turnips, collards, and to my palate dinosaur kale. The sweetness is a perfect complement to the bitter greens.

I'll be perfectly honest: I do not always keep a bottle in my pantry. That said, I find myself buying this at least monthly when the mood strikes me because it is delicious and is definitely different from the other curries I serve.

title: Sweet and Lowdown
text:
With apologies to Woody Allen the best way I can describe this delicious sauce is sweet and lowdown.

Sweetness dominates the flavor profile. It's definitely not syrup sweet, but is thick and viscous and gets that aspect from the cane sugar and raisins in the mix. The lowdown comes from the balance of tart and sour that the cane vinegar and tamarind contribute. Also, although this is not by any means spicy there is a hint of pepper that adds the lightest touch of the piquant.

Salt, too, is evident in the flavor profile. However, the sodium content is still a manageable 50mg per tablespoon serving. The tomatoes add a little acidity, but also flavor that is augmented and enhanced by onion and spices. Combined, this is a rich and thick sauce with a lot of flavor.

I love this with two dishes - one traditional and the other a family recipe. The traditional one is cream cheese and lox. A little dribbled over the cream cheese with capers and chopped red onions is delicious.

My family recipe calls for mixing chopped black olives and pimentos into a soft cream cheese, spread on celery and dribble a little of this sauce on it. It's both delicious and healthy. In fact, a tablespoon of this sauce is only 5 calories and despite the sweetness it only contains a single gram of carbs.

There are many more uses for this sauce that the ones I cited, but regardless of how you use it - as an ingredient or as a condiment - it's delicious.

title: One great sauce and two excellent variations
text:
Disclaimer: I purchase these sauces locally and individually, so this review is going to focus on each product and not address price, shipping or other variable factors.

Each of the two sauces is an interesting variation on the original Pickapeppa sauce. This sampler allows you to conveniently compare and contrast them to the original.

First up is the [[ASIN:B000ZD752S Jamaican Original Pickapeppa Sauce]]. It's sweet, thick and has interesting nuances of spices and a contrasting tang and sourness in the flavor profile. It is not at all spicy, although there is a subtle hint of piquancy. Of the three this one has the highest sodium content, which is still a fairly low 50mg per tablespoon serving.

Second is [[ASIN:B001FPGYJ0 Pickapeppa Gingery Mango Sauce]]. Still sweet and a little spicy, which mainly comes from the ginger. It has some pepper, but like the Original it's just enough to detect in a subtle way. It shares the same thick, rich base with the original, but has a 'tropical' flavor that I cannot fully identify. Probably because more mangos were possible used. The 20mg of sodium is less than half of what the Original sauce contains, which is a big plus for me. Despite the low sodium it still has a salty characteristic that makes it ideal on just about anything.

Third is [[ASIN:B001FPGYLI Pickapeppa Hot Mango Sauce]]. It's close to the same basic formula as the Gingery Mango sauce, but the peppers dominate the piquant component of the flavor profile while the ginger is relegated to a complementary role. The dominant flavor is still sweet with sour and tang closely behind. And despite the name it is still relatively mild. If you can eat Tabasco then this one will seem even milder. It's slightly salty, but it only contains 10mg of sodium per tablespoon, which is more than acceptable for most sodium restricted diets.

Overall this is a great set of sauces, especially if you've only tried the Original and wanted something with the same great flavor, but a little more kick. All three occupy a permanent place in my pantry.

title: Sweet and mid way between the original and hot versions
text:
On the spiciness scale this is mid way between the [[ASIN:B000ZD752S Original Pickapeppa Sauce]] and the [[ASIN:B001FPGYLI Pickapeppa Hot Mango Sauce]].

Like all Pickapeppa sauces this one is sweet and relatively mild when it comes to spiciness. Even the hot mango sauce is not very spicy. However, the spiciness of this one is mainly from the ginger. There is some peppers, but the dominating component of the flavor profile is sweet instead of piquant. More importantly, ginger is a more dominant flavor in the piquant component than the peppers.

The mango gives this sauce a little more complexity than the regular sauce, and there is a touch of tang and sour from the vinegar. The onions and garlic pull the sweetness a little towards pungent, and the raisins certainly contribute to the thick, rich qualities of this sauce. What I love is the very low sodium content. Despite being salty enough to eliminate the need for adding more to your food, a tablespoon only contains 20mg of sodium (about half the amount of other sauces.) Also, even though this contains cane sugar, there are only two grams or carbs and 20 calories per serving. It's one of the few sauces I enjoy that is guilt free.

If you want a little spiciness but only a very little - but a lot of flavor that follows the original sauce's recipe - this is a great one to try. Like the other Pickapeppa sauces it is relatively low in sodium, calories and carbs. I know that my cardiologist appreciates that.

title: Delightful condiment
text:
This is a constant condiment in my house. I love the seemingly simple first taste that turns into a complex array of flavors. It's basically sweet and very thick.

The best way to describe it is to break down the flavor profile. The dominate taste is sweet that comes from cane sugar and raisins. There is also a distinct sour and tart component that is from the vinegar and tamarind. Those two alone are an interesting contrast, but when the pepper is added it has a touch of the piquant as well. Not truly spicy, but just a hint to make it interesting. It is a little salty, but the sodium content is still a manageable 50mg per teaspoon serving. The tomatoes add a little acidity, but also flavor that is augmented and enhanced by onion and spices. Combined, this is a rich and thick sauce with a lot of flavor.

Of the multitude of uses I have two main dishes I always use this on. The first is cream cheese and lox. A little dribbled over the cream cheese with capers and chopped red onions is delicious. My other favorite is to mix chopped black olives and pimentos into a soft cream cheese, spread on celery and dribble a little of this sauce on it. It's both delicious and healthy. In fact, a teaspoon of this sauce is only 5 calories and despite the sweetness it only contains a single gram of carbs.

To my palate this is a wonderful touch of the Caribbean and a nice counterbalance to some of the spicier meals I typically eat.

title: For those who love the traditional version but want heat
text:
Disclaimer: I purchase this locally, so my review is going to strictly focus on the product and not the price or shipping.

This is a variation on the traditional Pickapeppa sauce, which has a flavor profile on the sweet side of the spectrum, and a close cousin to the [[ASIN:B001NADFD0 Pickapeppa Spicy Mango Sauce]]. That sauce depended more on ginger for it's piquant component while this one is heavier on the peppers. Not terribly hot, but it still has a kick. Also, it does not have a bite, but more of a spreading heat.

Like the spicy sauce the mango gives this one a little more complexity, and there is a touch of tang and sour from the vinegar. The onions and garlic pull the sweetness a little towards pungent, and the raisins certainly contribute to the thick, rich qualities of this sauce.

Although the spicy version has excellent nutritional values, this one is even better! It's still salty like the spicy version, but it only contains 10mg of sodium per tablespoon (half that of the spicy version), along with only 10 calories and a single gram of carbs.

This one has flavor and heat. I will forewarn you that if you are expecting blazing hot you will be disappointed. However, if you want an interesting flavor combination with some heat - and especially if you are already a fan of Pickapeppa sauce - you will probably love this.

title: A wonderful variation on the traditional Pickapeppa sauce
text:
Note: I purchase this locally, so my review is going to strictly focus on the product and not the price or shipping.

This has the same, thick viscosity as the regular [[ASIN:B0001CVIE4 Pickapeppa Sauce]], but with a much different flavor profile.

First, the product name on this page is 'spicy', but the real name is 'Gingery Mango Sauce' and the spiciness is mainly from the ginger. Like the traditional one this one tends towards sweet, but the piquant component is from the ginger and pepper.

The mango gives this sauce a little more complexity than the regular sauce, and there is a touch of tang and sour from the vinegar. The onions and garlic pull the sweetness a little towards pungent, and the raisins certainly contribute to the thick, rich qualities of this sauce.

What I love is the very low sodium content. Despite being salty enough to eliminate the need for adding more to your food, a tablespoon only contains 20mg of sodium (about half the amount of other sauces.) Also, even though this contains cane sugar, there are only two grams or carbs and 20 calories per serving. It's one of the few sauces I enjoy that is guilt free.

If you love the original give this one a try - it's not going to replace the original recipe in my condiment cabinet, but it is a sauce I will continue to buy and enjoy.

title: Interesting variant of curry
text:
I've tried curry from India, Malaysia, Thailand and South Africa and each is different. The same can be said for this one. While it has the characteristic turmeric as one of the main ingredients, the blend of the other spices gives this a distinct personality.

The flavor profile is dominated by a slightly bitter aspect from the turmeric, but that also adds to an overall pungent flavor from the way that the turmeric enhances the cayenne pepper and the other spices - especially the anise, coriander and fenugreek. It's the blend's proportions that make it unique. The allspice and cane sugar give it a sweetness that is typical of Jamaican (and general Caribbean) cuisine. There is a slight saltiness in the flavor profile as well, but the sodium content is fairly low at 30mg per tablespoon. The earthy flavor of cumin is also easy to detect.

Note that this is not especially spicy. The sole source of the piquant component of the flavor profile is the cayenne pepper. That has a bite that the Scotch bonnet peppers common to most Jamaican fare lacks, but it is also a lot less spicy. Also, like any curry hot oil pops the flavors and intensifies them, so take that into consideration when cooking with this.

Thus far I have used this to make fish curry and to also make an interesting lentil soup. It also worked well in a modified version of aloo palak (an Indian dish of curried potatoes and spinach). Not the same as any Indian recipe, but still flavorful.

I am still experimenting, but have made up my mind that this is a spice blend that I want to keep handy. This is definitely worth a try if you enjoy curries, but want something a little different.

title: Balsamic style vinegar that mixes with oil!
text:
This is an interesting product that is made from grape must - the same base for grappa - and balsamic vinegar. It has a subdued flavor of balsamic vinegar and the added benefit of mixing well with oil.

For personal use this is wonderful as a flavor enhancer for fresh strawberries. For friends, especially those who love mixing balsamic vinegar, olive oil and spices as a bread dip, I use this instead. One reason is that it actually mixes with the olive oil, giving a more uniform dipping sauce. Of course, another reason is that it has the expected flavor that is unique to balsamic style vinegars.

I use a little of this (along with lemon juice) as a marinate before cooking the fish. This reduces the 'fishy flavor' that some of my friends dislike. However, it also enhances some types of fish, especially salmon. It's also ideal with vegetables such as zucchini, peppers, eggplant and similar to be grilled over a charcoal fire. I usually mix a little of this with some olive oil, which as I stated above, it blends with perfectly, and a little crushed garlic. Baste, grill and enjoy. Conversely, you can grill the vegetables plain and use the mixture as a dipping sauce, or just a few drops of this balsamic glaze as a condiment.

Bottom line: this has advantages over regular vinegar when you been to blend with olive oil, and it is thick and viscous, so it makes a perfect basting sauce too.

title: Delicious blend and good source of protein
text:
I love this particular mix because I'm fond of almonds and cashews. The blend of nuts - as others have mentioned - seems skewed towards almonds, with cashews coming in second and macadamia nuts a distant third. For me this is perfect. It all depends on your tastes and preferences.

What I love most, though, is the relatively low sodium content that is 50mg per serving. According to the can a serving is approximately 21 pieces, which comes to a hand full for me.

If you are allergic to peanuts do be aware that while this mix does not contain any it does use peanut oil (along with cottonseed oil) as part of the roasting process. Also, if you are carefully controlling fat intake, 130 of the 170 calories per serving is from fat. While each serving contains 15 grams of fat, only two of those grams are saturated fats. Carbs come in at 7 grams.

Nutritionally, a serving provides a fairly high amount of copper, magnesium, manganese, phosphorous and iron, and is high in vitamin E. I use this as a protein boost since I am mainly a vegetarian who also eats fish a few times a week.

Like most nuts these are a healthy addition to a diet when eaten in moderation. I typically enjoy a single serving per day as a supplement to my overall diet plan. Of all of the mixes I have tried this is the tastiest (to my palate) and one of the healthiest.

title: Hot, tropical and delicious
text:
The flavor profile captures the flavor of authentic Jamaican jerk. The piquant element is strictly from the Scotch bonnet peppers, which are both hot and flavorful. There is a touch of sweet from the cane sugar that is complemented by some of the aromatic spices (allspice and nutmeg.) In fact, the flavor profile is very complete because there is a touch of bitterness from the nutmeg, and sour from the citric acid. Salt is also prominent in the profile, with 540mg per two teaspoon serving. The final savory components come from the spring onion, black pepper and thyme.

This is definitely spicy. If you have an aversion to hot food you may want to try the [[ASIN:B004GIKSJ0 Walkerswood Jamaican Mild Jerk Seasoning]] instead. It has the same basic flavor profile, but with a diminished piquant element.

However this is for much more than jerk barbeque though. Walkerswood provided a tip that I followed - mix a little of this into mayonnaise - that makes a perfect condiment. In fact it complements aioli (a French twist on mayonnaise).

Bottom line: This is probably the best blend for making authentic jerk and can be used to 'spice' up other dishes and condiments in ways only limited by your imagination.

title: Delicious taste of the Caribbean
text:
I've been focusing on Caribbean cuisine and specifically Jamaican fare lately and this is a perfect sauce for my kitchen. I use it as both a cooking sauce and as a condiment (I am still experimenting.

What I love is how this perfectly complements my meal planning philosophy. I love contrasts and this allows me to contrast a spicy dish with one that is savory, but with a full flavor profile. This one has the acidity and rich flavor from the tomatoes, and a tangy sour flavor from the vinegar, tamarind and citric acid. Those combine beautifully with the sweet nuances from the cane sugar and fruits that add a complexity of their own. There is a little piquant from Scotch bonnet peppers and an array of flavors from the spices. Even the nutmeg adds a touch of bitter.

A few things that make this wonderful to my palate are the way the mango adds a blast of tropical fruit while the raisins make this sauce rich. You can taste the banana, but the dominant flavor is mango. There is also a defined saltiness, which completes the flavor profile.

For all of the sweet ingredients and saltiness this is surprisingly low in calories, carbs and sodium. A teaspoon contains only 5 calories, a gram of carbs and 40mg of sodium.

If you are looking for spicy this is not for you. It has a touch, but not enough to register as anything other than a interesting component of the flavor profile.

You can use this on meat, but I do not indulge. It does, however, go perfectly with both white and dark flesh fish, and is wonderful as a 'secret ingredient' in soups, sauces and stews.

title: Same flavor profiles at two ends of the heat spectrum
text:
I love the hot mix, but have to accommodate friends and guests, so this pack is an ideal way to do that.

You get one jar each of the [[ASIN:B004GIKSJ0 Mild Jerk Seasoning]] and the much spicier [[ASIN:B0000DG586 Traditional Jamaican Jerk Seasoning]]. Both share basically the same flavor profile, but the piquant component is greatly diminished in the mild blend.

Basically its piquant element is strictly from the Scotch bonnet peppers, which are both hot and flavorful. These are at the top of the flavor profile for the traditional blend, and at the very bottom for the mild mix.

There is a touch of sweet from the cane sugar that is complemented by some of the aromatic spices (allspice and nutmeg.) In fact, the flavor profile is very complete because there is a touch of bitterness from the nutmeg, and sour from the citric acid. Salt is also prominent in the profile, with 540mg per two teaspoon serving. The final savory components come from the spring onion, black pepper and thyme.

Either is for much more than jerk barbeque though. Walkerswood provided a tip that I followed - mix a little of this into mayonnaise - that makes a perfect condiment. In fact it complements aioli (a French twist on mayonnaise). However, I digress. This is probably the best rub for making authentic jerk and can be used to 'spice' up other dishes and condiments in ways only limited by your imagination.

Bottom line: if you want to explore the tastes and flavors of Jamaica and the wider Caribbean this is a wonderful way to do that. It's authentic and delicious. If you love to barbeque, then you may find yourself stocking up because it's that good.

title: Perfect for those who love jerk but cannot tolerate too much heat
text:
From a flavor perspective this is near identical to the spicy version, [[ASIN:B0000DG586 Walkerswood Traditional Jamaican Jerk Seasoning]], but toned down for folks who cannot tolerate overly spicy food.

The ingredients are identical in both versions, but in this one the proportions are altered to diminish the piquant component of the flavor profile. It does that while retaining the other ones: a touch of sweet from the cane sugar that is complemented by some of the aromatic spices (allspice and nutmeg.) In fact, the flavor profile is very complete because there is a touch of bitterness from the nutmeg, and sour from the citric acid. Salt is also prominent in the profile, with 540mg per two teaspoon serving. The final savory components come from the spring onion, black pepper and thyme.

To be sure, there is a touch of spiciness in this, but only enough to impart a genuine taste of Jamaica. Also, like its hotter sibling this seasoning is for much more than jerk barbeque. For example, mix a little of this into mayonnaise. It will make a perfect (and exotic) condiment. In fact it complements aioli (a French twist on mayonnaise).

I use this on salmon. For me and other guests who like their food spicy I use the hot and spicy version, and this one for guests who want to enjoy the same flavor without the burn. I hand coat the fish with a thin layer of olive oil, then rub in this seasoning. I let it sit overnight and - viola! - the flavors have married deeply with the fish and come out beautifully when grilled or broiled. Don't get me wrong - I am sure it's wonderful on meat, but I do not indulge in that.

Bottom line: if you want to explore the tastes and flavors of Jamaica and the wider Caribbean this is a wonderful way to do that. It's authentic and delicious. If you love to barbeque, then you may find yourself stocking up because it's that good.

title: A little on the mild side
text:
The heat is there, but this sauce lacks the fire of some of the other Jamaican sauces I have been recently sampling. If you can easily tolerate Tabasco sauce then this will provide a Caribbean flavor without overwhelming your palate.

The flavor profile is somewhat two dimensional, tending towards both sweet and piquant as the dominating flavors. There is a touch of saltiness and the faintest hint of sour.

I love this on more delicate white fish like flounder because it does not mask the flavors of those types of fish. This goes wonderfully on eggs, and is a flavorful base for beans. It works very well in soups and stews, and, of course, as an all-purpose condiment.

One more thing I love is this is friendly for those of us whose diets restrict sodium. At only 40mg per teaspoon serving you can indulge without worry. The same serving is also a scant 5 calories.

Although I prefer a lot more heat I still enjoy this sauce because of the flavor. I also keep it around for guests who may not enjoy super-spicy, but want a little kick to snacks and meals.

title: Deliciously hot
text:
This takes the [[ASIN:B000MGSRBG Walkerswood Hot Jamaican Scotch Bonnet Pepper Sauce]] to the next level. It shares the same wonderful flavors, but is significantly more spicy.

In this sauce the Scotch bonnets do dominate the flavor profile, which is counterbalanced by a little sour tang from the cane vinegar and citric acid, and sweetness from the cane sugar. The savory components of the flavor come from the onions, garlic and thyme. All of the flavors combine into a sauce that is hot and tasty. Even though the Scotch bonnets dominate this mix, they do not reach out and grab you by the throat the way some hot sauces do. This has an immediate bite, but it's more of a tang, and it spreads into a warm glow.

I use this on eggs, in beans, on some vegetables, and on some fish dishes. It does not work well to my palate on delicate white fish like flounder because it overpowers the flavor.

If you are in a never ending quest for hotter and hotter sauces you may not like this one as much as I do. However, if you value flavor equally with heat then you will probably find this to be perfection.

title: Jamaica in a bottle
text:
This brand is my favorite and this sauce in particular is a true winner. Among the reasons I love this sauce is the flavor profile is a near perfect balance. Sweet and heat dominate, which takes care of sweet and piquant components. However, there is a hint of sour and a lot of salty. The savory aspects come from the spices, and the touch of bitter in particular is from the nutmeg that is included. In fact, a look at the ingredients evokes West African and even Middle Eastern influences.

I especially love the lower sodium content in this sauce. At 230mg per tablespoon it is low compared to other sauces I enjoy, although it's still nothing to brag about to my cardiologist. I use this in moderation, so it is not a problem for me despite sodium restrictions in my diet.

While this is packed with flavor, it has some heat to it. It's certainly much more piquant than Tabasco sauce, but in a different way. First, it does not have the pronounced bite. It's more of a heat that builds and spreads, almost as though its releasing a constant stream of endorphins. And the spices and sweetness truly counter the Scotch bonnet peppers.

You can use this on practically anything. I use it on eggs, fish, some vegetable dishes and as a part of a base when cooking beans. It's a perfect hot sauce for those of us who value flavor as much as we do the heat.

title: One of my favorite brands
text:
I can purchase this locally from a number of sources, including the dominant supermarket chain in Central Florida. Therefore my review will focus on this fish sauce and not address price or shipping.

Not all fish sauces are created equal. I spent a lot of my life in Asia and was first introduced to this in the Philippines where it's called patis. This is identical to a high quality patis in all respects. Do be aware that this, like patis or other Thai brands, is extremely high in sodium. A single gram of this sauce contains 890mg. That means that a teaspoon contains a whopping 4450mg, so use it very sparingly if you have sodium restrictions.

My main use is to chop fresh bird's eye peppers and make a combination dipping sauce and condiment that is called phrik nam pla in Thai. It's also delicious by itself on on grilled eggplant and zucchini, and especially pork (which I have not eaten in decades but did enjoy with this sauce when I did consume it.) Actually, this is perfect on mixed grilled or fried vegetables and will enhance many dishes if used in lieu of salt or soy sauce.

Bottom line: this is a quality fish sauce that is identical to patis and the equal of any brand I have used.

title: A lot of bite for jalapenos
text:
Disclaimer: I purchase this locally so am focusing this review on the product and not variables like price and shipping.

These have a surprising bite for jalapenos. So much so that I sometimes substitute this product for freshly cut bird's eye peppers when I am making a condiment called phrik nam pla from peppers and Thai fish sauce.

The reason I like this brand is because these jalapenos have a firm texture, and because they are packed in water instead of pickled in vinegar to retain the true flavor of the peppers.

I especially love the low sodium which is a total of 20mg for the entire can. I normally consume a can in a day if I am using this for cooking, but as a condiment I can stretch it for a few days. It keeps well refrigerated in a jar or sealed plastic container. In one case I went a week before finishing a can and it remained fresh and maintained the flavor and texture.

title: Superb quality and flavor
text:
Disclaimer: I purchase this locally so this review will focus on the product and not price or shipping. That said, I am thrilled that ackee is now readily available. Not too long ago it was banned and was difficult to get at any price.

This brand has the 'scrambled egg' consistency and the characteristic nutty flavor hints of quality ackee. I use it exclusively to satiate my appetite for salt cod - a dish I love and totally different from the Italian baccala I grew up eating.

In addition to flavor and consistency, I love this brand because it's simple and natural. The can contains only ackee, water and salt. More importantly - for me - is the sodium per serving is only 125mg. Each can contains about five servings. Another thing is this is pretty high in good minerals and vitamins like potassium (270mg) and calcium (83mg) and has 30mg of vitamin C.

As I said above, I am fortunate that I can get this locally. However, considering how scarce ackee was during the ban I would have gladly paid a premium price and am happy that I can order it online if I cannot find it locally. This is one of my favorite brands, which adds to my perception of value.

title: Superlatives do not begin to describe
text:
I am going to avoid gushing superlatives because all of the good ones have been used in other reviews. Instead I want to extol the virtues of this blend on fish. Specifically on salmon. Don't get me wrong - I am sure it's wonderful on meat, but I do not indulge in that.

When I prepare this I hand coat the fish with a thin layer of olive oil, then rub in this seasoning. I let it sit overnight and - viola! - the flavors have married deeply with the fish and come out beautifully when grilled or broiled. This is definitely spicy. If you have an aversion to hot food you may want to try the [[ASIN:B004GIKSJ0 Walkerswood Jamaican Mild Jerk Seasoning]] instead. It has the same basic flavor profile, but without the piquant element.

It's the flavor profile that not only sets this apart, but also captures the flavor of authentic Jamaican jerk. The piquant element is strictly from the Scotch bonnet peppers, which are both hot and flavorful. There is a touch of sweet from the cane sugar that is complemented by some of the aromatic spices (allspice and nutmeg.) In fact, the flavor profile is very complete because there is a touch of bitterness from the nutmeg, and sour from the citric acid. Salt is also prominent in the profile, with 540mg per two teaspoon serving. The final savory components come from the spring onion, black pepper and thyme.

This is for much more than jerk barbeque though. Walkerswood provided a tip that I followed - mix a little of this into mayonnaise - that makes a perfect condiment. In fact it complements aioli (a French twist on mayonnaise). However, I digress. This is probably the best jerk mix for making authentic jerk, and can be used to 'spice' up other dishes and condiments in ways only limited by your imagination.

title: Hot sauce lover's hot sauce + unbelievable flavor
text:
I've tried numerous hot sauces and too many have 'hot' as their main claim to fame. Unlike those this one's as hot, but has an amazing flavor that is like Jamaica in a bottle.

What I love is the Scotch bonnets do not dominate the flavor profile. You can actually taste the way a hint of sweetness counterbalances the piquant aspects, but also the nuances of garlic, onions and thyme. You can also detect a hint of sour and tang from the vinegar that actually flavors as well as preserves this sauce. Those all combine to be an intriguing and delicious hot sauce.

The sauce itself if pretty thick so a little goes a long way. I was also surprised that despite the heat this did not scorch or have a sharp bite. Certainly if Tabasco sauce is your limit this will probably be far too hot for you, but if you do like it hot you'll enjoy it. And also marvel at the smoothness because the heat builds instead of grabbing you by the throat.

One final note: a teaspoon has a scant 45mg of sodium and despite the cane sugar the carbs do not even register.

If you want a hot sauce that is hot, but want maximum flavor too this is it as far as I am concerned. It just does not get any better to my palate.

title: Disappointing
text:
UPDATE: 7 OCT 2013 - please see my comment below for two alternatives that I do recommend.

I truly hate giving less than positive reviews, but I have reviewed three other 'Saigon' (also known as 'Vietnamese') cinnamon products and all were remarkable. This one falls short.

Here are my impressions of this one and a comparison to the others. To be sure this one is a high quality cinnamon. It has a strong aroma that has the fragrance of a premium jar of regular ground cinnamon. The word 'regular' is the key word. True Saigon cinnamon is significantly more aromatic - it hits you the second you open the jar - and has a far more intense flavor. Once you have tried it you will never forget it and will probably not settle for anything less.

With respect to the difference between my experience with this one and the other three brands I have tried I am willing to concede that I may have gotten a bad jar, which happens. Ironically I do not feel cheated because this is still very high quality cinnamon - just not what I was expecting.

I would be interested in comments from others who have tried this and other brands to determine if I did get a bad jar.

title: A quality source of the real thing
text:
I have tried a few different brands of this incredible type of cinnamon and have not been disappointed with any of them. For me it now comes down to price and availability among those I have tried - this one included.

The first thing I look for is aroma, then taste. Both indicate freshness and authenticity. This one has the characteristic aroma that conveys at a whiff that this is not only fresh, but the real thing. Tasting this - if you never have tried Saigon (also known as Vietnamese) cinnamon - is like tasting this spice for the first time. The flavor is vivid. That is the best way I can describe it.

A little goes a long way. You will probably find that you only need half as much of this than a recipe calls for. Certainly no more than two thirds. Another thing to consider is most folks only purchase cinnamon in sticks. This is far more potent that any stick I have ever ground, and it disproves the adage that pre-ground spices lose their potency. More importantly, the nature of the bark of this wonderful spice makes it impossible to get it in stick form, so if you are offered it that way it's not the real thing.

I use this mixed with either honey or unsweetened applesauce as a topping on baked sweet potatoes. It adds a pleasurable flavor that allows me to get by without butter. It is also a pleasure when I add a pinch to coffee grounds before brewing.

The bottom line is if you have never tasted Saigon cinnamon you are in for not only a treat, but a completely different flavor experience with this. It's packaged fresh and fragrant, so I do not think you will be disappointed.

title: Very delicious
text:
I love hot sauces and love experimenting with various ones. Lately I have been using a lot of products from this brand and this one is among my favorites.

The reason I love it is the flavor and the piquant character balance one another. Of course the piquant factor dominates the flavor profile (although this is not super spicy to my palate). The garlic is easily detected, but the surprise is the sweet aspect of the flavor profile, which seems to dominate more than the salt.

About the piquant quality - this does have a slight bite and some spiciness, but if you can tolerate a serrano pepper you will not have any problems. For me I prefer a little more spiciness so I will often add some finely chopped bird's eye chilis to the sauce. Of course spiciness is both subjective and relative. If a jalapeno is too hot for you may want to avoid this. On the other hand, if a habanero is not enough, you will have to kick it up with additional peppers.

To me it's all about flavor and this one has it. It not only works with stir fry dishes, but also in American dishes like grilled beans and as the base for stews and soups. A dab of this when making scampi will add a lot to that dish as well.

Nutritionally a teaspoon contains only 10 calories and a single gram of carbs. However, it also contains 410mg of sodium, so if you have restrictions note that and use this sparingly. In fact, use it as a condiment in lieu of salt on some dishes for a real treat.

If you love spicy sauces and want to fuse Chinese flavors into your tried and true menus, or to make authentic Chinese dishes this is a great shortcut. It's earned a spot in my pantry.

title: Truly natural and perfect for some diets
text:
Disclaimer: I purchase this locally and will focus solely on the product and not address variables like cost and shipping.

I've grown to love the taste of this brand because even though it's called 'unsweetened' that only means that no additional sweeteners are added. In fact, after trying a number of different brands I keep coming back to this one because of both the flavor and the texture.

The apples from which this is made are sweet in their own right. In fact, the ingredients are both natural and simple: apples, water and ascorbic acid. The latter is not some chemical additive - it's vitamin C that is a natural part of an apple.

Even though this is a sauce there is a certain texture that is slightly coarse. This is neither good nor bad, but some folks prefer a much smoother texture and others - like myself - prefer it the way this brand is.

I mentioned that this is perfect for some diets. I use it as a substitute for butter and sometimes cream in many recipes. For example, I will use this over a sweet potato instead of butter, and also will substitute it for cream when I am making rice pudding or similar dishes. The only possible red flag is the carbs which comprise 13 grams per half cup serving. Of those eight grams are from sugar (naturally occurring in apples, of course). Those numbers are nominal and for most folks are very low, but if you need to micromanage carb and sugar intake it's useful to know the numbers. One added plus is a serving contains one hundred percent of the recommended minimum intake of vitamin C.

title: Delicious (but with caveats)
text:
For flavor this easily merits five stars according to my palate. However, there are a few red flags that need to be spotlighted. First, this contains peanut products, so if you have allergies to those then pass this by. Second, there are about fifteen 1 teaspoon servings in this jar and each contains 740mg of sodium. If you have restrictions then factor that in because it's fairly high.

Nutritionally, each teaspoon serving is 40 calories, 25 of which are from fat (which is 2.5 grams). There is no cholesterol, and the three grams of carbs per serving are offset to a degree by the 1 gram of protein. So aside from the sodium level the nutrition profile is reasonable.

For most folks the two red flags I cited are non-issues. The sauce itself is simply delicious, especially if brought to a boil in a water mix per instructions. It is not especially spicy, but that is a relative term. Put another way, if you can eat a jalapeno, this the heat from this sauce will not pose a problem. Salt is the dominating characteristic in the flavor profile, although the sauce is not particularly salty to the taste. There is a nice touch of garlic, and other ingredients that are not easily identifiable on their own, but combine to give this sauce it's wonderful (and exotic) flavor.

This is made to be mixed with water and used as a base for noodles. In that respect it is perfect. However, a teaspoon mixed into a soup right before serving adds a nice flavor - and the soup does not have to be from a Chinese recipe. Try it in a tomato-based vegetable soup. Or add two teaspoons to a stew. I use it as a base for beans which comprise a large part of my diet and it adds a great deal of flavor. Of course, for authentic Sichuan-style noodles this is a great sauce.

title: Not bad for something from a jar
text:
Note: I purchase this locally, so this review will only address the product and not pricing or shipping costs.

All of the key flavors are there: you can taste the blend of eggplant and tomato, the tang of vinegar and the saltiness of the capers. This also has a good base of other flavors from celery, olives and seasonings. In other words, it may not be close to home made, but it is tasty and definitely convenient. It has that distinctive Sicilian flavor that makes it perfect for last minute entertaining when you need to put out antipasti or meze.

There are approximately three servings per can, with each serving coming in at about 140 calories. Not bad for something so delicious.

What I truly love, though, is the reasonable levels of sodium, which is a fraction of the fried eggplant I mentioned above, and other nutritional values. Sodium is 310mg, which is less than half of the same serving of the fried eggplant, although the carbs and fat are still a tad high at 7 grams each. If you are watching cholesterol there is zero in this product. Do be aware that the sugar content is 8 grams.

As an antipasti or meze - hot or cold - this is an excellent choice to accompany breads for dipping and scooping, and it goes well with other servings that are Mediterranean (olives, pickled peppers, cheeses, dolmas, etc.) Of course it's great to make this delicious dish yourself, but these jars are convenient for putting something together on short notice.

title: Inexpensive and perfect for tuna salad
text:
This is not tuna I would use to make tapas or to create a culinary delight. For something like that I would use [[ASIN:B001LMKG5K Ortiz Spain El Velero Yellowfin Ventresca De Atun Claro]]. For a nice tuna salad served as a sandwich or over a bed of greens, though, this not only perfect, but in some ways better.

I am not implying that this is better than a ventresca cut of premium tuna. Instead, when I make tuna salad I use a little olive oil and mayonnaise, onion and relish, a touch of lemon and some seasonings. By the time all that is mixed in the flavors and nuances of a fine cut are so masked that you would be wasting your money on a better grade.

What I love is this has pretty good nutritional numbers, is almost shredded so it easily mixes into a traditional tuna salad, and has a nice, mild flavor.

Nutritionally each five ounce can contains two 50 calorie servings. Granted the cholesterol and sodium levels are slightly high at 30mg for cholesterol and 180mg for sodium. However they are not show stoppers as long as you are aware of them and adjust your recipes accordingly. On the plus side there is nominal fat (registers zero on the nutrition chart) and no carbs. Plus it has some good stuff like 90mg of potassium, 11 grams of protein. Add in selenium and omega-3 and you are getting a healthy base for tuna salad.

Another big plus for me is price. I am on a fixed income, so I have to balance culinary delights with some occasional compromises in order to eat healthy as well as enjoy my meals. This tuna is one of those compromises. Save money here and get something truly delectable for special dishes and occasions. Like I mentioned, the flavor of a better cut and grade of tuna would get lost in the ingredients.

If you are looking for a budget-priced, tasty and healthy source of tuna for quick salads this is as good as any and better than some.

title: A good way to stock up on a great oil
text:
Normally I stay away from boutique olive oils for two main reasons. First, some more common brands are good enough to be a well kept secret. Second, I have purchased boutique oils in the past only to be disappointed because they were stale. This one, though, is an olive oil lover's dream come true. More importantly, I have never gotten a stale or disappointing bottle.

It has the grassy notes that characterize Ligurian oils, and that back of the mouth burn is perfect. I'll admit that I rarely purchase this because I am on a fixed income, but there are times during the year when I absolutely have to treat myself to something nice, and this is it. Not my favorite wines or cheeses, but this.

One reason for the freshness and consistently great flavor is the care taken to protect the oil. The foil wrapped bottles are not marketing hype (well, perhaps partly), but a means to completely block light and extend the life.

At this point I need to set expectations: If you love high quality olive oils and have not tried this, I recommend that you do. If all olive oils taste the same to you then, perhaps, you should save your money. If you do go for it, this four bottle deal is a real bargain.

I use this over a Caprese salad or to make bruschetta, and I happily drizzle it over arugula salads. Heaven, though, is mixing it with [[ASIN:B000C1U83Q Bottarga Di Muggine (Grey Mullet Roe) - Grated - From Cabras, Sardinia]]. Personally, I will continue to treat myself to a bottle (or four in this case) every year. It's one of the things that make life worth living.

title: Impressive flavor and bite
text:
This is not like that 'other' sriracha sauce - this has a nice bite and lingering heat. The only thing it shares with the competition is superb flavor.

The flavor profile is dominated by the piquant quality from the chilis, but I was surprised that sour was not as dominating as the ingredients would normally indicate - especially since vinegar is only second to the chilis in the ingredient list. The garlic is easily detectable, as is the salt. The overall flavor allows this to go with just about any dish from eggs to noodles.

My main use is as a substitute for harissa (a Tunisian hot sauce). I also mix this with Thai fish sauce for seasoning grilled or broiled fish and vegetables and as a general condiment.

There are about fifty 1-teaspoon servings per container, each of which is a mere five calories. Sodium is a little high at 180mg per serving.

Overall this is a wonderfully (to my palate) sriracha sauce that has become my hand's down favorite. If you like a little more bite than that 'other' brand give this one a try.

title: Tasty, but some nutritional red flags
text:
Disclaimer: I purchase this locally so this review will focus solely on the product without comment on pricing or shipping factors.

This is a delicious treat that I keep in my pantry to go with quick meals. The 'smoked' flavor is a little heavy, but the texture of the salmon is dense and juicy and it's a delicious pairing with a light salad.

Ingredients are straightforward: salmon, soybean oil, water, salt and smoke flavoring. The salmon is also color-enhanced. This is about par for most canned fish.

Nutritionally this is a mixed bag. On the plus side it contains a full gram of omega-3, which is especially important in my diet. It also has a whopping 20 grams of protein and 240mg of potassium.

However, there are some red flags. First is half of the 160 calories are from fat, which totals 8 grams (probably from the soybean oil). Of the fat 1.5 grams are saturated fats. Sodium is 390mg, which is acceptable because I can manage that level with trade-offs in other dishes. Although, the 35mg of cholesterol is another concern for me because of my age and certain health conditions.

Red flags notwithstanding, I still think that the pluses balance out the negatives. Also, I consume this in moderation and only occasionally. It's a perfect source of a quick protein boost and some of the negatives can be diminished by draining the oil and blotting the salmon before serving.

title: Much wider use than just Szechuan cuisine
text:
It goes without saying that this is an important ingredient in some Szechuan dishes, but it has a much wider potential for other cuisines.

Since I am new to this spice I am going to take it as a matter of faith that the aroma is a true indication of freshness and strength. It has the characteristic sizzle effect inside your mouth, and also a lemon-like taste in the flavor profile. In Szechuan it is usually paired with star anise and ginger. It is a perfect counterbalance to truly hot chilis, which opens the door to the other cuisines that I mentioned.

Let's start with North African - add this to any tagine dish and it will enhance it. It also works wonderfully in dishes in which you would add harissa, including using it as a spread.
