title: Nice blend for making consistently good rouille
text:
This is a great blend of rouille spices that is both fresh and in generally good proportion. What I mean by 'generally good' is that is is good as is, but I augment this mix with a little more saffron and cayenne pepper. Otherwise, it is a great convenience to have a ready mixed blend that is fresh and aromatic.

About the way I augment this: when I am ready to add the spices to the base of my rouille (more about the base below), I use a quarter of a vial of [[ASIN:B008ZLNC5G Powder Saffron, organic premium Persian powder saffron]] and an additional half teaspoon of cayenne. The powdered saffron is actually not significantly more than the three percent of saffron that is already in this mix. Regarding the cayenne - I find that the extra that I add gives the rouille a little more bite, and especially if I am making rouille the traditional way with bread crumbs instead of egg yolks.

I mentioned a 'base' for my rouille. I make it the traditional way with fish stock, olive oil, bread crumbs and spices. I also make it using egg yolks as a base. This, too, is authentic, but I think the bread crumb recipe is the original. Finally, when I am pressed for time and want to set the rouille out as a spread over baguettes I simply mix the spices into store bought mayonnaise. Blasphemy, I know, but sometimes one needs to break rules. In all cases this mix works perfectly. To my palate the end result is as close to authentic I am likely to achieve.

The bottom line is this blend is both fresh and aromatic, and works well even without my changes and augmentations. I always keep some on hand in my spice cabinet.

title: Quick and inexpensive way to use high quality saffron
text:
Disclaimer: I was provided with a review sample by the manufacturer in exchange for a candid review.

This is my first time using powdered saffron so I tested it in simple dishes and a tea. The first thing I did was examine the color and to breathe in the aroma. The color is not the deep red that characterizes this company's saffron stigmas, but I expected some loss when it was ground into powder. The aroma was fainter than stigmas of saffron, but seemed to be fresh.

My next step was to make a simple saffron rice. I used aged basmati rice and prepared this powder the same way I would stigmas of saffron (stigma is a term for the thread or strand). Before starting I did some research and found out that only half as much powder is required than if you were using stigmas. The end result was a nice dish of rice that I ate without anything other than a little sea salt. The flavor and aroma were what I would expect from a top quality saffron - and what I would expect from any top grade Iranian saffron.

The next test was to use a pinch in tea. Aside from the tea and a little honey I used no other ingredients. Absolutely perfect.

My conclusion is this is a high quality saffron powder. The reason I had avoided powdered saffron in the past is there are too many low-grade ones on the market, and worse, cut with other ingredients like annato (achiote). fortunately this turned out to be the real thing - and high quality too.

Will I continue to use the powdered form? Frankly, no. My reasons have nothing to do with quality and everything to do with the fact that I am old and set in my ways. I gave this five stars because preparing saffron stigmas properly can take time and experience, whereas this powder is simple to use. Another reason I awarded this such high marks is the price is excellent. Although you are getting 1.5 grams of powder, it is the equivalent of three grams of stigma. And it is convenient to use.

I've uploaded a picture in customer supplied images at the top of this page that shows the size of one of the vials relative to a US quarter dollar coin. That will give you an idea as to how much power you will be getting in the three vials. Bear in mind that these vials are the equivalent of the company's [[ASIN:B007P4W0OI Persian Saffron, organic & pure Mehr sargol saffron / 1/9 oz (3 Gram)]] product.

Powder or stigmas is a personal choice. I imagine cooks who are experienced with cooking with saffron will opt for the stigmas. However, a few vials of this powder is handy to have in your spice cabinet for quick indulgences like saffron infused tea.

title: Wonderful addition to my pantry - but 'Balsamic' is loosely used
text:
Before I get to the part about Balsamic being loosely used I want to extol the virtues of this vinegar.

It can be the base of an amazing marinate, especially if you love the fragrance and taste of figs which are prominent in the bouquet. One tried and true recipe that I use for marinating fish is one third this infused vinegar and two thirds soy sauce. I crush in three or four cloves of garlic and add a bay leaf. I marinate the fish in that mix overnight. The results are delicious.

Used very sparingly it can also be the base of a salad dressing. The reason I say sparingly is because this is a strong vinegar that can easily overpower delicate leafy salads. Mixing this with equal parts water and olive oil and a few chopped herbs makes for a great dressing. Even a few drops over an insalada Caprese (sliced tomato topped with fresh mozzarella and basil leaves, and drizzled with olive oil) will add an interesting nuance to that dish.

It can also be used by adding a few drops to olive oil and grinding [[ASIN:B001SAWHPM Alessi Dipping Spice]], which will do wonders to a baguette.

I could go on and on, but the bottom line is this vinegar is sure to please anyone who also loves figs. It is a bit strong and pungent, so take that into account. Its uses are only limited by your imagination.

Now about the use of the word 'Balsamic'. This is not a true Balsamic vinegar in the strictest sense of the word. In fact it cannot be called 'Traditional' under Italian law, which regulates such things. This is more of a condiment grade vinegar. The traditional stuff sells for significant bucks. I mention this to differentiate this product from a traditional; i.e., geniune, balsmic vinegar from Modena or Reggio Emilia), so you will not be disappointed. Even though this is a condiment grade vinegar, it still has many valuable uses in the kitchen and at the dining table.

title: Excellent deal
text:
These larger capacity grinders of the Himalayan salt are better deals than most I've come across. At 10 ounces, each grinder holds two to two and a half times the salt of others I have purchased for about the same price. In fact, there are 283 quarter teaspoons (one gram) of salt per container.

What I love is these grinders have an adjustment mechanism that turned clockwise will give you a finer grind. For coarser grinds simply turn it in the other direction. I have uploaded a customer-supplied image at the top of this page that shows this adjusting mechanism.

Note: the grinders themselves are disposable. Once it's empty you simple throw it away, which is a shame because they work well. Unlike some refillable grinders I have owned these have a smooth action and do not get stuck. The large cap keeps moisture out of the salt when it is stored.

The salt itself does have a different flavor and one that I personally like. The flavor may be due to the iron oxide, which also colors the rocks pink. The actual sodium chloride content - the salt itself - comprises 95 percent of the product. Do be aware that there are no magical properties to this salt.

If you are on a restricted sodium diet this is as bad for you as sea salt or Kosher salt if used in excess. Each quarter of a teaspoon serving - one gram - contains 416mg of sodium. I have included a customer-supplied image at the top of this page showing the actual nutrition label that is affixed to the grinders.

If you compare prices of pre-loaded grinders of this salt you will quickly discover that this one is a bargain. I love mine for the convenience, but I also purchase additional salt in bulk for salt cellars and preserving.

title: Great flavor, a little heavy on the vinegar though
text:
To my palate these are a little too sour from the vinegar, but personal tastes vary so I still think it merits five stars.

One reason is the cherry peppers used are high quality. They have a plumpness and great texture that I love in pickled peppers. And sourness (to my palate) aside, these are a nice addition to any antipasti or meze spread for guests. In fact, the sourness is a nice contrast to oil based snacks like olives or fire roasted peppers, as well as meze that are flavored with oil and lemon.

Another reason I think these rate highly is my trust in the brand. I use a lot of Mezzetta products and have come to expect them to be made from the best ingredients. These peppers are no exception.

It should go without saying that there are perfect in salads, and if rinsed, make a wonderful garnish for many main dishes.

The ingredients are fairly straightforward: peppers preserved in water, distilled vinegar, sea salt and calcium chloride. There are seven 3-piece servings per jar, with each serving coming in at 15 calories. Each serving contains two grams of carbs, and zero fat or cholesterol. Sodium is fairly high at 340mg per serving (about 113mg per piece). This is on par with similar products from other brands, so just be aware of it if you are watching sodium intake and enjoy these in moderation.

title: Took me completely by surprise
text:
Note: I purchase these locally so am going to focus on the product without discussing price or shipping.

My first jar of these was an impulse buy. I wanted something to set our for guests along with other meze/antipasti snacks and figured that japapenos would be mild enough for most folks. How wrong I was. I was delightfully surprised at my first bite. These things pack a wallop. In fact, instead of a mild mannered jalapeno these came awfully close to habaneros. I may be exaggerating a bit, but they are a lot hotter than any jalapeno I have eaten in the past. And a lot more flavorful than any habanero.

What I love, aside from the slight endorphin rush from the heat, is these are not overpowered by vinegar. In deed, these are packed in brine with a simple list of ingredients that allows the pepper flavor to stand out. The brine is water, salt and citric acid. Nothing more.

Nutritionally there are eleven 10 calorie servings per m jar. Each serving contains zero fat and cholesterol and a manageable 90mg of sodium. Carbs come in at a scant 2 grams.

I use these in omelets (either as an ingredient or as a garnish), and as part of a soffrito when I am making pinto beans. In all cases I rinse off the brine before cooking or serving them.

If you love habaneros for their heat, but hate the flavor, give these a try. They are much hotter than most jalapenos, have a wonderful flavor from the roasting process, and fall somewhere between a serrano pepper and a habanero in heat.

title: I cannot believe the flavor from canned olives!
text:
I normally turn up my nose at any olives that come out of a can, but am delighted that I tried these because I love them.

The flavor is different from other olives I had while living in the Middle East, but perhaps since I was in the Gulf region (Kuwait and Dubai) that may account for the uniqueness to me.

What immediately grabbed me was the skillful balance of lemon, a little bite from the pepper and the saltiness. In fact, the flavor reminded me more of Moroccan or Tunisian fare. Regardless, if you want to taste olives that are 'different' from the ones you normally encounter - even from fresh olive bars - these will be a treat.

Ingredients are both simple and natural: Olives, Water, Salt, Acetic Acid, Garlic, Hot Pepper, Lemon. Nutritionally there are twelve servings (5 olives per serving), and each serving is 15 calories - all of which are from fat. Fat content is 1.5 grams per serving, but there is zero cholesterol. Sodium is 200mg per serving, so if you are on a sodium-restricted diet you need to consume these in moderation. And if you are like me and love them that may be somewhat difficult.

I am fortunate in that I can readily buy these locally at close to the same price. My advantage is I don't have to wait, and do not have to deal with the inevitable dented cans. However, if they were not locally available I would not hesitate to order them here.

title: The best deal for one of the best ras el hanout mixes you will find
text:
Not too long ago I proclaimed that [[ASIN:B008437X78 Mediterranean Gourmet Ras El Hanout, 2.46 Ounce]] was one of the best deals you were likely to find for a quality ras el hanout. I was wrong. This larger canister of that same spice mix is the best deal - or the best I have come across anyway.

What I love about this brand is the quality of the mix and the specific proportions. The quality is evidenced by fresh ingredients that are highly aromatic.

It's the proportions that are problematic since there are no two blends of ras el hanout that are alike. To me this one is near perfect, but someone else may find it is too light on heat or some other flavor or characteristic, or too heavy on another. My recommendation is to try the smaller canister I linked to above first to see if this blend is for you. Personally I love it and have made it my favorite brand. Your mileage may vary.

Of course, the price is incredible. For less than twelve dollars at the time of this review you get 16 ounces of a high quality ras el hanout. The only good reasons to go with a smaller size is if you do not regularly cook with this blend. If that is the case, go with the smaller size because this will go stale and saving money by buying in bulk is really throwing money away if allowed to go bad.

Aside from Moroccan Berber and North African cuisines this spice would work perfectly with many Mediterranean, Persian and Indian dishes as well. I use it to add 'secret' flavors to some of the food I prepare. For example, if I am making aloo palak (an Indian curry of potatoes and spinach) I mix this into the curry.

A recent dish I used it in is an Italian-American fish stew from San Francisco called cioppino. I browned garlic, shallots and thinly sliced fennel bulb in olive oil, added shellfish, quarters of other fishes and their stock, thickened it with tomato paste. I cooked it until the stock reduced, and chopped tomatoes. I continued cooking with a touch of red wine and two tablespoons of this spice mix and red pepper flakes. Before serving I added a little sea salt and the meal was perfect. It kept my guests guessing what the secret ingredient was.

Enjoy!

title: A delicious addition to a meze spread
text:
I set out a can in a dish with other morsels for meze when I am entertaining guests. To be fair some folks love them and others do not much care for them. It's all in the palate and individual tastes.

The reason I love them is they have a fairly pungent flavor that comes from the garlic, with a nice bite from whatever pepper they used to spice it up. They are a bit salty, so I let guests know that they are very high in sodium. Every can I have opened is consistent. In every case every pickle had the same flavor and the same 'perfect' crunchiness.

Personally, I enjoy them in moderation (and my cardiologist would not have it any other way.) The ingredients are simple enough: cucumbers, water, salt, acetic acid, dill, garlic and pepper. Calcium chloride is included as a firming agent.

Nutritionally there are eleven servings per container, so three quarters of a pickle constitutes a serving, which is a scant 5 calories. There is zero cholesterol, carbs or fat, but each serving contains 340mg of sodium. That looks high - and is - but is no worse than any other brand of pickle.

A few parting notes: first, I purchase mine locally. In fact I am surprised by how many chain and big box stores in my area carry these. This means that my costs are lower (no shipping) and I do not have to put up with dented cans and other issues, which increase my perceived value. Second, although I lived in the Middle East I cannot compare these canned pickles to ones I had there. These are close I suppose, but there is so much variation among brands or vendors that it's hard to compare. I will say that these reminded of of my stay in that region in a very good way.

title: Fresh and high quality
text:
These chilis have a wonderful aroma that indicates their quality. Unlike some I have purchased in the past, each one has a near uniform color without brown, dry blotches, and the skins have a natural oily feel instead of being overly dried and crumbly.

What I love is they are full flavored with a little bite, but still mild enough to use in dishes you will be serving guests who do not care for overly spicy food. You can always add spiciness to a cooked dish, but it's nearly impossible to take it out.

It goes without saying that these are great for Mexican cuisine, and especially for making sauces. However, they also go well in Middle Eastern and Mediterranean dishes. I will finely chop a few and add to bases and sofritos when I am making soups, sauces or even marinates for fish.

Here is one of my favorite bases that will go with any Mediterranean style soups, as well as a marinate for fish: I coarsely chop six garlic cloves and two shallots, four of these chilis and crush cashews. I saute those in olive oil until the garlic is golden brown. I add a cup of chopped cilantro and three diced, large, vine ripened tomatoes. After it has cooked down I add sea salt to taste, and to make it spicy I add [[ASIN:B0050IKSBI Harissa Paste]] to taste. From there I can continue by adding ingredients for a soup or stew (or beans), or marinate a nice cut of fish. It goes perfectly with salmon.

If you use pasilla and cannot get it locally, this one is a high quality choice that has never disappointed me.

title: Ain't nothing like the real thing baby
text:
With apologies to Marvin Gaye and Tammi Terrell, but the title of their hit song sums up this sauce. It is nothing like the same sauce made by the same brand for the French market.

First, this one contains rapeseed oil instead of olive oil - a cardinal sin in my opinion - and, second, it does not contain lemon! At the time of this review the product page contained the wrong ingredients. The actual ingredients are rapeseed oil, water, egg yolk, vinegar, garlic and Dijon mustard.

My complaints notwithstanding, I still gave this four stars because it is delicious and the manufacturer did claim it was specifically made for the American market. So, if you have had the real thing you are probably not going to like this one at worse, or will be disappointed at best. If you have not had the real thing and love a nice, garlic infused sauce that has the consistency and shares the base with its sibling, mayonnaise, then you are in for a treat.

Here is the lowdown on nutrition (which may seem over the top, but not bad if compared to mayonnaise): 180 calories per 2 tablespoon serving. 171 of those calories are from the 19 grams of fat of which 2 grams are saturated. Cholesterol is 18mg and sodium is 200mg. Be aware that this sauce is made with egg yokes and modified food starch, so if you avoid those you may want to avoid this product.

If you've never had aioli, but love both mayonnaise and garlic, give it a try. Mix in a little lemon juice and you will get close to the real thing. Not one hundred percent, mind you, but close.

title: Disappointing, but still flavorful
text:
I'll address my disappointment first: this is not a real Aioli sauce. True, it has a wonderful flavor, but anyone who has tried the real thing - including this same brand for the French market - will be disappointed.

To be fair, the maker does state that this was designed for the American market, but even Americans like olive oil, which is a key ingredient in authentic aioli. This one contains rapeseed oil. And to be even more fair (and why I still awarded this four stars), if you have never tried the real thing you will probably fall in love with this. I will concede that there is a hint of Provence in the flavor. A minor hint, mind you, but a hint nonetheless.

Since I have vented my negativity I will balance it with something positive: the sauce has a wonderful balance of mustards and garlic. Not as strong as the real thing, but perhaps to an American palate used to less pungent sauces it is close to perfect.

Nutritionally the values are 180 calories per serving (2 tablespoons). 171 of those calories are from the 19 grams of fat of which 2 grams are saturated. Cholesterol is 18mg and sodium is 200mg. Be aware that this sauce is made with egg yokes and modified food starch, so if you avoid those you may want to avoid this product.

If you have had the real thing you will probably complain about the same thing I did. If you have not, you are in for a treat.

title: I would not think of enjoying Mexican cuisine without this nearby
text:
There is an authenticity in this hot sauce when paired with true Mexican cuisine. For the record the cuisine with which I am most familiar is Baja, but I have been served this sauce in restaurants all over the US, as well as some of the Mexican border towns.

True, it is not very spicy. What it is, though, is flavorful. Also, unlike Tabasco, peppers dominate the flavor instead of vinegar. But the best thing is how it manages to enhance any dish from seafood to soups and main courses.

I mentioned that this is not very spicy - that is a relative statement. One person's spicy is another person's bland. This is not as spicy as Tabasco, but is a little spicier than a pickled jalapeno pepper. If you want truly spicy sauce with a good flavor you will probably have to try an Asian sauce like [[ASIN:B001FB68FO ABC Indonesian Extra Hot Chili Sauce - Sambal Extra Pedas]] or a North African/Mediterranean sauce like [[ASIN:B0050IKSBI Harissa Paste]]. You will get the heat and flavor with those, but you will lose that ineffable flavoring that is truly a flavor of Mexico.

The bottom line is if you love Mexican cuisine this sauce brings out the best in any dish with which you would use a hot sauce. It may not be the spiciest, but to my palate it's the best.

title: Handy for whipping up raita on short notice
text:
This mix is excellent for making raita or even a sauce on short notice. Up front, though, you need to know that despite the claims to the contrary it does contain a trace of salt - 2mg per teaspoon, of which there are 24 one-teaspoon servings per jar. Frankly, it's such a minute amount that you could make the claim that a single serving is sodium free. You decide.

In addition to using it to make raita, I use it to infuse olive oil as a topping for soups or to flavor rice. Basically I use a teaspoon of this in a quarter of a cup of olive oil that I bring up to medium heat. Some of the ingredients will pop, at which point I remove it from the heat and allow to cool. I'll sometimes squeeze the juice of a whole lime into the infused oil and use it as a marinate or even a quick salad dressing.

However, this blend is primarily for raita. While most raita dishes are made from either tomato or cucumber, I only make the cucumber variant. Here is my recipe using this blend (when I am making it from scratch I prepare it differently. I start with two cups of plain yogurt. Avoid 'Greek' style yogurt because it's too thick. I peel, deseed and grate a cucumber and finely chop a spring onion (using as much as the darker stem that I can). I mix those ingredients into the yogurt along with two teaspoons of this mix. I squeeze the juice of a whole lemon and thoroughly mix it in. If I have either fresh mint or cilantro handy I will finely chop a quarter of a cup of one or the other and mix it in. Since this blend is essentially salt free you will need to add that to taste.

Is this as good as made from scratch? Of course not. It is, however, an excellent blend for raita when you are in a hurry or unexpected guests drop in. It has earned a place in my spice rack.

title: Authentic Indonesian and Malaysian flavor
text:
This is the real thing and I am happy that I stumbled across it. It has a perfect balance of very hot and very flavorful. It's the spiciness that makes this such a treat. I would put the heat of this on par with a habanero sauce, but with a much better flavor. This is definitely much hotter than jalapenos.

I've compared it to [[ASIN:B001MGEU0W Huy Fong Sambal Oelek Sauce - Fresh Ground Chili Paste]] which is relatively hot, but also one dimensional when it comes to flavor. And totally different from the authentic flavor that this sambal imparts.

While this is perfect for many Indonesian, Malaysian, Thai and Philippine dishes, it's not limited to that region or even Asia. This sauce makes a great base for marinating fish, is perfect in soups and stews, and fits right into Mediterranean style cuisine. Speaking of Mediterranean, if you use harissa - in paste form like [[ASIN:B0050IKSBI Harissa Paste]] or ground like [[ASIN:B001E48ASU Dry Harissa]], substitute this for it. The results are pleasing to my palate and may be to yours as well.

If you are looking for an authentic sambal this is it.

title: Relatively mild, but heavenly flavor
text:
I normally love extremely hot and spicy dishes, but sometimes I just want a mild kick with a lot of flavor. This sauce delivers. My primary use is on eggs or in some soups, but I also use this as a base for other sauces - some very spicy and some not.

It's difficult to communicate levels of spiciness in words, but I would put this at about half the heat of a jalapeno. Another comparison would be to Tabasco sauce - this one does not have the sour, overpowering taste of vinegar like Tabasco, nor the bite. It does, however, have a pleasant warmth that augments the flavor.

One way I use this as a base is to saute some chopped shallots and garlic in olive oil, add crushed cashews, then four tablespoons of this sauce. I add [[ASIN:B001E48ASU Harissa]] to increase the spiciness. Sometimes I will add chopped cilantro to the mixture, but the key to the flavor is this Sriracha sauce.

This is also a perfect condiment to set out for guests who are adverse to overly spicy foods. Personally, I always have a bottle on hand and it usually does not last long. It's one of the best condiments in my pantry.

title: Decent flavor and wonderful memories
text:
I'll confess up front to only drinking this coffee a few times a year, and I do so more as a ritual than because I enjoy flavored coffees.

First, the coffee itself: the beans used in this grind are 100% arabica, so there is a characteristic smoothness. The flavor of the coffee itself is not particularly deep or rich, but the chocolate and other flavorings result in a nice brew of overall flavor and richness.

I do enjoy how the flavor and coffee are balanced. Neither overpowers the other. This has been skillfully blended to have all of the ingredients complement one another, which is why I gave it five stars.

Aside from the beans the package claims natural and artificial flavors. I am always on the lookout for nutritional issues with ingredients, but the packaging was vague about what exactly constitutes what are listed as artificial flavors. A check of a third party site devoted to nutrition info had zeros all the way down the list of values, including cholesterol and fat. That is encouraging, and especially considering that if the flavorings contained lactose or other allergens they would probably have been noted.

Bottom line regarding the beverage: I enjoy it, but not enough to habitually drink it. My biggest pleasure comes from the memories. My departed soulmate loved this coffee and the aroma of it brewing and the many cups I shared with her evoke priceless memories that are made more vivid when I smell the aroma of it brewing and sip a cup. I have a cup on her favorite holidays (Thanksgiving and Christmas), and on her birthdays and anniversary of her passing. I am enjoying a cup as I write this and dedicate this review to the memory of Karen I. Karr November 1, 1953 - April 12, 2010.

title: Impressed! This is a GREAT olive oil.
text:
I do not impress easily when it comes to olive oils. I can put up with mediocre wine, but will not tolerate anything less than the best when it comes to olive oil, and this one qualifies.

While most of my favorites are Spanish oils I tried this one and was blown away. It has that back-of-the-palate burn that I look for in a quality oil, and it has just a touch of grassiness that I normally associate with the Ligurian oils from Northwestern Italy. I'm officially impressed.

Other things that I love about this oil are freshness and value. Too often when I try a new brand of olive oil it's stale in the container. The problems are usually exceeding shelf life (very common with slow selling brands), or mishandling in shipment (usually allowing pallets of the product to set exposed in the sun. Neither was the case here. The oil is consistently fresh and flavorful.

With respect to value, this one is a bargain when you compare it to bulk brands that are in the same price range. Some of the bulk brands are admittedly good (there are some gems among them), but it's usually a crapshoot regarding quality. Factor in the fact that this qualifies for Super Saver shipping (at the time of this review) and the value proposition is attractive.

It's said that there are three things that make Sicily great: olive oil, citrus and almonds. Having tried this oil I agree.

title: Worth every penny
text:
These preserved lemons are essential for North African cooking, and are also indispensable for authentic Sicilian and Mediterranean dishes.

I've tried making my own and cannot come anywhere near achieving the texture and flavor of these. One can almost taste Tunisia in the jar. If you are cooking Moroccan or own a tagine these will add a lot to many meals. The brine is also useful if you use a teaspoon (or less) to add flavor to a sauce or soup. In fact, if you keep searching for the key to making a Sicilian style pasta sauce, use a little of the brine in the sauce - you'll be amazed by the results.

My main use is on fish. I usually coat the fish in olive oil and rub in some spices, and set it on a bed of thickly sliced red onions with some of these lemons sliced on the top. I then bake and - voila! - a wonderful and healthy dinner. Of course if you truly want to get authentic, especially if you own a tagine, prepare your fish with a marinate of [[ASIN:B000GGWCW2 Chermoula]] and slow cook with slices of these lemons on top.

Do not let my focus on fish dishes lead you to conclude that these will not work with meat. I do not eat meat, but friends who cook with preserved lemons rave about how well they go with chicken, lamb and other meats. Of course these would also add a lot of flavor to strictly vegetables. In fact, they are common in vegetable dishes made in a tagine.

I tried the pepper that is in the jar and was not impressed one way or the other with it. It's too mild and it did not seem to impart any flavor to the lemons or the brine.

One thing to note is you need to rinse off the lemons before using them in cooking or your food may be either too salty, overpowered by lemon, or both.

title: Very high quality and definitely piquant
text:
There are three things I look for in ground cayenne pepper and this brand has them all:

Freshness comes first. Many people cannot tell the difference between fresh and stale ground cayenne because they are distracted by the spiciness. I can, and I can assure you that this is fresh.

Aroma comes in a close second. This pepper has an aroma that indicates both the freshness and the quality of the peppers used. Some brands of cayenne fall a bit short in this area.

Spiciness. This brand stands out when it comes to heat. Cayenne pepper ranges from somewhat mild (and bland) to scorching hot. This one is closer to the scorching end of the scale, but its freshness and aroma come through as a wonderful flavor.

Aside from how pleased I am with the quality of this pepper, it's gratifying to find it in 16 ounce packaging. I use cayenne like many people use salt of black pepper, so the choices are usually narrow: purchase a lot of expensive two ounce jars or one bland large container. This one solves that problem because it's priced like the bulk containers that are typically low quality, but the ground pepper is of the same quality as some of the best from boutique (and expensive) brands.

If you use this pepper mainly for medicinal purposes to lower blood pressure and promote cardiac fitness, you may not see the spiciness as a big plus. On the other hand, if you use a lot of cayenne pepper for seasoning and as a condiment, and love the ones that are on the spicy side, this is a bargain and one that I recommend

title: Delicious, but beware ...
text:
Easy five stars for flavor. This is delicious. The main two ingredients are figs and cane sugar. Unfortunately (and the reason that I subtracted a star) is this treat also contains high fructose corn syrup (HFCS), which is something many folks avoid.

However, if you love figs and have no aversion to HFCS then you are going to love this jam. The natural flavor of ripe figs come through, and it goes with just about anything on which you would spread a jam.

Aside from the HFCS the caloric content is not terrible. A tablespoon is about 50 calories, with zero cholesterol, sodium of other things one should be watching if they are eathing healthy. That same tablespoon full has 12 grams of carbs.

If only they had left out the HFCS ...

title: A pantry staple in my house
text:
The uses for these seeds are nearly infinite - toss them in salads, process them into a paste with herbs and spices as a rub, and the list goes on. My primary use is to make za'atar.

What I love about these seeds is they are not stale. They have a nice texture, and they are not hulled, which improves their shelf life. I do transfer mine to an airtight jar for storage because as much as I love za'atar a two pound bag lasts a long time.

Another use for these seeds is to encrust a nice fish filet before baking or broiling, and if you love pan seared ahi, then you already know how well teriyaki and sesame seeds go with that.

Probably the best thing about these seeds, though, is the price. At less than fifteen bucks (at the time of this review) for almost a kilo of high quality, freshly toasted sesame seeds is a bargain. If you are a high volume consumer of these seeds this is possibly the best deal you are going to find.

title: Good quality and a great value
text:
This saffron is pretty close to the quality of the Iranian saffrons at close to the same price point. This one is harvested in southern Morocco and at one gram for less than seven bucks (at the time of this review) is a bargain for a decent saffron.

The color is a little lighter than my preferred brand - [[ASIN:B0071DSIL2 Persian Saffron Organic & Pure Iranian Bahraman Saffron]] - but still imparts the delicate and nuanced flavor that makes saffron such a valuable spice.

One reason I tried this was to ensure that I had alternate sources of high quality saffron. There are always regional issues that can disrupt the importation of the most prized saffron. I can say that this one measures up completely. The quality is up to my demanding standards, and the price is a bargain. An added plus is the container in which this ships - it will keep your precious saffron fresh.

If you occasionally use saffron then the one gram size is perfect. If, like me, you are also looking for alternate sources give this one a try. I am impressed with the quality of Moroccan saffron!

title: Very versatile spice - one complaint
text:
I'll confess that I am more familiar with North African cuisine than dishes from the Horn (although I have spent time in both Kenya and Somalia many decades ago.)

I love the quality of the herbs and spices that comprise the blend. The flavors are vivid and fresh, and the mix is aromatic. I also love the way the many ingredients seem to be in harmony. Considering that Ethiopia is one of the oldest areas of human civilization they have had thousands of years to perfect the blend. And to my palate it is perfected because it goes with just about any dish, including common Mediterranean fare. A little in a red pasta sauce will have your guests scratching their heads while effusively complimenting the chef. That is but one example.

In the header I mentioned that I had one complaint: salt is added to this mix. Granted it is not a lot, but for those of us who want to have absolute control over sodium in our dishes adding salt to a pre-blended mix is worthy of a complaint. I hope the owners consider this by either making a salt-free version or eliminating sodium altogether. You can always add salt to a dish, but removing it is not so easy.

The one recipe in which this excels is in simlins - a common dish from the US South that is made of squash and onions. The authentic recipe calls for fatback as the base, but I do not eat meat, so I make mine with olive oil. I layer yellow squash and onions sprinkled with salt and pepper for the traditional way. However, I eliminate the salt and pepper and use this instead (in much smaller amounts because it does not take much). I cook over a low heat - uncovered - for two hours and the results are fantastic.

My inspiration for using this mix stems from my late grandmother's habit of sprinkling nutmeg over the traditional way before serving. This blend takes that to a whole new level.

A little of this in a hearty soup like pasta e fagioli is perfect. In fact, even in a simple potato and leek soup this blend will add flavors, as well as draw out nuances from otherwise bland ingredients.

Enough said! Take a chance and let your imagination run amok.

title: A welcome addition to my spice rack
text:
Disclaimer: I primarily purchase my harissa as a paste and prefer this brand: [[ASIN:B0050IKSBI Harissa Paste]]. However, having this on hand is a convenient way to 'roll your own' on short notice. A key advantage to the dry spices is you can make a paste as strong or mild as you like. The disadvantage is getting the proportions right. For that reason I will always prefer the paste that I purchase, but will always keep some of this on hand too.

Like all Zamouri spices and blends that I have tried in the past, the spices in this one are fresh and aromatic. Sometimes the brand takes liberties with ingredients in some of their mixes, but in the case of this harissa I think the mix and proportions are nicely balanced.

If you followed Zamouri's recommendation of mixing equal proportions of this mix, olive oil and water you will be rewarded with a decent harissa paste that has both flavor and a bite. In this particular mix cayenne pepper and paprika dominate the flavor, with easy to identify garlic and salt. There are other peppers in the mix that add piquant nuances, as well as hints of spices that impart interesting flavors.

While this is a North African/Mediterranean spice, it easily complements any cuisine, and especially Mexican and Caribbean. Of course, it is perfect for any Middle Eastern dish that calls for flavorful spiciness. That means it is perfect with Palestinian and some Turkish dishes. In fact, do not be limited by my narrow recommendations - if you live a little heat in your food let your imagination run wild with this.

title: A brand I trust and an excellent tahini
text:
This is one of two brands of tahini that i trust (the other is [[ASIN:B000HQL51U Joyva Tahini]].) The reason I am so loyal is the consistent quality. I have purchased other brands in the past only to be pleased with some batches and upset because others had a staleness to them.

This one has a nice aroma that only freshly ground sesame seeds impart. I also love the viscosity of the paste, which is not too thick nor too thin. In other brands I have found that some are actually runny and others are super thick or dried out. So I appreciate that aspect of this tahini, and especially when I am making a simple lemon sauce with water, lemon juice and garlic. I can actually mix this brand by hand with a whisk instead of resorting to a food processor.

One disclaimer: I get mine locally at a specialty store in the local area, so I avoid shipping costs. This naturally increases the value to me. Still, when it comes to selecting ingredients I will pay a premium price for quality and this particular brand is definitely worth a premium price in my opinion.

title: Simply magic
text:
This blend \consists of very fresh and aromatic spices that are mixed in authentic proportions. In other words, this is a high quality chermoula that will magically transform your fish into an exquisite meal.

If you follow the basic directions in the product description on this page you will be rewarded with one of the best marinates imaginable.

Mix one and a half tablespoons of this blend into a puree of a cup each of fresh cilantro and parsley, a few garlic cloves and three tablespoons of olive oil. Spread this paste in both sides of your fish and let sit in the refrigerator overnight.

You can then cook the fish in a tagine, grill or broil it. Or do like I and prepare it en papillote using parchment paper.

En papillote works for any type of fish and is - in my opinion - second best to using a tagine. I place a layer of thickly cut slices of red onions of the bottom and drizzle them with a little olive oil. I then layer the marinated fish, followed by thinly sliced lemon ([[ASIN:B005XGR43C Les Moulins Majoub Preserved Lemons - 7 ozs.]] is perfect). I layer medium sliced tomatoes on top of the lemon, drizzle a little more olive oil and garlic cloves, and season with [[ASIN:B008437X78 Mediterranean Gourmet Ras El Hanout]]. I then fold over the parchment paper and slow cook in the oven at 325 degrees for two hours per pound of fish.

Regardless of how you prepare your fish, marinating it first in a paste made from this spice mix as described above will greatly enhance the flavor and wow family and guests.

title: Surprising uses
text:
Lately I have been experimenting with various Spanish and Hungarian brands of paprika. I purchased this on a whim the last time I was in our local chain store to see how it compared to [[ASIN:B003G50HPE La Chinata Hot Smoked Paprika by La Tienda]], which I very much liked.

This one is sweet and mild compared to the La Chinata brand, but still has that smokey flavor that is pronounced enough to make it interesting. This can replace saffron in paella, if you are on a budget, as well as serve as a substitute in recipes that call for annato.

One surprising use I found is it works with some Middle Eastern and other Mediterranean recipes that you would not normally think of adding paprika. One example is a tahini dressing that is a puree of a garlic clove, a half cup of tahini, a third of a cup of fresh lemon juice and a third of a cup of water, and a teaspoon of this smoked paprika (salted to taste.)

While I prefer the spicier La Chinata style, I love having this one around for when I cook for guests who do not like their food to be very spicy. It still has a lot of flavor and the smokey nuances add a lot to many dishes.

title: I've gone to heaven
text:
I love spicy dishes, but the problem with many is the peppers and mixes have the heat without flavor (or terrible flavor if, for example, the peppers are habaneros.) This is a dream come true for me and I purchased a tube on a whim. What a serendipitous find!

To be sure this is not for folks who like a touch of Tabasco or jalapenos. This paste is up there with habeneros for heat, but imparts wonderful flavors that you would never obtain from anything made with that pepper.

Since I've not been using this that long I've only had occasion to use it in an omelet, beans and a fish stew. Believe me, even if you love your food super spicy a little of this goes a long way. It overpowered the first omelet until I figured out how much was enough (about an eighth of a teaspoon works well). A tablespoon mixed with 16 ounces of pinto beans cooked in a recaito sauce like [[ASIN:B003T0E1ZS Goya Recaito - Cilantro Cooking Base]] makes for a perfect side or main dish.

What sets this apart from every other hot sauce or paste I've tried is the interesting way it teases your palate. The label claims that in addition to peppers it contains carrots, turnips, tomatoes, coriander and caraway seeds. While I do not doubt that, the flavors become almost ineffable when blended with the dish in which it's used, and as spicy as it is, that aspect does not overpower the flavor. If anything it enhances it.

title: Quickly became my favorite
text:
Crushed red pepper is a staple in my house - I use it as a condiment, and in moderation in some dishes I prepare.

When I came across this I had to try it. It's nothing like my usual brand, [[ASIN:B003L8R7TU Badia Crushed Red Pepper]]. This one is slightly salty and has a different texture.

I would rate it as medium hot, which is a subjective term. It's slightly hotter than a jalapeno and nowhere near as spicy as a habanero (sorry, but that's the best I can do to peg the piquant quality.)

What sold me on it is the flavor. Unlike crushed red pepper, which provides a bite, this provides the bite, but also has an interesting flavor. I cannot describe it, but there is a subtle sweetness. Another thing I love is when I make a sofrito (a base for stews, soups and sauces) I was unable to add crushed red peppers because they would stick to the pan. These do not. In fact, they quickly infuse the olive oil and blend perfectly with garlic when I am starting the sofrito.

Thus far I have been able to substitute this for any recipe that I would have used crushed red pepper. It is also the perfect condiment (assuming that you like red peppers.)

title: One of the best deals ever for a quality ras el hanout mix
text:
At the time of this review an almost three ounce canister of this spice is going for less than four bucks shipped if purchased as an add-on of an order that qualifies as super saver shipping.

Of course it would not be a deal if the mix was badly done or the spices stale, which is not the case on either count. The mix, like any ras el hanout, is as individual as snowflakes, so expect the blend to reflect the unique recipe of the manufacturer. Personally I was more than satisfied with it.

What I especially love is the quality of the spices that are blended into this mix. They are fresh (for ground spice anyway) and aromatic. Another big plus for me is this ships in a canister that tightly seals to keep the blend fresh.

I personally use this blend to add 'secret' flavors to some of the food I prepare. For example, if I am making aloo palak (an Indian curry of potatoes and spinach) I mix this into the curry. A recent dish I used it is is an Italian-American fish stew from San Francisco called cioppino. I browned garlic, shallots and thinly sliced fennel bulb in olive oil, added shellfish, quarters of other fishes and their stock, thickened it with tomato paste. I cooked it until the stock reduced, and chopped tomatoes. I continued cooking with a touch of red wine and two tablespoons of this spice mix and red pepper flakes. Before serving I added a little sea salt and the meal was perfect. It kept my guests guessing what the secret ingredient was.

Aside from Moroccan Berber and North African cuisines this spice would work perfectly with many Mediterranean, Persian and Indian dishes as well.

title: Good basic blend
text:
I frequently make my own za'atar, but keep this around for when I am pressed for time.

Like all Zamouri products I have tried, the ingredients in this are fresh and aromatic. I am pretty loyal to this brand because of that, and this Za'atar is no exception.

The blend itself - how best to put it? - is basic. This is not a severe criticism of this brand as much as it is a reflection of my personal tastes. It is also an acknowledgement that there are as many variations on the proportions and even the spices as there are snowflake patterns.

Personally I prefer a little more sumac in the mix when I am making it myself, as well as some oregano. I usually add those to this mix, and especially when I am making manakeesh. However, for sprinkling over humus or other dishes.

Overall, though, I like the convenience of this because it is made from high quality ingredients (thyme, sesame seeds and sumac). I can quickly add my own touch of to get the flavor I want from it. More importantly, it's inexpensive as well as convenient.

title: High quality grade
text:
This is a high quality sumac in that it has a nice aroma that indicates that the sumac is fresh. In addition the flavor has the characteristic citrus in perfect balance.

Freshness aside, this price is also right. At the time of this review this is actually less expensive than other quality brands, and is also part of the Add-On program that eliminates shipping if you add it to orders over a nominal amount.

Sumac is one of my essential spices that I use on everything from garnishing humus and rice, to preparing fish. Of course this is also necessary for za'atar.

One note: this is claimed to be organic. I have no reason to doubt it, but cannot tell the difference between this and other brands of high quality sumac.

title: One of the best sweet paprikas on the market
text:
I am fortunate in that this is readily available locally. Much of my cooking does not require paprika, but I keep three different kinds in my spice rack because each is an indispensable flavor for some dishes.

This one is the sweetest grade of the eight Hungarian grades and is called Különleges. I use it as a garnish mostly; typically over deviled or hard boiled eggs and occasionally over other types of egg dishes. At the other end of the Hungarian paprika spectrum is another of the three types I use. It's from the same brand and is called Erős in Hungarian (see [[ASIN:B0043U7GHI Traditional Hungarian Paprika - Hot]] for a description.) It's much spicier. The final type of paprika I use is a Spanish grade called pimentón de la vera. This one is smoky and hot, and vastly different than the Hungarian grades. My favorite brand is [[ASIN:B003G50HPE La Chinata Hot Smoked Paprika by La Tienda]].

About the weevils. There are two products in which you can expect the pesky things: rice and paprika. I suppose some of the Americanized brands of paprika are weevil free, but they also lack the deep flavors of Hungarian (or Spanish) brands, and most fall far short of this particular brand. As one other reviewer recommended: keep it in the refrigerator and the problem will go away. The alternative is to use a bland variety and forgo the wonderful flavor this one imparts. To me that alternative is unacceptable.

This is the real thing and is worth every penny.

title: Hard to beat for paella
text:
There is something magical about this rice. Like all rice from Calasparra this one is super absorbent - even more so than [[ASIN:B000FDLAWY Arborio]] rice we Italians use for risotto. In fact, this grain will absorb three times its volume in liquid compared to arborio's 2-to-1 ratio.

This particular brand is of the highest quality and consistency. Some rices - even the best ones - will grow stale from storage before you ever get it, or, worse, be infected with weevils. This is fresh, wonderfully aromatic and it perfectly absorbs.

Unlike when I prepare risotto in which I am frequently stirring, I take the opposite approach with paella. Once it's in the pan I leave it alone to get the crisp bottom very much like tahdig in Persian rice. Using the low heat that is required for a great paella, this method works beautifully.

As long as you are aware of the absorption rate of this grain, and the low heat cooking requirements of paella in general you're set. This rice makes a perfect paella every time.

title: Unique flavor
text:
I was hesitant to try a Spanish paprika, believing that the Hungarian paprika was the original. How wrong I was because a little research revealed that this magnificent spice has its origins in the New World and it was the Spanish (and Portuguese) who introduced it to Europe.

This particular brand is exceptionally high quality and is a grade called 'pimentón de la vera'. It is different from the normal picante grade in that it has a smoky flavor that is supposed to be used for meats and sausages.

Among my uses are in lieu of saffron in paella and a substitute in recipes that call annato. In the paella it imparts a flavor that I cannot achieve with any other spice. You cannot use this together with saffron though because it will completely overpower the subtle flavors of that very expensive spice. As a substitute for annato this will color rich more red than yellow if used in the same portion size, but also has a spicy, smoky flavor that will change the flavor of the dishes in which it's substituted. Mostly for the better, but it's wise to experiment before serving at larger gatherings.

This and two other grades of paprika (Hungarian sweet and Hungarian hot) have permanent places in my spice rack. This one is the most unique in my opinion, as well as the most perfect for paella.

title: Highest quality
text:
This is a high quality paprika that is the top of the spiciness grade from among eight grades ranging from this mildest called Különleges to this one called Erős in Hungarian. This is also close to the Spanish grade called pimentón picante, which is the spiciest in that country.

I mix mine with a little hot olive oil when making a sofrito for some soups and sauces, and it can be sprinkled on deviled eggs and other dishes as a garnish in lieu of sweet paprika if a recipe calls for it. Regardless of the cuisine, this grade goes beautifully with sweet peppers, onions, garlic and tomatoes in any combination.

While this is the spiciest grade it is not terribly hot compared to ground cayenne pepper. This allows it to work well for providing a little bite to a dish without overpowering the palate of folks who are not used to overly spicy food. Of course every palate is different, so you may want to experiment before using it with wild abandon.

title: Excellent substitute for spaghetti in some dishes
text:
Mezze means half, so this is a miniature penne. I love this shape more than spaghetti or regular size penne for any dish that has a rich red sauce. The reason is they are less filling (and less carbs), while still providing the key advantage of the penne shape: they collect the sauce and bits of the sauce ingredients for a more focused flavor.

Of course this is a perfect shape for any ragu, but I also use it frequently for sugo alla puttanesca that I make with tomatoes, garlic, capers and fresh olives sauteed in olive oil. I also prefer this shape as the pasta for alla cecca, which I make by chopping tomatoes, basil and garlic, quartering fresh mozzarella, and tossing them into cooked and drained pasta.

These are almost small enough to use in pasta e fagioli, but I have not tried that yet. They will work in other hearty vegetable soups, though, which I have tried. In fact, if you put them in twenty minutes before the soup is ready the extra time will reduce some of the semolina and thicken the soup.

Experiment by substituting this shape for spaghetti or regular penne in some of your recipes that use thick sauces. You may be surprised by how well this shape works.

title: Great for rustica and heavier sauce pasta dishes
text:
This pasta is readily available locally so I am not going to address shipping or other ordering factors. The shape is 'little bells', but also looks like a horn or even a flower. That is why this particular shape is perfect for heavier sauces or rustica-style disher that contain ingredients such as mushrooms, zucchini and similar.

I use it to make simple dishes. One example is I will chop some sweet peppers and quarter grape tomatoes, then saute whole garlic cloves in olive oil. After the cloves are browned I will add the peppers until they are cooked, then mix in the uncooked tomato quarters and season with grated cheese. The mouth of these shapes will collect the ingredients and the result is an intense burst of fresh flavor without overwhelming or competing tastes. Sometimes I just toss rapini con aglio (rabe broccoli with garlic) into this pasta for a perfect, quick meal.

Since this shape was designed to 'collect' ingredients into the mouth of the pasta, substitute this for linguini when serving a white clam sauce - it's a perfect shape for that style of dish.

The possibilities for this shape are endless. If you make sauces with small chunks of vegetables, fish or meat, then this will probably work perfectly.

title: A perfect balance for my tastes
text:
When it comes to espresso my tastes are pulled in two directions. I grew up drinking the European roasts that have a pleasant bitterness to them. However, after discovering the Cuban roasts I fell in love with the rich, deep flavor that characterizes those.

This roast has the best of the European and Cuban coffees: that wonderful bitterness that manages to also be smooth, and the rich flavor. When I am brewing a pot the aroma fills the house like no other coffee, and this is strong in caffeine as well. The perfect way for me to start the day!

I use a moka pot to make mine. Specifically, a [[ASIN:B000CNY6UK Bialetti 6800 Moka Express 6-Cup Stovetop Espresso Maker]] for which the grind of this coffee is perfect. It's not too fine, not too coarse for the basket that functions as a filter. I have not tried this coffee in a pressurized espresso machine, so I cannot say one way or the other how well the grind will work in those. I do know that with drip-style coffee makers this coffee comes out too bitter and loses a lot of its richness.

If you like the slight bite of European coffees, but also love the richness of the Cuban ones, give this one a try. I personally think it works best in a moka pot.

title: An oblong Kiss
text:
These taste identical to the ubiquitous Kiss drops that we all grew up with in the US. I loved those as a child, but as I grew older I gravitated towards dark chocolates. Especially the rich, dark and bittersweet European ones.

Compared to European and some domestic chocolates these are very sweet. However, they are pure milk chocolate and do NOT contain high fructose corn syrup or other 'improvements' like some confections. While the title - Milk Chocolate - may be obvious it's easy to forget the basic ingredients if one is a vegan. Fortunately I am merely a vegetarian.

The nutritional values need to be closely examined if you are watching calories, fat or carbs. The package claims that the serving size is four pieces and there are eight servings per twelve ounce bag (32 pieces in all). Each individual piece is 50 calories, of which about 27 of those calories are from fat. Also, of the three grams of fat per piece, nearly 2 of those grams are saturated fat. Cholesterol and sodium are nominal, weighing in at 2.5mg and a little over 8mg respectively. Carbs, though, are 12.5 grams per piece (nearly all of which are from sugar.)

While the nutritional figures look bleak, they are not terrible for 10 gram pieces of milk chocolate. While these are too sweet for my taste, some of my guests love them. And they do evoke a certain nostalgia since they taste like the Kisses Hershey made famous. I always keep a bag on hand - served in a dish - for guests who cannot resist them.

title: Heavenly - rich and wonderful
text:
When I saw the name I immediately thought Belgium. When I tasted my first one I was convinced they were from Belgium and was surprised to find out these are from Germany. Regardless of where they were made they are the work of a company that knows chocolates.

I put this assortment out in the a dish much the same as shown on the packaging - see my customer-supplied image at the top of the page for a visual. And to be honest I only serve these when I have guests because left to my own devices I would gobble them up myself.

This is a variety pack that consists of seven different styles: milk chocolate, Coffee and Cream, Hazelnut Almond, Hazelnut Cream, Dark Cream, Dark Mousse and Praline Cream. There are twenty pieces in a box.

If you have lactose issues or are a vegan know that each style contains milk products. Thankfully these do NOT contain high fructose corn syrup (something that cannot be said about some other premium, flavored chocolates). While the box claims a serving size of four pieces I am going to provide the nutritional values for a single one. Each contains 75 calories, of which 45 of those calories are from fat. There are 5 grams of fat per piece, of which 3 grams are saturated. There is less than 2mg of cholesterol in each one, and 7.5mg of sodium.

The above nutritional values are not terrible for flavored chocolates, and are actually better than competing chocolates. As long as you are aware of what you are consuming and do so in moderation this is a wonderful treat that is rich and creamy, and of the highest quality.

When I do indulge it's with an espresso. These go perfectly with any coffee and are a touch of both luxury and decadence that we all need periodically. In that respect these are worth every penny.

title: Superbly made and perfect for some dishes
text:
Disclaimer: I almost always use Barilla brand pasta, but this was available locally and I could not find Barilla spaghettoni. It was serendipitous because I fall in love with these noodles.

The first thing I noticed is the slightly rough texture of the noodles. These make them perfect for sauces that contain finely chopped ingredients because they will cling to the pasta. Cooking time for al dente is about on par with other spaghettoni I have used: 11 minutes.

I love this style of pasta because the thicker noodles go perfectly with simpler sauces. I am not big on red sauces, and as a vegetarian I also eschew meat sauces. My favorite recipe for this type of noodle is to saute garlic and coarsely chopped tomatoes in olive oil. I season the saute with red pepper flakes and freshly ground black pepper. Once the saute is finished (the garlic is uniformly golden brown) and the pasta is cooked and drained I toss finely chopped fresh basil into the pasta along with a few handfuls of fresh baby spinach. I next mix in the saute and serve with grated Pecorino Romano cheese.

When preparing the above recipe I noticed just how effective the texture on the noodles are at attracting clinging pieces of basil. This is a key difference to this noodle from my favorite brand and why I gave this one five stars.

If you cook with spaghettoni this one is worth checking out.

title: Perfect for Florentine and similar style dishes
text:
The shape of this pasta is perfect for any dish that is centered on spinach (Florentine style) or any other leafy vegetable like arugula - or a combination. It is also perfect for rapini con aglio (rabe broccoli with garlic).

Up front - I am very loyal to Barilla brand because it is consistent. What I mean is I can obtain the same al dente firmness by cooking a package of this pasta using the same temperature and time that I used twenty years ago on a package. That consistency is why I use Barilla (with a few exceptions) for all of my pasta.

I mentioned that this is perfect for Florentine and similar dishes. This is because as the leaves wilt they wrap around the shapes, catching in the twists and making a perfect morsel that is hard to obtain from other pasta shapes. These shapes are also excellent for heavier ingredients found in rustica-style dishes.

Here is how I prepare rapini con aglio and serve it with this pasta. First I steam the rapini until it's cooked, but still firm. I then brown whole garlic cloves in olive oil, and after they have turned a golden brown I add in the rapina and continue on medium low heat until it's well cooked. I toss this into cooked and drained pasta, toss with sea salt and black pepper and serve. I often will squeeze a lemon wedge over the dish before serving.

If you are making Florentine style dishes, instead of cooking the spinach (or other leafy vegetable) in the sauce, toss it raw into the cooked and drained pasta, then add the sauce. The heat from the pasta plus the sauce will cook down the leaves, but their flavor will be more prominent in the dish.

Regardless of how you use this shape, it's interesting and - as I have hopefully shown - perfect for certain types of dishes.

title: The best of the best
text:
For most of my pasta I use Barilla brand, but for bucatini this is THE ONE to buy in my opinion. It has the perfect texture, shape and flavor for bucatini all'Amatriciana or deriviative dishes, and is consistent.

What I mean by consistent is I will get the same al dente firmness each time I cook this pasta as long as I use the same time and temperature settings. Not all pastas are like that. Some vary by the batch and require that you carefully monitor it through the cooking cycle.

As for the bucatini all'Amatriciana here is my recipe: I start by sauteing guanciale in olive oil if I am cooking this for guests. If I cannot get guanciale I substitute pancetta. If I am preparing this for myself I omit the meat since I am a vegetarian.

I next add two cans of high quality tomatoes like [[ASIN:B005IE1JDK Napoli Italian San Marzano D.O.P. Whole Tomatoes]] and simmer for an hour.

I thoroughly mix this into the cooked and drained bucatini and grate in a copious amount of Pecorino Romano and serve. If for just me I add red pepper flakes and a little black pepper after I've grated in the Pecorino Romano.

Regardless of whether you are loyal to another brand - as I am to Barilla - for the absolute best in bucatini this is the brand to buy in my opinion. You can actually taste the difference.

title: Dilemma - in a good way
text:
I am increasingly torn between the Italian and other European coffee roasts and Cuban ones. This is my latest indulgence in my quest for great espresso.

First, let me clarify what I mean by espresso. I am not talking about the brew from high pressure steam, but the ubiquitous, aromatic (and delicious) brew I make with my [[ASIN:B000CNY6UK Bialetti 6800 Moka Express 6-Cup Stovetop Espresso Maker]].

The grind of this coffee is perfect for my moka pot, and the aroma it produces while brewing is heavenly. Comparing this (or other Cuban roasts) to European ones is like comparing apples to oranges. The European ones - and especially the Italian coffees - have a characteristic bitterness. That is one of the many reasons I love them. This is richer and smoother, though, and why I am drawn to this and other Cubans. In fact I would put this and [[ASIN:B004SVMAOG Cafe Pilon]] as my favorites, but this one seems to be even richer to my palate.

Frankly I am not going to choose - I will continue to enjoy this and the other ones I routinely brew because each has merit of their own. This one, though, is on my short list of excellent roasts. More importantly, if you use a moka pot the grind is ideal for that type of brewer.

title: Heavenly - with some caveats
text:
I'll get the caveats out of the way first. If you are a vegan you need to know that these delightful squares contain milk by-products. Or more accurately, 'may contain' them. The labeling is equivocal, but at least the warning is there. Also, if you have allergies to tree nuts (of which peanuts are NOT a member), they are included in the somewhat ambiguous warning too.

If you are not a vegan or have tree nut allergies you are in for a treat. These are dark, rich, bittersweet pieces of heaven to my palate. I enjoy them with a morning cup of espresso. I'll also confess that I indulge in one as a late night snack when I am struck by an overwhelming need for something sweet.

Nutritional values are sobering. One square has around 77 calories of which nearly 57 are from fat. Fat content is around 7 grams, of which four grams are saturated. Carbs per square are slightly more than 6 grams. I am not providing these numbers to discourage, but instead to let folks who are watching their intake know what's in store. Besides, anything this delicious has hidden costs, and, frankly, these are relatively healthy compared to some 'chocolates' sold as candy bars.

The bottom line is these are delicious, and if you watch your consumption actually has some health benefits from the relatively high cacao content, which can help suppress appetites if eaten in moderation. I, for one, will continue to enjoy a square with my morning espresso.

title: Excellent as a table or as a grating cheese
text:
I use this for both grating and as a table cheese - and especially as an accompaniment to some wines.

What I love is this is a piquant, salty cheese that adds a lot of flavor to any dish into which it's grated, and it makes an excellent salt substitute. More importantly this is essential for carbonara-style spaghetti dishes. I do not eat pork, which rules out spaghetti alla carbonara, bucatini all'Amatriciana and similar dishes, but a pasta with olive oil, a beaten egg and a copious amount of this cheese and black pepper is simple and superb.

As a table cheese the saltiness and sharpness are an excellent contrast to some fruits - especially melons, grapes and even figs. Those same qualities make it perfect with wines. A medium bodied Sangiovese goes perfectly, as will a white gavi with it's hints of pear.

A burning question that I am frequently asked is which is better: this or Parmigiano-Reggiano? Personally the Parmigiano-Reggiano is too valuable to use as a grating cheese. It's far better suited as a table cheese in my opinion. And it's nearly the polar opposite in flavor with a sweet nuttiness that is nothing like the sharp Pecorino Romano. And while both cheeses are deemed to be salty, the saltiness of the Parmigiano is significantly subdued in comparison.

Of course it all boils down to personal taste and I can envision dishes in which the Parmigiano would be better suited, but I still go for this cheese for grating.

Either way this is a wonderful cheese that will work with any dish that calls for grated cheese, as well as a delightful addition to a cheese and fruit plate.

title: Perfect for some sauces and soups
text:
While I normally use black or red pepper for seasoning this is essential for some dishes. Any dish that uses a lot of butter or a white or cream sauce is a candidate for this pepper as a seasoning.

First, the quality is excellent. This grind, like all Badia brand spices, is aromatic and fresh. It is not as good as freshly ground pepper corns, but I have not come across any white ones and depend on this spice for my country-style French onion soup.

Second, since I do not use this type of pepper often a 2 ounce container lasts a long time and the packaging does keep it relatively aromatic and fresh.

White pepper imparts a slightly different flavor than black pepper. It's more subtle and blends into white sauces from both a visual and flavor perspective better than black pepper.

Here is one recipe in which I use this, and it is typical of when this is a better choice than black pepper: French onion soup. Bear in mind that it's not Americanized, but does represent typical French country fare, which is hearty. I start with melting four ounces of unsalted butter in a soup pot. I next chop four medium size yellow onions and add it to the melted butter and cook uncovered on medium low for 90 minutes until the water in the onions has been cooked out and the onions caramelized. During this period I add a pinch of this white pepper and a pinch of sea salt. I occasionally stir and every 30 minutes add in a tablespoon of Chardonnay (sometimes I use sherry). After the onions are completely done I add 5 cups of water and bring to a boil for 1 minute, then simmer covered for ten minutes. I place toasted slices of baguettes in the serving bowls, ladle a serving of soup over them, then top with Gruyere cheese and bake until the cheese melts.

title: Pricey, but worth it for the pleasure
text:
Granted, personal tastes are as individual as snowflakes, but to me the added cost of these is worth it because not all sugars are created equal.

Until discovering these at a local international foods market I assumed that sugar cubes were all alike. How wrong I was.

Compared to the brand I had been using - [[ASIN:B0005Z7IAA Domino Sugar Cubes Dots]] - these are a little denser and imparts a slightly different flavor. I use them with espresso (rarely for me, but frequently for guests) and they have elicited remarks and questions about the sugar. This piqued my interest because I served the cubes in a dish and they looked like any other cubes. I did a side-by-side comparison and these did impart a slightly different flavor to the espresso.

They dissolve quickly, which is a big plus when serving it with Moscato d'Asti, which has a very gentle fizz.

If you are considering these and do not have a good pair of sugar tongs I recommend also checking out these [[ASIN:B0000CFTNR Stainless Steel Sugar Tongs]], which are perfect for serving the cubes.

title: Outstanding Cuban grind and roast
text:
While I have pretty much settled on [[ASIN:B001EQ5ERI Lavazza Caffe Espresso Ground Coffee]] as my daily coffee I also experiment (and always will). This one is so rich in flavor and aroma that I'm tempted to call it lush.

I grew up drinking Italian and other European roasts - all of which were designed for what are called moka pots (see [[ASIN:B000CNY6UK Bialetti 6800 Moka Express 6-Cup Stovetop Espresso Maker]]), and I have found that the European roasts tend towards a little bitterness. Not in a bad way, mind you, because that characteristic is one of many things that make such coffee a pleasure. Cuban roasts tend towards deep, rich flavors. I personally enjoy both, and this particular brand is perfect for my palate.

Since I use a moka pot that is pretty much the same as the one shown in the excellent video review on this page I cannot vouch for how suitable this grind is for regular drip pots. I am assuming that it's a bit too fine. However, with a moka style pot this grind is perfect.

Luckily I can get this from just about any local store that carries coffee, so not only is it readily available, it's also less expensive because there are no shipping charges. Like another reviewer, though, I think the quality of this coffee would warrant a premium price if you could not obtain it locally - assuming you love rich, strong coffee.

title: Another milestone in my quest for the daily grind
text:
Coffee is a passion, so I am forever experimenting for various grinds and roasts for my [[ASIN:B000CNY6UK Bialetti 6800 Moka Express 6-Cup Stovetop Espresso Maker]] (and my 12-cup model too!)

At the pinnacle - for me anyway - is [[ASIN:B001E5DYTE illy Ground Espresso Coffee, Fine Grind (Dark Roast, Black Band)]]. If I weren't on a fixed income my quest would be over. Sadly, I can only afford it on weekends and special occasions. This one, on the other hand, is perfect for daily brewing. It's rich, has a balance of both bitter and smoothness, and brews perfectly in my moka pot.

While I still experiment with various brands this has quickly become my 'house coffee' that I enjoy every morning. It is one of my favorite grinds and roasts from Lavezza for everyday use and competes nicely with some of the excellent Cuban coffees that are locally available. More importantly the price is more than reasonable.

title: My private reserve
text:
I do not drink this every day because I'd soon go broke. It's a private reserve that I save for weekend mornings or capping off an intimate dinner with special friends.

When I do indulge this is the perfect ground for the perfect espresso. I have tried Illy's [[ASIN:B000S75D66 Moka Ground Coffee]] that is supposed to be perfect for my [[ASIN:B000CNY6UK Bialetti 6800 Moka Express 6-Cup Stovetop Espresso Maker]], but it falls short. This one, though, has the perfect balance of bitterness and richness that I have come to expect since taking my first sip in Europe years ago. Frankly nothing else comes close as far as my palate is concerned.

If you are not used to authentic espresso, European style, you may not immediately discern why I (and others) rave about these grounds. Indeed, you may find it too bitter. The reason I am so passionate about this particular coffee and its grind is, first, how the aroma grabs me. Next, the bitterness that contains a wealth of complex, earthy nuances, and the overwhelming richness that is almost velvety.

As for the bitterness that puts off some folks, that can be cured with a single lump of sugar or - better - a dollop of anisette. Perhaps it's an acquired taste. I do know that if you discovered this wonderful coffee on a trip to Italy or France, and enjoyed it there, then you know that this is as good as gold and worth every penny.

Although I cannot afford to drink this every day on my fixed income, my life would be much the poorer if I did not have a stash as my private reserve.

title: These are guilty pleasures
text:
I serve these as a treat with espresso to guests (see my customer-supplied photo at the top of the page.) Of course there are many more reasons to enjoy them that that - but if I did not exercise self discipline I would be a diabetic by now!

The flavor is bitter sweet, but not overly bitter like chocolates with higher cocao content in the 80%-90% range. It's this combination of sweetness and bitterness that makes it a perfect complement to espresso (or any strong coffee.)

As some other reviewers pointed out, you need to be aware of what constitutes these squares. They not only contain milk byproducts, which rules out vegans, but according to the packaging may also contain tree nuts. That eliminates peanuts, which do not grow on trees, but if you have any other nut allergies you probably want to avoid these.

While the packaging claims four squares as a serving size I serve them singly because they are high in calories. Each square contains close to 53 calories (not bad, but consider a serving of four is 210 calories). Of those 53 calories approximately 38 are from fat. Total fat is 4 grams, 2.5 of which are saturated, and each square contains 6 grams of carbohydrates, 4 of which is sugar.

Don't me wrong, the nutritional values above are actually pretty modest for chocolate, but you should be aware of them if you have any dietary restrictions.

A word about dark chocolate: yes there are health benefits, but these bars are more a confection than a health aid. If you want chocolate for health purposes look for bars or squares with 85% or higher cocao content. Those contain less sugars and fats and do have benefits. If you are looking for a guilty pleasure that epitomizes the art of confectionery chocolate making this is it.

title: Sweet and refreshing
text:
Disclaimer: I get these locally, so am not going to delve into areas like how shipping costs make this expensive. My focus is on the product itself. Compared to the [[ASIN:B0075LIHUC San Pellegrino Aranciata Rossa (Blood Orange) Sparkling Water]], which is bitter (in a good way), this one is light and sweet. It's perfect on a hot humid day.

As noted by others this (and the rest of the juice flavored sparkling waters from San Pellegrino) have a high sugar and calorie content.
