At 140 calories and 32 grams of sugar this is not a drink you want to toss down one after another if you are watching your caloric or sugar intakes. Put another way, a 12 ounce can of Classic Coke contains less calories (90) and sugar (27 grams). I am saying this to show a stark comparison, not to promote Coke (which I do not drink at all.) Just be aware of the nutritional values and then enjoy a can when you want to treat yourself.

What I love is the flavors of Italy in the can. This has the sparkling mineral waters from Northern Italy's Lombardia region and the citrus of Sicily. To my palate it's a perfect combination.

See the photo that I uploaded at the top of this page and you will note the color. It's not artificially orange, but natural as though you used fresh oranges and a juicer to squeeze them. It's the natural look and flavor that keeps me addicted.

See the photo I uploaded at the top of this page for a visual of how the juice color is a natural, pale as though you extracted it from fresh oranges. No artificial orange coloring was used, which is a plus in my opinion.

title: Absolutely refreshing if you like grapefruit
text:
Combining the sparkling mineral waters from Northern Italy's Lombardia region with the citrus of Sicily is a marriage made in heaven. This is one of a number of flavors from San Pellegrino that is based on that combination.

Unlike the tart limonata and bitter aranciata rosso flavors, this one is smooth and subdued. In fact, there is a more subtle grapefruit flavor that is significantly less acidic than straight juice. That makes this particular sparkling fruit drink both refreshing on a hot, humid day, and a wonderful mixer for drinks that you would normally mix with grapefruit juice.

As much as I love this (and the other flavors) they are heavy in sugar and calories. So if you are controlling your sugar or caloric intake you need to be aware of the following: each 11.15 ounce can contains 150 calories and 35 grams of sugar. Considering that this is not an overly sweet drink the large amount of sugar is surprising. A 12 ounce can of Classic Coke contains less calories (90) and sugar (27 grams), but also contains sodium, which this sparkling juice does not. I am not advocating that you drink Classic Coke instead - I just want to graphically illustrate the nutritional values. One thing to remember is this product is all natural: juice and mineral water.

Despite the sugar content I still enjoy this and the other flavors offered by San Pellegrino - I just enjoy them sparingly. And there are always at least a dozen (or more) cans in my refrigerator to enjoy or serve to guests. It's one of my guilty pleasures.

title: Perfect for Italian moka makers and a great coffee
text:
In the Italian definition of espresso this is more a moka pot-style coffee than espresso, but that is indulging in semantics and not worth quibbling.

What is important is this is the perfect grind of coffee for my [[ASIN:B000CNY6UK Bialetti 6800 Moka Express 6-Cup Stovetop Espresso Maker]]. And grind is important for that style of maker. Equally important is the rich flavor and balanced acidity. The aroma while slow brewing in my moka maker is a treat as well.

To be honest I do hop around when it comes to brands, and am especially fond of some of the popular Cuban brands like Pilon and Bustelo, as well as some Italian ones. This one, however, is my favorite. It may be because I broke in my moka maker with this a long time ago and the flavor somehow lingered. Or simply that this one is perfect to my taste buds.

If you love rich, strong coffee give this a try. If you want to truly enhance the experience brew it in a moka maker.

title: One of my guilty pleasures
text:
I've become addicted to this slightly bitter mixture of the sparkling mineral water from Northern Italy's Lombardy region and the blood orange (aranciata rossa) from Sicily.

The problem is, at 140 calories per 11.15 ounce can (and a whopping 32 grams of sugar), I have to watch my intake. If you are watching either calorie and/or sugar values of what you consume this is one to occasionally enjoy. The real irony is I am attracted by the bitterness which is predominate despite the high sugar content.

I will admit that this is refreshing, and especially so on a humid Florida day. However, since it is a guilty pleasure I have a ritual in which I serve mine in a fancy [[ASIN:B007JBR5K6 flute]] to remind myself that enjoying one is a special occasion to be savored.

In a perfect world I could drink as many as I wanted with no adverse affects. Alas, I do not live in such a world - but mine is made a little brighter when I have one of these.

title: Excellent value for a quality cut and grade of cheese
text:
Although the description claims that this is a 'top grade' it's actually mid-grade and because of its 18-20 month aging period. Technically it's vecchio grade, which is a step above the minimum aging requirements per Italian law, but not quite aged sufficiently to qualify for the top grade called [[ASIN:B001LM0ZY2 Parmigiano Reggiano Stravecchio]].

That said, this is one of the best values in Parmigiano Reggiano - outside of Italy - that I have come across. The grade is unquestionably good, and the extra aging for vecchio cheeses makes this one impart a nuttier flavor than the younger ones, but still more piquant than the older stravecchio grade.

I almost never use Parmigiano Reggiano as a grating cheese, unless I am topping a soup with it - and then I grate sparingly. For me this is mainly a table cheese. I also love pairing it with equally complex wines such as amarone or barolo (although I also enjoy it with a much lighter and simpler sangiovese such as a [[ASIN:B0062TZOPY 2010 Antinori Santa Cristina Sangiovese Toscana]]).

This is an ideal cheese for any cheese and fruit platter because it pairs nicely with red and green grapes, figs, pears and even citrus.

The rind is also useful for adding to the soffritto when you are making soups, and especially the hearty ones like pasta e fagioli.

Bottom line is this is an excellent grade of Parmigiano Reggiano at a bargain price (even when shipping is factored into the overall cost.)

title: Essential for French onion soup and melting
text:
This is a firm and dense cheese that is slightly more piquant than [[ASIN:B005NMTAYC Raclette]], but has a more pleasant aroma when preparing it. This particular one - cave-aged - seems to be slightly drier and less piquant than others I have tried.

Most folks use this cheese for either fondues or as a topping on French onion soup. I am not a fondue person, but I do love authentic, country-style French onion soup and this is the only cheese I deem worthy of topping it. See the customer-supplied photos at the top of this page for some photos that I have uploaded.

Nutritionally this cheese will make your cardiologist go crazy. For one thing, a little over two ounces - a quantity that is perfect for topping the baguette in a bowl of French onion soup - contains the following: 272 calories of which 190 are from fat. Speaking of fat, the two ounce serving contains 21 grams, 12 of which are saturated. Add in 73mg of cholesterol and 222mg of sodium and you have a cheese that is a guilty pleasure. Indeed, that describes it because it is one of my true pleasures in like, but I only have it on special occasions.

Regardless of the nutritional values, this cheese is the key ingredient of my recipe for French onion soup. Bear in mind that it's not Americanized, but does represent typical French country fare, which is hearty. I start with melting four ounces of unsalted butter in a soup pot. I next chop four medium size yellow onions and add it to the melted butter and cook uncovered on medium low for 90 minutes until the water in the onions has been cooked out and the onions caramelized. During this period I do grind in some black pepper and a pinch of sea salt. I occasionally stir and every 30 minutes add in a tablespoon of Chardonnay (sometimes I use sherry). After the onions are completely done I add 5 cups of water and bring to a boil for 1 minute, then simmer covered for ten minutes. I place toasted slices of baguettes in the serving bowls, ladle a serving of soup over them, then top with this cheese and bake until the cheese melts. I somethings use a [[ASIN:B005009WDQ raclette grill]] to melt the cheese and then pour it over the soup and serve.

This particular cheese is of the highest quality and is an example of a great cut of Gruyere. It has many uses and will work perfectly in any recipe that calls for a melted-cheese topping, as well as fondues.

title: Uniquely Sardinian and exquisitely delicious
text:
It's probably silly to wax enthusiastic over little semolina balls that are both a pasta and a couscous depending on your perspective. However, both the shape and flavor make this one of my favorites, and especially as a substitute for rice or more traditional pasta shapes when I am serving seafood.

Nutritionally there are about 8 servings to a bag. Each is 190 calories and 41 grams of carbs, which is standard for most semolina-based pastas.

Cooking time is ten minutes for al dente firmness. Unlike most couscous you need to drain this after it's been cooked, and I recommend a mesh type colander because the tiny balls can slip through the holes in some colanders.

This is a versatile ingredient in that you can make cold salads or hot dishes with it. I use it to make a side for steamed shellfish using this recipe: chop a half cup each of fresh basil and mint, finely chop spring onions (a small bunch will do) and set aside. After the fregola has been cooked, mix the chopped herbs and 1/3 cup of extra virgin olive oil into the fregola, squeeze the juice from a large lemon and mix that in. I also sprinkle about 3/4 of a teaspoon of [[ASIN:B00AQ3B4U6 Bottarga Di Muggine]] in lieu of salt to give it an authentic Sardinian flavor, plus a pinch of black pepper. Sometimes I add some high-quality capers like [[ASIN:B004T345GO Mediterranean Organic Wild Capers]], which needs to be rinsed of brine before adding if you do use them. Serve with the steamed shellfish by adding some sliced tomatoes as a second side and you have a perfect summer meal.

title: A taste of Sardninia
text:
This is one of two major pasta types associated with Sardinia. The cuisine of that beautiful island is truly ancient. The other is an interesting type of couscous called Fregula Sarda.

In the strictest sense this is a gnocchi. Indeed, it;s also known as gnocchi Sardi. One interesting characteristic is the shape, which is like a small closed shell. The slit in the pasta collects sauces, and herbs adhere to the ridges on the outside of the shape. Taste-wise it is slightly different than any other high-quality pasta made from pure semolina. However, when prepared in the traditional Sardinian manner by flavoring it with saffron, it becomes a culinary experience. As a side note this is the saffron I normally purchase because of its high quality and reasonable price: [[ASIN:B0042ZF6B2 Iranian Saffron]]

While the slight saffron flavoring truly sets this pasta apart from all others, it's the shape that I find interesting. Aside from the functional aspects of the shape that I described about, it makes for a somewhat weighty dish because of the thickness of each piece, and, of course, visually it clearly associates your dish with Sardinia.

One recipe that perfectly complements this pasta that I love is: brown shallots or onions in high quality olive oil, add fresh tuna and braise on all sides. Then add capers and chopped tomatoes. Toss into this pasta, season with grated [[ASIN:B00AQ3B4U6 Bottarga Di Muggine]] and serve. Usually the bottarga is sufficiently salty to preclude adding salt, but I do season mine with a little black pepper and red pepper flakes. This is not only authentic Sardinia fare, but it's fast and easy to make and delicious.

Nutritionally there are about eight servings to a bag, and the calorie count is 200 with 42 grams of carbohydrates. This is standard for just about any brand of pasta made from 100% semolina.

I do not often make this type of pasta, but on the occasions when I want to make the recipe cited above (or a handful of other Sardinian dishes) this is the only type I use. As for brands, this one is locally available and is high quality.

title: Perfect for laying out spreads and raclette
text:
Regardless of whether you call it antipasti, meze, tapas or hors d'oeuvres these cocktail onions have a place among the olives, cheeses, dried meats and dips and spreads.

Also, along with new potatoes and gherkins, these are essential for serving [[ASIN:B005NMTAYC Raclette]], which is popular among the Swiss and French. Melting that cheese over these and the other ingredients produces an almost decadent tasting experience that is true comfort food to my palate.

What I love about this brand and these particular onions are their flavor, texture and low calorie count. There are 8 five-piece servings per jar, with each serving coming in at a scant 5 calories. On the other hand, you need to be aware that each serving also contains 300mg of sodium. There is no cholesterol, so that is a plus.

These are indispensable for laying out spreads - especially for Mediterranean style appetizers - and go with just about any cuisine or culture. I am loyal to the Mezzetta brand because their products are not only consistent in quality, but have been readily available in just about every state and city in which I've worked, lived or visited.

title: A Swiss tradition and a wonderful melting cheese
text:
I only discovered this cheese and how to prepare and serve it less than a week ago when a friend came over with an [[ASIN:B005009WDQ Indoor Electric Raclette Grill]] and a sizable piece of this cheese.

She prepared it with steamed new potatoes seasoned with paprika and used the coupelles (the small, wedge shaped pans that came with the grill) to heat the cheese and then pour it over the potatoes. I loved both the process and the flavor and aroma of the dish. Not so my friend who brought the cheese over, nor another friend who was visiting. They loved the taste, but hated the aroma (they called it an odor) of the cheese as it was being cut and cooked. I found it savory, so be aware that in the very unscientific poll at my house 2/3s thought the cheese was smelly. Of course 100 percent found it to be delicious.

About the cheese and flavor: this is a wonderful melting cheese that is as good as Gruyere for melting, but this one has a distinctive flavor. I detected a little nuttiness to the taste. It is supposed to be served with white wine (or even tea), but never water according to my friend. She had a sparkling wine - Moscato d'Asti - and I enjoyed my plate with a Beaujolais-Villages, which is the closest I will get to a white wine. Perfect in my opinion.

Since I was gifted the grill my forays into the more traditional ways of serving this cheese, which includes over pickled cocktail onions (superb), gherkins (I did not care for it), and if ever I have guests again I will try it with an assortment of dry Italian sausages and meats. I am a vegetarian so I will forgo those.

If you love melting type cheeses and want to try a Swiss favorite that is also popular in France, this is a 'must try'. If you already know about raclette, this is a quality piece of the cheese that you will not regret buying.

title: If you love Parmigiano Reggiano you will probably love this
text:
A few notes about this cheese. (1) This is not the domestic asiago that you find in the dairy section at your grocery store. There is no comparison. (2) There are various grades of Asiago d'Allevo: the youngest is called Asiago Mezzano, this one is called Asiago Vecchio and the oldest aged grade is Asiago Stravecchio. I love the way the brand named this oro del tempo, which means golden age because this grade has developed beyond the younger Mezzano, but has not yet evolved into the very bitter and granular Stravecchio that is truly an acquired taste.

This grade is just beginning to acquire a slightly bitter taste, and also the texture is starting to resemble that of Parmigiano Reggiano, but there is still a smoothness to it.

Compared to Parmigiano Reggiano this is a sharper cheese with some hints of the nutty flavor of a 12-month old Parmigiano Reggiano. While both make excellent table cheeses and both are wonderful grated, that is where the similarity ends.

Asiago Mezzano - this grade of Asiago d'Allevo - also makes a wonderful melting cheese, and when serving cheese and fruit this makes a great addition to the cheeses that you may want to lay out because its bitter notes contrast well with sweet fruits. While many folks recommend pairing this with a white wine I am too old school for that - I love this with a non-intrusive wine like sangiovese that allows the complex flavors to dominate. If you insist on a white wine why not try a Beaujolais, which is a white wine that happens to be red (some wine guru said that and I have to agree). A good vin de pays grade of Beaujolais, such as Beaujolais-Villages, is a perfect match in my opinion.

I love this grated into soups and light pasta dishes, or for 'dusting' foccacia. However you use it, I think you will be impressed by this particular grade and brand because it's light years away from the domestic asiago cheeses.

title: Essential for pasta e fagioli (a.k.a. pasta fazool)
text:
For some soups I use [[ASIN:B005W0Q7GO Barilla Pastina Pasta]] or the more traditional shaped [[ASIN:B001871AQC DaVinci Pasta Soup Cuts, Acini Di Pepe]], but for heartier soups like pasta e fagioli this is the pasta shape to use. Pasta e fagioli means pasta and beans in standard Italian, but it's also known as pasta fazool (sometimes spelled fazul) in southern dialects like Neapolitan. Regardless of how you pronounce it, the dish is a mainstay of Italian cuisine and is perfect for cold days.

I personally prefer Barilla brand pastas because they are consistent. What I mean is any batch cooks to the same level of firmness assuming identical cooking times as the last. This is truly a pasta that you can time to yield a perfect al dente firmness, which is important in soups because they tend to get reheated a number of times.

In the customer-supplied images at the top of this page I've provided a photo of how my own recipe for Pasta e fagioli turns out. The recipe itself is relatively simple and quick to make. The vegan version is: saute garlic and finely chopped onion, carrots and celery in extra virgin olive oil until they are semi-soft, then add six cups of water and bring to a boil adding in spinach and arugula.

Once the greens are reduced I add crushed tomatoes and ditalini, reduce to medium heat and continue for ten minutes.

Finally I add in cannellini beans and chopped tomatoes, season with a pinch of sea salt and black pepper and oregano to taste. I simmer for twenty minutes more and serve.

If you substitute grated Parmigiano-Reggiano cheese for the sea salt you have a vegetarian version of the dish that is a little more friendly to those who need to watch their sodium intake. Another way to serve this is with a touch of Sardinian flavor, although it is not strictly vegetarian: substitute [[ASIN:B00AQ3B4U6 Bottarga Di Muggine (Grey Mullet Roe)]] or the more distinctive flavored [[ASIN:B00AQ3D2QU Bottarga Di Tuna (Tuna Roe)]] for the sea salt or Parmigiano-Reggiano cheese.

If you manage nutrition, the box contains approximately eight 200 calorie servings. Each serving contains 42 grams of carbs. A serving also contains a gram of fat. On the plus side there is zero cholesterol or sodium, and there is a decent amount of vitamins and minerals per serving: 10% iron, 35% thiamin, 15% riboflavin, 15% niacin and 30% folic acid of recommended daily requirements. Each serving also contains 7 grams of protein.

title: My favorite pasta shape
text:
Since I eat a lot of vegetarian sauces this shape is perfect. Technically this particular shape is called penne rigate because it has ridges. The tubes will accumulate sauce and pieces of vegetables, and the ridges on this shape also hold lighter particles of spices such as fresh basil as well as sauce. This allows you to prepare a pasta that is not drowning in a sea of sauce, but not dry either.

Although I make vegetable-based sauces, the shapes are equally perfect for meat sauces. They also are very sturdy, making them a good choice for pasta dishes with heavier sauces that are laden with larger pieces of meat or vegetables.

To best illustrate how well this shape works with sauces I have uploaded a photo in the customer-supplied images at the top of this page. You can clearly see from the photo how beautifully the sauce coats and clings to the pasta, and also how easy it is to make a quick dinner since I also provided an ingredient list.

If you are counting calories or carbs be aware that the box contains approximately eight 200 calorie servings. Each serving contains 42 grams of carbs. A serving also contains a gram of fat. On the plus side there is zero cholesterol or sodium, and there is a decent amount of vitamins and minerals per serving: 10% iron, 35% thiamin, 15% riboflavin, 15% niacin and 30% folic acid of recommended daily requirements. Each serving also contains 7 grams of protein.

Buon appetito!

title: A quality semolina pasta
text:
A few disclosures first: this is readily available locally, which is where I normally purchase this product. Also my preferred brand is Barilla. However, I prefer the more traditional shape of this brand than the star-shaped style that Barilla sells when I am making certain soups. Acini de pepe is Italian for peppercorns. This style of pasta is sometimes called pastina (little pasta).

The soups I make with this style are typically clear or semi clear broth types where I want the texture of the semolina pasta, but not necessarily the thickening that Barilla's star shape style will impart. One recipe in which I use this is to chop a leek, carrots and celery and saute them in extra virgin olive oil until they are soft. I then slice five or six pieces of Parmigiano-Reggiano cheese rind in 2 inch pieces about 1/16th inch thick. As a side note, the safest tool for cutting such thin pieces of the rind is a [[ASIN:B001WSL66Q Boska Holland 5.91 Inch Dutch Cheese Knife for Semi Hard and Hard Cheese]]. After that I quickly saute the rind in the vegetable mix until it softens, and then add two quarts of water to the mix and bring it to a boil. I next add a fresh leafy vegetable - usually arugula to impart a slight touch of bitterness - and continue the boil until the leaves have wilted into the water. Finally I add a half bag of the acini de pepe and continue boiling uncovered for 6 minutes. If you substitute chicken for the rinds this recipe makes a relatively tasty chicken soup.

I usually top the soup with ground mixed peppercorns like from a [[ASIN:B005VHFRV4 Mccormick Peppercorn Medley Grinder]] and grated Parmigiano-Reggiano cheese. Served with a baguette topped with bruschetta will provide a healthy, light and easy to prepare meal.

Nutritionally there are eight 210 calorie servings in a bag, each of which contains 43 grams of carbs and a gram of fat. So if you are on a diet that restricts carbohydrates or caps your daily intake of calories do be aware of these facts. There are some pluses though. Each serving provides the following percentages of of vitamins and minerals: 10% iron, 35% thiamin, 15% riboflavin, 15% niacin and 35% folic acid of recommended daily requirements. Each serving also contains 6 grams of protein.

This is a high quality pasta made with 100% semolina and is perfect for any recipe that requires traditional shaped acini de pepe.

title: A real star in soup recipes
text:
This small pasta also goes by the name acini de pepe (Italian for peppercorn) and is a great way to thicken home made soups or even as the main ingredient for a soup. While most acini de pepe is shaped like tiny little tubes, these are star shaped.

My favorite use is in most clear broth type soups - a few ounces added early will boil down and thicken the broth into a hearty soup that is perfect for a cold day. It's also indispensable for making Italian Wedding Soup. My favorite recipe, though, is a simple, yet tasty soup that features this as the main ingredient: I start by sauteing finely chopped carrots, celery and shallots in extra virgin olive oil until they begin to soften, then adding whole garlic cloves and browning them. I next add two quarts of water and 12-16 ounces of fresh spinach and bring the mixture to a boil. Finally, I add the contents of this box and continue for 10 minutes (the instructions on the box recommend 6 minutes, but I go longer to dissolve some of the semolina to thicken the soup.) The result is a soupy pasta dish that is easy to digest, packed with vitamins and quick to make. Salt and pepper to taste, and even better: grate some Parmigiano-Reggiano cheese in lieu of salt. Or a pinch of grated [[ASIN:B00AQ3B4U6 Bottarga Di Muggine]] for a taste of Sardinia.

Nutritionally a box contains eight 200-calorie servings, so be aware that using the entire box is going to add 1600 calories to whatever dish you are preparing. Moreover, each serving contains 42 grams of carbohydrates. On the plus side there is zero cholesterol or sodium, and there is a decent amount of vitamins and minerals per serving: 10% iron, 35% thiamin, 15% riboflavin, 15% niacin and 30% folic acid of recommended daily requirements. Each serving also contains 7 grams of protein.

I am loyal to Barilla brand because I love the quality of their products. However, if you prefer the more traditional acini de pepe shape, especially for salads, you may want to check out [[ASIN:B006K3SHL0 Da Vinci Acini Di Pepe]], which I also use when my local grocery store is out of stock of Barilla.

title: Consistent quality and a perfect shape for some dishes
text:
Know up front that I only use Barilla brand for pastas because it has been both consistent and repeatable. What I mean by that is if you prepare pasta by boiling for 11 minutes (in the case of this particular shape) it will come out with the same al dente firmness that it did the last time you made it. I have been using this brand for well over twenty-five years and if I use the same time settings for a specific pasta shape it comes out the same every time. Of course that is assuming I am not doing this in some high-altitude location which does require that you adjust the times.

Using this shape is not a haphazard choice. Farfalle (means butterflies in Italian) is perfect for tomato- and cream-based sauces because the ridges catch and retain the sauces. Also, this shape is good for pastas that contain heavier pieces of vegetables, such as rustica, or pieces of meat or fish. This is because not only will the ridges catch and retain the sauce, but they also reinforce the strength of the pasta.

I've included a customer-supplied photo at the top of this page that depicts one of the many variations of rustica that I make with this pasta. However, it goes best with a rich cream sauce. Here is my recipe:

SAUCE: melt three tablespoons of butter and heat until it clarifies, then mix in two and a half tablespoons of this flour and whisk until it's even. Next I add two cups of light cream and four tablespoons of finely grated Parmigiano-Reggiano cheese (the real thing, not imitations like parmesan). A little white pepper, sea salt and a pinch of nutmeg and you have a white sauce to die for - and this flour is the key because of how well it mixes into the butter.

PASTA: cook per directions (they call for boiling for 11 minutes for al dente firmness - I use 10 1/2 minutes). After the pasta is cooked, immediately and thoroughly drain and DO NOT run cold water over it. Place it back into the pot in which it was boiled and immediately mix in a half pound of fresh spinach and toss into the pasta. Let sit for three minutes - the heat of the pasta will semi-cook the spinach. Mix in the cream sauce and serve.

Of course, the above recipe can be varied by adding different sauteed or steamed vegetables.

A word about nutritional values: like all pastas this is high in carbs, so consequently is also high in calories. Not that the cream sauce recipe helps things right? The box contains approximately eight 200 calorie servings. Each serving contains 42 grams of carbs. A serving also contains a gram of fat. On the plus side, there is zero sodium or cholesterol.

I am and always will be loyal to this brand for the reasons I cited above. Since I often cook the types of dishes this pasta shape is perfect for I always have a few boxes in my pantry.

title: Top quality for a number of recipes
text:
First let me agree with every review that has extolled the virtues of this flour for making perfect pizza crusts. It proves that all flour is not created equal because this one makes consistently perfect crusts.

Pizza aside, I use it most for making focaccia. Here I use the standard pizza dough recipe of yeast, water, flour and olive oil, but I also whip an egg into the mixture. This makes a perfect focaccia every time.

Another use (and I hope my cardiologist is not reading this) is for making cream sauces for pasta in which I melt three tablespoons of butter and heat until it clarifies, then mix in two and a half tablespoons of this flour and whisk until it's even. Next I add two cups of light cream and four tablespoons of finely grated Parmigiano-Reggiano cheese (the real thing, not imitations like parmesan). A little white pepper, sea salt and a pinch of nutmeg and you have a white sauce to die for - and this flour is the key because of how well it mixes into the butter.

Regardless of how you use it, this is one of the finest grades of flour I have come across. Since the key to Italian cooking is to use only the finest ingredients, you can be assured that this flour meets that criteria.

title: Exceptional quality
text:
I am fortunate in that this (and other products from the Ducktrap brand) are readily available from my local grocery.

What I love about this smoked salmon is there are no added preservatives. In fact, except for salt used as part of the smoking process and some spices there is nothing that is artificial. More important to me is this salmon is gluten-free.

Another factor that makes me loyal to this brand is their smoking process does not mask the natural flavor of the salmon. In addition, the color and texture is - to me - perfect and adds greatly to the dining experience.

Finally, the packaging is convenient and will keep the salmon fresh if you only use a portion of the salmon. This is a big plus for folks like myself who live alone and do not consume a whole package at a single meal.

Although everyone has their own serving and recipe ideas I have provided a photo of my favorite way to serve smoke salmon when I am not enjoying it the traditional way on a bagel with creamed cheese. I hope that sparks ideas.

title: Perfect for cheese tastings
text:
When I am enjoying cheese I prefer it with bread - there is nothing like a baguette, or tearing off a piece of French, Italian, Cubano or Puerto Rican bread to pair with an excellent cheese and a well chosen wine.

However, bread can quickly become filling at cheese tastings, so I prefer crackers. Of course you want a cracker that does not compete with the cheese (or wine). These crackers are light and neutral enough to use with even the mildest cheeses and still savor the flavors.

Although these are not as filling as bread they can contribute to pounds because they are deceptively high in calories. Four crackers is considered a serving, which is 60 calories (and nine of those calories are from fat.) Carbs per serving is 12 grams and sodium is a manageable 40mg. I suppose if you are tasting some of the double- and triple-creamed cheeses like Saint Agur or a nice brie the nutritional figures for the crackers pale in comparison. However, for folks who have dietary restrictions these figures are useful.

Another characteristic of these crackers is they are sturdy enough to spread some of the denser creamed cheeses on without breaking.

I am fortunate in that these are readily available locally, so that saves me in costs and worry about them arriving broken. I will say that I've never had an issue with freshness and have come to prefer these crackers for tastings for all of the reasons cited.

title: A treat for salmon lovers
text:
I first discovered Copper River salmon when I worked on a consulting assignment and tried some at a great little fish place in Kirkland, WA. I was hooked (no pun intended). Much to my chagrin I discovered that the season for this particular species was less than a month and, worse, most of the catch went to eager buyers in the Pacific Northwest.

Fast forward: my wife found out about my addiction and each birthday for years would treat me to this exact package. It's not as good as fresh, but well worth it if your palate can detect the nuances of this fish.

The ingredients are fairly simple: salmon with a little sea salt. The flavor is incredible, and while I prefer fresh, the smoking is even, does not mask the Copper River flavor that is unique to this fish, and the fish itself is succulent.

If you've tried Copper River salmon, then you will enjoy this. If you are new to it, this is the second best thing to fresh and it's always available.

title: This is the gold standard in paste tomatoes
text:
A large amount of San Marzano tomato production goes to producing world class tomato paste. Cans like this fortunately escape that fate. The good fortune comes from the fact that these plum tomatoes are superb in sauces, are preferable to my palate to fresh, vine-ripened domestic tomatoes that you can buy in a supermarket. When I am making a sauce or any dish that calls for tomatoes these are what I use.

What I have found is not all San Marzano tomatoes are created equal. For one thing there can be deceptive labeling such as 'San Marzano' style tomatoes, or the same species of tomato from a different country. The real thing has the D.O.P. designation, which indicates that they are authentic. Also, under Italian law only the real thing can bear the following designation: Pomodoro S. Marzano dell'Agro Sarnese-Nocerino. These tomatoes have both markings on the can, and as importantly, are of the highest quality.

The tomatoes are technically a species of plum tomatoes like the common roma species, but have a different texture. Also, they are somewhat less sweet than the more common roma. Interestingly, your taste buds seem to remember the flavor and aroma of high quality San Marzano tomatoes like these, which renders all other tomatoes - including even the highest quality roma - second rate. Or that is the case with me.

Frankly, I have tried other brands of this tomato that share the D.O.P. designation and they have all fallen short in flavor and texture, so if you are going to invest in the best this is the brand that I recommend. Also, the price is not bad, even with the high shipping rate. I still recommend that you try to source them locally if possible since cans can become dented in shipping. Otherwise, this is a bargain and this particular brand is among the best available in my experience.

title: Good value and reasonable quality
text:
This is a denser, richer paste than what you normally get from cans, including a similar product from the same brand: [[ASIN:B0005ZH9XG Cento Tomato Paste]]. The key reason is this paste is double concentrated.

It's much thicker than most canned pastes, and allows you to control the thickness of sauces by using all or a portion of the paste in this tube. In fact, the slight more than 4.5 ounces in this tube is about the equivalent of two six ounce cans of the thinner, single-concentrate pastes like the one linked to above.

While the only two ingredients in this tube are tomato and salt, this paste has a sweetness that comes from high-quality tomatoes.

For people like myself who need to watch nutritional values, a tube of this paste is about 140 calories and contains about 260mg of sodium. There is no fat or cholesterol, but it does contain a little less than 30 grams of carbs and 16 grams of sugars (natural).

Aside from the denser paste that this tube provides, it has another advantage in that if you do not use the whole tube you can recap it and refrigerate it.

If you normally use canned paste, give this a try - for thick, rich sauces it cannot be beat.

title: Essential for Sardinian cuisine (as well as a secret ingredient for other recipes)
text:
I only recently discovered the joys of Bottarga when I started using the tuna roe version in some of my recipes. That style of roe proved to be a little too bitter for some palates, so I gave this one a try.

Frankly I prefer the tuna roe (I use the same brand: [[ASIN:B00AQ3D2QU Bottarga Di Tuna (Tuna Roe)]], but this one has has a lot of merit as well. Especially when grated into salads or as a substitute for anchovies in some recipes like spaghetti alla puttanesca or spaghetti con aglio e olio (spaghetti with garlic and oil.) Especially in salads or in spaghetti alla puttanesca the tuna roe version does not marry well with the other ingredients and can mask flavors if you are not careful. This roe, on the other hand, seems to go perfectly with those dishes.

First rule of using this or any bottarga: do NOT cook with it. Instead grate it over a finished dish before serving in much the same way you would a fine, hard cheese. I learned the hard way that cooking it into a recipe guarantees you will have a salty, bitter dish that only a Klingon would enjoy.

When I was researching this product I learned that Cabras, Sardinia is renowned for their high quality bottarga, and it shows in the quality. In the process I also came across a recipe that proved to be delicious beyond my imagination and is now fare that I serve guests whom I really want to impress: brown shallots or onions in high quality olive oil, add fresh tuna and braise on all sides. Then add capers and chopped tomatoes. Salt to taste (I also use black and red pepper). Toss into an authentic Sardinia pasta like [[ASIN:B005R3Z1PO La Casa del Grano Pasta - Is Malloreddus]] (also known as gnocchetti Sardi), season with this grated bottarga di muggine and serve. This is not only authentic Sardinia fare, but it's fast and easy to make and delicious.

Compared to a slab of bottarga di muggine this jar is more convenient because you do not have to shave it since it's pre-grated. Since I do not use this all of the time the jar is perfect.

Experiment and add a dash over savory dishes and you may discover some recipe secrets that you can either share or jealously guard.

title: One of the higher quality brands that is a constant in my kitchen
text:
Anchovies are common ingredients in Mediterranean dishes, but are especially valued in Spanish cuisine. Ortiz is a Spanish company that I have come to trust for quality, and fortunately can purchase these locally for a fraction of the price and no insane shipping costs. Still, I am so sold on this brand and product that I would probably be coerced in paying whatever I had to to get them.

What sets these apart from the slimy, salt laden anchovies that wind up on pizzas is they are packed in oil. The cheaper anchovies that send a lot of people running are packed in salt and are way too salty (and, frankly, gross in my opinion). These, on the other hand, are mild in flavor, slightly salty, and have a wonderful texture.

It is this grade of anchovy that I use in Caesar salads, and use as a base for dishes like spaghetti con aglio e olio (spaghetti with garlic and oil) and other dishes. It is also an essential ingredient in my spaghetti alla puttanesca recipe. Indeed, since in that dish I use expensive San Marzano tomatoes, and the highest quality capers (like [[ASIN:B004T345GO Non-Pareil Wild Capers]]), along with garlic and a quality olive oil, it does not make sense to use anything but high quality anchovies like these.

As I said, these are not overly salty and not at all slimy compared to some of the cheaper brands and all that are packed in salt instead of oil. The flavor is totally different from those that you find on pizza. But what I really love about these is the fact that they are packed in a jar instead of a can. Since I use them for bases and in moderation in the dishes mentioned above, a small amount goes a long way. When I was buying them in cans I would toss the unused ones - often half a can - but here I can take a few strips and reseal the jar and refrigerate it. These are good for about six months after opening, so you will not be wasting high quality filets that you may not use up in a recipe.

These do not disappoint and are worth every penny if you want to use nothing but the best ingredients in your dishes.

title: Pricey, but worth it
text:
At slightly less than four ounces this is an expensive can of tuna. On the other hand, it is a premium cut from one of the top grades of tuna. Since I purchase mine locally (about the same price as here, but without the exorbitant shipping cost) a can is indeed worth it in my opinion.

Describing the taste to someone who has never tried the ventresca cut from a solid piece of yellowfin tuna is difficult. If you love high-grade tuna I am reasonably sure you will love this. It's succulent, flavorful and delicate. Even the texture is superior.

This is a step down from the more prized (and expensive) [[ASIN:B004OHGOY6 Ortiz Ventresca White Tuna Belly in Oil]], which is from the same cut, but from albacore tuna. That is not to say that this is inferior - it's anything but! I will say that you have to have a well developed palate to appreciate the differences between the two, and when you objectively compare the cost versus the pleasure you will find that this yellowfin is a viable alternative. That said, I think that if you like this one you owe it to yourself to also experience the other.

I've been babbling a bit about cuts and grades. Here is what I am talking about: the particular cut is called ventresca and is from the choicest part of the fish. To Spanish consumers who are very particular about these things (and rightfully so), this term alerts the consumer that this is a cut from the tender belly area of the fish. Grading the tuna is done by species. bonita del norte (the expensive one I mentioned above) is at the top of the tier and is what we commonly call albacore in English. The grade in this can is the next down and known as claro (yellowfin in English.) It's still a quality species and is highly valued. All other species are lumped into 'rojo' (red).

When I am entertaining and put out tapas (snacks) this is the one I use and guests rave about it. I reserve the more expensive one I mentioned above for pampering myself and special occasions. But back to this one: if you can purchase it with better shipping terms or locally I am confident that you will know why a small can of tuna can cost nearly ten bucks because it's exquisite.

title: The holy grail of tuna
text:
There is no tuna (to my palate) that comes close to a ventresca cut from a quality piece of bonita. It simply has to be experienced to make a believer out of most. This brand, cut and grade of tuna are my favorites and combine to be one of my pleasures in life.

This is the pinnacle of tuna and the top tier of Spanish grades of both cut and tuna species. As for the cut, it is from the choicest part of the fish and accounts for the term 'ventresca', which alerts the consumer that this is a cut from the tender belly area of the fish. This term works with lesser grades of tuna as well, including [[ASIN:B001LMKG5K Ortiz Spain El Velero Yellowfin Ventresca De Atun Claro]]. Indeed, the cut is what sets this apart. Even a ventresca cut from a lesser grade, such as the bottom rung rojo grade, would be a delicacy (though I doubt that any canning company would even bother with that since the difference between the two top grades and rojo is vast.)

Grading the tuna is done by species. This one is at the top of the tier and is what we commonly call albacore in English. The next down and still highly valued is the claro grade known as yellowfin in English. All other species are lumped into 'rojo' (red).

So, when you add the fact that the fish grade used in this product is top tier, with the fact that the cut is from the most desirable part of the fish you have something special. Add in that Ortiz is a quality brand and this becomes a real treat that you can set out for tapas when entertaining guests. And I guarantee that it will be quickly consumed. Personally, when entertaining any group larger than two I use the less expensive yellowfin I cited above. For special occasions, more intimate settings or when I am in the mood to pamper myself I use this one though.

If you love tuna and want to see what the hoopla is about it's worth the price to try at least one can. Beware, though, of liking it too much because it can become an expensive addiction.

title: Tasty source of dietary fiber
text:
After reading over some of the complaints about this product I am somewhat puzzled. I have been purchasing this brand for some time and have experienced nothing but consistent quality. Perhaps because I am buying locally I am not getting a product that has exceeded its shelf life. Regardless, the figlets have always been sweet, soft and free of any dirt or other impurities. I will say that the stems, which are a natural part of this dried fruit, are a little tough.

I am a vegetarian who carefully watches what I eat, so I pay close attention to nutrition facts. Each 8 ounce bag contains a total of 550 calories (five 110 calorie servings), so snacking through a whole bag of these could wind up becoming a big portion of your daily caloric intake if you are managing calories. Also, at 26 grams of carbs per serving you are looking a whopping 130 grams if you eat a whole bag in a day. Frankly, I have done just that more than once because they are delicious. Each serving contains 20 grams of natural sugars too. In fact, aside from potassium sorbate that has been added as a preservative, the figs are natural.

On the plus side, there is zero cholesterol, sodium or fats. Additional benefits include 5 grams of dietary fiber per serving, as well as 1 gram of protein. Vitamin and mineral benefits as a percentage of daily values are: calcium, iron, magnesium, and vitamin B6: 6% each, and 8% of copper.

Aside from fresh figs when they are in season, these are the figs I consume and are a regular part of my diet. When I am craving something sweet I grab a few (and they go very well with some cheeses too). Just be aware of the calorie and carbohydrate values because what can be a healthy snack can, in fact, wreck a diet if not consumed in moderation.

title: Not bad for a caponata out of a jar!
text:
While I love fried eggplant products like [[ASIN:B000H7F5J2 Galil Fried Eggplant]] I also enjoy caponada. I usually make mine from scratch, but I have never succeeded in correctly making it Sicilian style. Incredibly this one has that distinctive Sicilian flavor and is a real treat.

About the flavor - there is something about Sicilian fare that sets it apart from other Mediterranean cuisine. It has ineffable flavors from spices like cinnamon that show the influence of many cultures ranging from African, Arab, and Greek to name a few. I honestly do not know which spices or combinations were used, but I can tell authentic Sicilian flavor when I taste it and this product has it.

There are approximately three servings per can, with each serving coming in at about 140 calories. Not bad for something so delicious.

What I truly love, though, is the reasonable levels of sodium, which is a fraction of the fried eggplant I mentioned above, and other nutritional values. Sodium is 310mg, which is less than half of the same serving of the fried eggplant, although the carbs and fat are still a tad high at 7 grams each. If you are watching cholesterol there is zero in this product. Do be aware that the sugar content is 8 grams.

As an antipasti or mezze - hot or cold - this is an excellent choice to accompany breads for dipping and scooping, and it goes well with other servings that are Mediterranean (olives, pickled peppers, cheeses, dolmas, etc.) Of course it's great to make this delicious dish yourself, but these jars are convenient for putting something together on short notice.

title: Delicious and convenient
text:
This fried eggplant is perfect for antipasti or mezze, and because it is delicious it's a convenient way to set out an impressive tray on short notice.

You need to be aware of some of the nutrition facts, though, if you or your family or guests have special dietary needs or restrictions. First off each can contains about 2 1/2 150 gram servings. That means you will probably be using more than a few cans if you have even a small gathering to serve. Sodium is a fairly high 645mg per serving, so if you have sodium restrictions this could be a red flag. I suspect the high sodium is also what makes this such an addictive and tasty snack. It's always the things that are bad for you that taste the best. The calorie count is 130, all of which are from the 16 grams of fat per serving. Also there are nearly 11 grams of carbs in each serving.

While the nutritional values seem bleak, if the servings are part of a more extensive spread of antipasti or mezze they are not as bad as they seem. And if this is an occasional indulgence then my take is to enjoy them without guilt (I have a lot of dietary restrictions and indulge in moderation without any side effects or guilt.) Of course, for those who can eat whatever they want this is a delicious addition to any spread and is sure to warrant a second serving. If you cannot live with the nutrition levels I recommend that you consider [[ASIN:B00498OI8O Alessi Sicilian Caponata - Eggplant Appetizer]], which has significantly lower levels of sodium and more reasonable levels of fat and carbs.

I always keep a few cans handy for guests and I have never had anyone not take less than two servings. Definitely recommended as a dip or hors d'oeuvres.

title: Spicy is a relative thing
text:
Another reviewer complained about this product being overly spicy while I could have used a bit more spiciness. If you do not like foods with a bite then you should take the previous review to heart and avoid this.

If you are like me, though, these are excellent out of the can. I prepare mine sauteed with garlic and olive oil, then mashed. I add a small quantity of red pepper flakes to mine to increase the spiciness, but I recommend that you try them as is before doctoring them.

For folks who are watching their nutritional intake each can contains about three half-cup servings, each of which are a reasonable 90 calories. Sodium is a reasonable 290mg, and there is zero fat or cholesterol. If you are counting carbs a serving is 14 grams. There are 7 grams of fiber and 8 grams of protein in each serving, so they are a good complement to most balanced diets.

To me these merit five stars for the nutritional values (and especially the relatively low sodium content for any kind of canned beans). But nutrition is not the only factor I took into consideration: they are flavorful, have a nice balance (to my taste buds) of spiciness, and excellent texture.

title: True Turkish flavor
text:
My favorite dolmas are based on Turkish recipes and this one does not disappoint. In fact, this is one of my two favorite brands when it comes to ready-made dolmas (see below for the other.) Fortunately I can readily buy these locally, which does drop the cost.

While I prefer homemade yalancı dolma, it's hard to argue with the convenience of this product: slice a lemon, lay out on a platter and serve. The spices used in this brand are unmistakably Turkish. About the only complaint I have is it is made with sunflower oil instead of olive oil - but still is delicious. In addition to the authentic flavor, the texture is perfect in my opinion.

Although most people immediately think dolmas are healthy, there are a few nutritional facts of which you need to be aware if you have special dietary needs. First, the serving size is five pieces or approximately 120 grams, and a little less than half of those calories are from fat. Speaking of fat, those five pieces contain 11 grams, but only 1 gram of those is saturated. There is nominal cholesterol (a serving size is considered to contain zero), and 23 grams of carbohydrates. These seem high at first glance, but if you keep your consumption to a single serving - easy to do if these are accompanied by other 'mezze' - then they are fairly safe. Compare the nutrition numbers to those of my other favorite brand, [[ASIN:B0084443G6 Al Wadi Gourmet Stuffed Vine Leaves]], you will see that both are in the ballpark for dolmas. See my review of that product for its nutritional figures to compare the two.

Regardless of whether or not you prefer Turkish recipes this is still a great product that will probably please anyone who enjoys Lebanese, Greek or other Middle Eastern and Mediterranean variants of this wonderful dish.

title: Delicious and authentic Lebanese style
text:
Having lived in the Middle East I developed a taste for specific cuisines with a penchant for the spicier Palestinian fare, while my favorite dolmas recipes were Turkish. However, I also learned that the gold standard in both Arab and Mediterranean cooking is Lebanese and this product proves it.

The flavor and texture of these are not only authentic, but to me a cut above most that I have tasted. That these are from a can blows me away.

There are, however, some nutritional facts that you need to consider. First, the bad news for those who are on low sodium diets: the sodium level is 611mg per serving. The good news is a serving is four pieces, so you can have a few without guilt or alarm. And while the calorie count is relatively low at a little less than 150 calories per serving, about a third of those calories are from fat, which is about 6 grams per serving - half of which is saturated fat. There are 7mg of cholesterol and a little over 20 grams of carbs per serving. While these seem to be bleak figures at a glance, bear in mind that there are only two and a half servings per can. Moreover, the values are about average for any dolmas brand or even homemade ones.

Used as a 'mezze' for guests the nutritional numbers are not so bad because dolmas are not going to be the main course and will be competing with other delicacies.

I am fortunate in that I can purchase these locally and manage to keep at least a few cans in my pantry for unexpected guests. For those impromptu occasions I also keep a few cans of [[ASIN:B000I07884 Alwadi Al Akhdar Baba Ghanouj]] on hand because the Alwadi Al Akhdar brand is one to which I am loyal.

title: Surprisingly good
text:
I purchased a can of this locally on a whim with low expectations since it was in a can. Frankly, I was delightfully surprised by how flavorful it is.

To the folks whose reviews claim that this is mis-labeled hummus instead of baba ghanouj - I disagree. Perhaps the confusion comes from the denser consistency of this product. If you follow the directions by adding some olive oil and lemon and thoroughly mixing it in, then the consistency will be that of a well made baba ghanouj. The directions also call for mixing in crushed garlic, which is essential to achieve an authentic flavor. I believe those ingredients were left out of the can and left to the buyer to increase shelf life.

After mixing in the lemon juice, olive oil and crushed garlic I also add a pinch of cumin into the mix. Right before serving I will sometimes sprinkle cumin or summac over the top for an added flavor as well as drizzle more olive oil over the top of the baba ghanouj in the serving dish or bowl.

There are a few nutritional facts you should take into account: there are about ten servings in a can, and each one contains 180mg of sodium. If you are on a low sodium diet you need to be careful of how much you consume. Also each serving contains 2.5 grams of fat of which a half gram is saturated. This is BEFORE you add olive oil, which will raise the fat content per serving by another 14 grams of fat per tablespoon of oil used when you mix the baba ghanouj. Each of the ten servings is 40 calories before adding in the olive oil, which contains an additional 140 calories per tablespoon.

While the above nutritional facts look dismal, bear in mind that they are about par for any properly prepared baba ghanouj - although you can control the sodium content by making this dish from scratch. Although my diet is restrictive I can break the rules occasionally when I want baba ghanouj but am too lazy to make it myself. Used in moderation this is an excellent alternative and one that is authentic if you follow the directions and mix in the missing ingredients and garnish to taste. And it's an inexpensive alternative as well as a convenient one.

title: Extremely convenient
text:
I love these because they have been conveniently cut into strips that are perfect for placing in serving dishes for hors d'oeuvres or antipasti (as well as tapas and mezze). They are also superb as either a garnish or an ingredient in a salad.

The flavor is superb and imparts that fire-roasted taste (although these are not claimed to be such.)

What I especially love, though, is the reasonable sodium levels in the serving. Too many peppers and similar antipasti ingredients have shockingly high levels. Each of the ten servings in this jar contain only 105mg of sodium (contrast that with the 450-500mg for my favorite brand of serrano and jalapeno peppers for the same serving size!) Since I need to carefully watch my sodium intake this is a major plus for me. Another plus is each serving is only 5 calories, making the entire 16oz jar a scant 50 calories.

All of the pluses add up to five stars for me. Do be aware that these are readily available locally where I live and at a lower price at that. If I had to factor in the high shipping cost imposed here I would probably balk or be less effusive in my comments. I never have less than a few jars in my pantry, and frequently have an open one in my refrigerator.

title: Versatile and convenient
text:
Although easy to make from scratch I always keep a few jars of this sofrito in my pantry for when I am too busy to whip one up myself.

The uses for this are as varied as patterns in snowflakes. I use it as a base for stews and soups, for basting fish before broiling or cooking it en papillote style, and even for adding to salsas and bruschetta to impart an ineffable flavor that never fails to please my guests.

You need to be aware of a few potential problems with this sofrito though. First is it contains MSG (monosodium glutamate). If you get a reaction from that then you may want to avoid this particular product. Second, it contains 2565 mg of sodium, which can be a problem for people on a low sodium diet. Finally it contains soy that can cause reactions in some people. These do not necessarily detract from the quality and flavor of this sofrito, but you should be aware of their presence if you or anyone in your family has issues with them.

Not only is this an essential ingredient for many Hispanic dishes, it also enhances a lot of Mediterranean and Middle Eastern recipes. I also keep a few jars of [[ASIN:B0004MXOG6 Goya Recaito]] around when I want a sofrito that is better suited for Puerto Rican cuisine.

title: Not as good as homemade, but ...
text:
This recaito is the next best thing to homemade in my opinion. I keep a few jars in my pantry for last minute dishes. Do note that this contains MSG, so if that ingredient causes any physical problems you should not purchase this product. It also contains some soy, another ingredient that causes problems with some people.

What I love is the versatility of recaito in general. And despite my preference for making it from scratch, Goya definitely does an excellent job with this ready-made one.

It is a perfect base for just about any soup or stew recipe you can think of, and is also an excellent garnish over the top of lentils, meats and entrees. I use it on fish when I am cooking it 'en papillote' style, which has always been a big hit among my guests.

A companion product that I always have on hand (and prefer making myself when I have the time) is [[ASIN:B0004MXOFM Goya Sofrito]], which is equally versatile and can be used for the same dishes and recipes as this recaito (although the recaito is a must for imparting an authentic flavor to Puertorriqueño cuisine.)

title: Blown away!
text:
I normally make everything from scratch and especially salsas and bruschetta so you can imagine my surprise and delight when I first tasted this salsa. Frankly, had I not opened the can myself I would have sworn that it was home made. Indeed, 'casera' implies just that and it is accurate in my opinion.

The can is labeled 'Hot' but that is a relative term. To me it's tangy, but not overly spicy. However, since I eat extremely spicy food that aspect of this salsa may, in fact, be spicy to many.

There are 26 servings in this 28 ounce can, so the nutritional info bears scrutiny. Each severing is a low 5 calories. What you need to watch, though, if you are managing your sodium intake is how many servings you consume since each contains 240 mg. It adds up quickly. On the other hand, there is zero fat and cholesterol, and only 1 gram each of carbohydrates and sugar per serving.

Basically (aside from the sodium level) this is not only delicious and close to home made quality, but healthy. When you factor in the cost per can versus what it would cost to make the same amount from scratch you win again.

Since I do not eat chips I use this as an ingredient in some fish dishes, as well as a topping for beans. Of course there are many more uses than those, but I can assure you that as a garnish for fish (or most any entree) this salsa will add a burst of fresh, tangy flavor.

I still make my salsas from scratch on special occasions, but I find myself using this more frequently. Even if you are a strict traditionalist have in a can or two in your pantry for unexpected quests is recommended. Don't let them see you open the can and you can fool most of them into thinking you whipped it up yourself.

title: The king is dead - long live the king
text:
My title is related to a review I did of [[ASIN:B001EQ5EHI La Piana Carnaroli Rice]] in which I proclaimed that was truly the king of rice. Shortly afterward a friend who grew up and still lives in Italy's Veneto region (in Padua) suggested that I try this grain before making sweeping statements. I managed to find this locally and I think I have found the perfect rice for making risotto.

While Carnaroli rice maintains its shape instead of melting away as you cook it, that grain did not absorb saffron which I frequently use, so I continued to use (and recommend) [[ASIN:B000FDLAWY arborio rice]] when cooking with saffron or other spices that you wanted to integrate with the rice grains.

This rice is the best of both worlds - it absorbs flavors, especially delicate ones like saffron, while remaining firm throughout the long cooking cycle for authentic risotto dishes. It also produces the same creamy consistency that is far superior to what you can achieve with arborio rice - and it will still turn out al dente.

For me I am going to stick with this style of grain for all risotto dishes. A plus is the bag which seals to keep the rice fresh. This is important to me because rice packaged in boxes tend to absorb aromas while they are stored.

title: High quality and consistent
text:
I have used many brands of arborio rice and this one is among my favorite because of the consistency. What I mean by that is each bag cooks the same way, using the same amount of stock and cooking time as the last. When you consider that I have been using this brand for years that is high praise. Contrast that with other brands that I have used in the past that have a wide variation in stock requirements and cooking time from one batch to another.

Another thing I love is the portion size and the packaging. Most packages of arborio rice are 16-ounce size. Vigo's 12-ounce bag is more than sufficient for serving eight to ten people, which means I do not have to measure or set aside a portion of the dry grains. And the sealed bag ensures that the rice will remain fresh for months (if not years), which is a major improvement over box packaging. This is especially important when you are purchasing in bulk like this 12-pack.

Another factor is the question of which is better: carnaroli or arborio rice for risotto? My answer is I use both. I definitely favor carnaroli for most types of risotto I make (my preferred brand is [[ASIN:B001EQ5EHI La Piana Carnaroli Rice]], but when I use saffron, arborio is my choice of rice. This is because arborio rice absorbs the saffron-based stock a lot better, which imparts a flavor that can only be achieved with saffron. And since this brand is consistent as I described above (and saffron is expensive), it's yet another reason to purchase this brand if you are making risotto with saffron.

The lot size - twelve 12-ounce packs - is nearly a year's supply for me since I also make risotto with carnaroli rice. Since each pouch is totally sealed that means that a year from now when I open one from my current supply it will be fresh and consistent - one more reason why I love and recommend this brand.

title: Truly the 'King of Rice'
text:
Flavor and texture of this type of rice make it perfect for risotto. For one thing, the grains maintain their shape better than arborio rice. This feature truly sets it apart and makes it perfect for certain types of risotto in the same way that some pasta shapes are better than others depending on the sauce.

I use carnaroli rice when I am basing the risotto on larger pieces of fish such as monkfish and mahi. The firmer grains work better with ingredients like that. I also use it when I want to make a very creamy risotto, which is another feature of this type of rice. It has an even higher starch content than arborio rice.

The only real drawback as far as I can tell is carnaroli does not absorb saffron nearly as well as arborio, so when I am preparing a risotto that has saffron I use arborio rice instead. As an aside, I recommend [[ASIN:B0042ZF6B2 Iranian Saffron]] for any dishes that call for saffron. That particular brand is of exceptional quality.

Regarding the portion size I think that the 16-ounce portions of this particular brand is about 4-ounces more than you need to make a risotto for up to eight people. I save the excess from each box in a sealed plastic container, so for me this six-box set is more like eight boxes. Since I do not cook risotto more than twice a month (and often less) this package is a six month supply for me, which makes the price a bargain.

One final note: I tend to use about ten percent more stock for this rice than I do for arborio grains, and I also tack on an additional five minutes of cooking time when using carnaroli. Your times will probably vary, but take into consideration that you may need a little more stock and cooking time if you are switching from arborio to carnaroli for risotto recipes.

Buon appetito!

title: One of my essential spices - both on the table and in the kitchen
text:
Besides black and red pepper this and cumin are my most used spices. I always sprinkle some over basmati rice, which is daily staple, as well as other dishes. It goes perfectly with fish. When I have guests over and fish is on the menu, I use a little of this as a rub for guests who do not like fish that tastes fishy (go figure!)

Other dishes that this goes perfectly with as a table spice are broccoli and rapini. I sometimes will sprinkle it on salads as well.

Because I use this as a table spice as well as for cooking I have found the perfect table shakers for sumac (and cumin - another spice I sprinkle on many foods): [[ASIN:B007T40P28 NEW, 6 oz. (Ounce) Swirl Glass Cheese Shaker, Pepper Spice Shaker w/ Perforated Stainless Steel Lid - Set of 2]].

If you are reading this review you are probably looking for a source of high quality sumac - this is it.

title: No substitute for fresh ground pods, but inexpensive for quick beverages
text:
This is a high quality, fragrant product that is fresh. Those reasons and the fact that it's also priced right are why I love this and gave it five stars. Another reason is most ground cardamom is not this fresh or aromatic.

I'll confess that I prefer whole pods, but occasionally I want to quickly brew a chai or a fast Turkish coffee (or even flavor regular coffee when brewing). This ground cardamom does the trick.

Turkish coffee with cardamom is both easy to brew and delicious to my taste. Just add cardamom to the grounds and make it your preferred way.

Cardamom is also a key ingredient in spiced chai (masala chai). I Normally grind a pod with a part of a stick of cinnamon, clove and a single black peppercorn. I mix it in a half and half water and milk mixture that I bring to a boil, add black tea and grate a piece of ginger). When I am lazy, use powdered ginger and this ground cardamom. Not quite as good as freshly ground pods (and grated ginger), but significantly better than most chai mixes you can buy off the shelf.

This spice is also used in sweet dishes and pastries, but I must confess that I have to forgo sweets for health reasons so know little about how it's used in that respect.

For sweetening coffee, chai or even desserts I recommend using one of the following in lieu of processed sugar: [[ASIN:B005F5K5N2 Goya Panela Brown Sugar Cane 1 Lb - Redonda]], known as "jaggery" in India. A convenient alternative is [[ASIN:B0050IM27Q Turbinado Sugar - 1 box, 1 lb]]. Either is especially superb with chai.

title: A lot more convenient than a communal dipping dish
text:
I frequently entertain guests who enjoy my cooking, Many of my guests have some to enjoy an dipping sauce for their bread, so I set the table with these.

While some restaurants that bring out a bread and a dipping sauce use a communal dish, I prefer to allow my guests to have more control over their sauce. Each guest gets one of these saucers, and I place the following on the table for their own mixing: a high quality olive oil, [[ASIN:B001SAWHPM Alessi Dipping Spice Grinder, 0.76-Ounce (Pack of 6)]], [[ASIN:B0019S5444 Alessi Whole Mix Peppercorns, 1.12-Ounce Grinder (Pack of 6)]] and [[ASIN:B001SB0DMU Alessi Grinder Sea Salt, 5.64-Ounce (Pack of 6)]]. For those who love to mix in basalmic vinegar I have a special treat awaiting them on the table: [[ASIN:B000CFO37Y Gia Russa Balsamic Glaze]].

Another way I use these is when I am measuring out spices for some dishes. I will measure out each spice into one or more of these saucers and mix them before adding them to whichever dish I am preparing. This prevents accidentally over spicing the meal because you can always pour too much spice back into its container a lot easier than removing it from a boiling pot!

The saucers are heavy duty (I love their heft), easy to care for and convenient. I have always cleaned mine in a dishwasher with no adverse effects, so I am reasonably certain that they are dishwasher-safe.

I usually do not entertain more than three people for dinners, so this pack is more than adequate for me. If you are used to larger parties, by additional packs.

title: Perfect complement to freshly ground coffee and spicing teas
text:
In a few words these pods are both wonderful when ground and are fresh. Once ground the aroma and flavor that are released make these among the best I have ever used.

I first acquired a taste for cardamom when I lived in the Middle East. Both Arabic coffee and Turkish coffee are made with cardamon. The Arabic coffee is difficult to brew because it is made from green coffee beans and green cardamom pods ground together. I have not found a source for green coffee beans where I live. However, Turkish coffee with cardamom is both easy to brew and delicious to my taste.

For regular coffee beans I grind a few pods when I am grinding the beans (a little of this goes a long way), and the brewed coffee has a wonderful flavor (not to mention a wonderful aroma while brewing.) Friends find the taste ineffable. I find it familiar and delicious.

Another way I use cardamom is to make spiced chai (masala chai). I grind a pod with a part of a stick of cinnamon, clove and a single black peppercorn. I mix it in a half and half water and milk mixture that I bring to a boil, add black tea and grate a piece of ginger (or, when I am lazy, use powdered ginger.) For the chai, a nice touch is to sweeten it with [[ASIN:B005F5K5N2 Goya Panela Brown Sugar Cane 1 Lb - Redonda]], known as "jaggery" in India. Or, for convenience, [[ASIN:B0050IM27Q Turbinado Sugar - 1 box, 1 lb]].

To be honest, I sometimes substitute powdered cardamom for pods, such as when I am making a quick Turkish coffee or chai, but when I want to treat myself, I use the pods. Frankly, there is not a ground cardamom I've tried that comes close to grinding the pods right before using them. And for company I never cut corners - these are an essential ingredient that is sure to impress and delight.

title: Perfect alternative to processed sugar
text:
This is healthier (and sweeter) than processed sugars as well as much healthier than artificial sweeteners. Panela is a household staple throughout Central and South America, as well as in India (where it's called jaggery.)

It can be shaved or grated to yield a serving, which is characterized with vivid flavor and sweetness. I use it for flavoring tea and for any cooking that calls for sugar (although I sometimes use honey instead.)

A more convenient form of this is called turbinado, of which this is an example: [[ASIN:B0050IM27Q Turbinado Sugar - 1 box, 1 lb]]. I keep it on hand in both forms, but the turbinado, while identical, does not impart the same flavor as a freshly grated portion of panela.

Either product is significantly healthier than processed sugar, and also has the advantage of being natural - many artificial sweeteners are actually carcinogenic.

This, its sibling called panela or honey are healthy choices when it comes to satisfying your sweet tooth. Also, if you compare the cost of these natural products to the processed or artificial ones, you will have yet another reason to go this route. I will not use anything else, except honey.

title: Among the best capers I have found
text:
I use capers in many dishes, including a meatless carpaccio, lox with cream cheese and bagels, and various salads and cold dishes (see my customer-supplied image at the top of the page for an example).

The problem, and especially in the backwoods of central Florida where I live, is finding high quality capers. There are a few brands that are acceptable to me, but since discovering this brand I am a loyal customer for life.

Key qualities of these include an excellent balance of acidity and saltiness (a little bite, but not obtrusive), and, of course, crunchiness. Compared to some other brands I have tried, many of which were very salty and not at all crunchy, this one stands out. And, of course, these are nonpareil grade instead of the gigantic capers that litter many supermarket shelves.

If you want a real treat use these with [[ASIN:B001LM5VFK Ortiz Atun Claro: Yellowfin Tuna in Olive Oil (7.8 ounce)]], Sliced, vine-ripened tomatoes, red onion, and, optional jalapenos. Drizzle with a high quality extra virgin olive oil and season with [[ASIN:B007BP3PF4 Herbes de Provence - Provence Herb 8 oz.]] ... or a high quality lox with cream cheese on a bagel. If you know capers you will immediately taste the difference and notice the texture and crunch that only the best capers have.

title: A special treat of exceptionally high quality tuna.
text:
When I want to treat myself this is one of the handful of ways I do so. I normally purchase [[ASIN:B004OHKKCI Ortiz White Tuna in Olive Oil Tin, 92-Grams (Pack of 5)]] for everyday use, but for special occasions this is how I pamper myself.

The quality of both the tuna and the olive oil are amazing. There are many ways of serving it, but one of my favorites is with sliced, vine-ripened tomatoes, red onion, capers and jalapenos, then drizzled with extra virgin olive oil and seasoned with [[ASIN:B007BP3PF4 Herbes de Provence - Provence Herb 8 oz.]]. I uploaded a customer-supplied image of just such a dish.

Another use is to top a paella with this tuna. Or serve it with a stuffed avocado. The possibilities are endless. This is not something I would waste on a sandwich, but for those times when you just want to treat or pamper yourself or someone special, this should do the trick.

title: Sometimes simple is better
text:
I love freshly ground pepper and especially love a little kick that having red peppercorns in a mix provide, so I normally use [[ASIN:B0019S5444 Alessi Whole Mix Peppercorns, 1.12-Ounce Grinder (Pack of 6)]]. There are times, however, when all I want is freshly ground black pepper, like when I am having vine-ripened tomatoes, insalada Caprese, and the such. That's where this product comes in.

The peppercorns are high quality and give off a nice aroma when ground. Like its more colorful sibling, the grinding mechanism tends to produce very coarse pepper, so if you prefer yours to be finer, a dedicated grinder may better suit your needs. I have had no problems with the grinding mechanism - I use a clockwise-counterclockwise motion and it works well. Too well if I am not careful because it will grind a lot of pepper with minimal motion. It does not clog like some dedicated grinders, which is another plus.

This is a convenient way to enjoy fresh ground pepper, and - in my opinion - is priced low considering that the grinder is disposable and I get nearly nine months of use from a package of six of these.

I always have one on my table (in the kitchen I use a dedicated grinder that allows me to adjust the grind.)

title: Perfect for dipping and much more
text:
This set of spices is designed for mixing with olive oil and used for dipping. Most folks think it's strictly for bread, but it is also perfect as a seasoning over oil and vinegar with pinzimonio (raw vegetables such as bell peppers, cauliflower, celery, etc.)

For bread, I keep it on hand for guests, along with a quality extra virgin olive oil, Since most of my guests are convinced that one must mix in balsamic vinegar, I also make sure I have [[ASIN:B000CFO37Y Gia Russa Balsamic Glaze]] on hand (read my review of that product for the reason why I use it instead of so called balsamic vinegars such as [[ASIN:B00759NNKI Balsamic Vinegar of Modena]].) For the record, I consider mixing either of the balsamic products I just mentioned in high quality olive oil to be a crime because those products mask the nuances of the oil. But that is just me.

Other uses I have for these dipping spices include: drizzle oil over indents in the dough, then grind the spices over it when making focaccia. Also, a few grinds over insalada Caprese, or even a fresh garden salad also works wonders, In fact, let your imagination run wild because these spices are fragrant and not overpowering.
