title: Easing into Darjeeling on a sweeter note - Not bad at all
text:
For the taste, I do find the price a bit high. Consider the 87 single estates of Darjeeling and then how many vendors blend their own at lower grades along with the different flush (season), there can be a lot of general Darjeeling. That makes it confusing. Anyone who wants to get into the better ones, you look for the single estates. When it's labeled Darjeeling, it's anyone's guess. Too often, they don't ever mention the tasting notes. It's good when they do.

This is what I like about this brand. It does have that classic muscatel note that's dominant in most Darjeeling teas. Not all of them have that note. Depends on the flush. What makes this one nice is it does have a light, sweet taste at the end. For anyone new to Darjeeling and they want an easier transition to the more prominent muscatel note, this would be the one.

Much of the time, Darjeeling has the Earthy, grassy, plant notes. Some are more floral and some are fruity. Often times, when they state almond, peach, muscatel and such, they refer to the skin, not the actual fruit or nut. The taste is more bitter.

Those into the Darjeeling have a darker, more Earthy palate. Unless it's a single estate that you're familiar with, majority are going to have heavier tasting notes.

If you like the aroma of Lavender, the Namring single est. offers that. For more almond note, Selim Hill single est.

This does have more taste than a certain brand sold on here in a blue bag. It doesn't taste as basic. There's a little more to this one that makes it enjoyable to drink all day. For many, this is a good tea. It's not bad at all.

So far between the Ceylon and this, it has been pleasant tea. For the quality of it and taste, the price is higher than it should be. That's having a lot of experience with tea.

It's much better than Lipton of course. But not the same as a single estate and the quality isn't as high as it could be for the price.

For some who tried a thousand teas, not sure that's valid. There are hundreds for sure. Anyone who as tried a lot of teas knows that a lot of teas overlap and it's a mix of grades and other teas to be a diff tea product, but not a whole entire type of tea bush.

87 Darjeeling estates. Break that into 3 seasons. Then break it into grades from how finely cut to whole leaves to how fresh it is to barely having any taste. 87 diff tea bushes is that. It breaks into the 3 seasons then you have 261 to choose from, but still it's 87 estates that have their own unique taste. Take the 1st or 2nd flush to blend, that's what you get. Blends.

Over a thousand blends from hundreds of different teas, yes. Thousands of tea as if there are that many different bushes, no. 87 diff tea bushes in the Darjeeling region alone can produce hundreds of blends. Anyone who has tried thousands of teas chances are only had hundreds.

Even then, no reason to review it as if this is to be the site for the top 100 teas of the world. You want the best teas, it's not sold in this site. Anyone who is really into teas would know that. If they're going to grade it in such a way as if every tea connoisseur thinks that way, then 99% of the teas sold on this site would be a 1 star to folks like that.

For all those who want a good tea to enjoy without it being on the same level as the ones sold in most chain stores, this is good. Just the price isn't so good. If the price was much lower, I think this would be a daily staple to have for many.

The Idulgashinna single estate Ceylon sold on here under Irish, English breakfast are good, sturdy teas for a good price. You have to find that marked on the bag. Technically it's not Irish or English blend. Single estates are not blends. That's why it's called single estate. If you blend them, you can't call them single estate.

The brand is good on its own. It would taste better blended with other teas for those who know how to blend. It's a good all day, any day tea. Not at the level to be addictive.

title: Taj by Moonlight - Subtle muscatel, lightly floral - not strong or distinctive blend
text:
Nice cloth bag. Nice gift for those who are not as particular about fine tea and used to drinking the generic teas or most brands sold in stores. It's a step up from the usual brands. For those who are into tea on a higher level, the grade is not high enough to stand out.

The floral note stands out more than the muscatel. Over all this tea is light in taste. If you make it more concentrated, it's more bitter and mutes the floral note and would go better with milk to balance.

Usually with single est. or higher grades, the floral notes are more prominent in which certain flowers stand out such as a rose or lilac. This is over all gen. floral. The aroma of dry leaves are lacking. The leaves are cut up small.

This is made cold brew so that the sweetness comes out more. No astringency when you do that. If you like it astringent where it grabs the back of your throat, then hot brew it.

The image of seniors having afternoon tea comes to mind. It would be considered a nice cup for those who grew up with fewer options.

For those into single estate Darjeeling and higher grade blends, I suggest other brands. The tea isn't bad. It's clean, natural and pleasant tasting. Pleasant fits. Not pleasantly surprised to be something more. The price is fair for the grade and taste. Don't expect any other tea to be much different in grade and taste. Usually many brands have a consistent theme.

It's kind of a step up from Twinings and few steps below Harney & Sons. Little more character and higher grade than Twinings. But not on same level as some of the Harney Darjeeling blends.

title: Strands and grainy texture - Zip bag doesn't close

title: Best Kee Mun Tea
text:
Tasting notes: Floral, deep dark sweetness, pronounced aroma and smooth.

Cold brew it for full potential sweetness without any astringency. Then dilute the concentrated tea with cold or hot water to your liking.

Best Kee Mun tea I ever had so far. High grade compared to the low grade that are sold often. Yes, the price is higher, but the taste is very different. Most are familiar with the cacao note of this tea. That is usual in the lower grades. It works well in terms of blending as breakfast teas or anything sturdy.

To enjoy the tea as is with all the floral, fruity sweetness, this grade is the one. It's very enjoyable as is, but can be blended with other teas as well.

What's the difference between a high and low grade Kee Mun?

Low grade has the Earthy, bitter cacao notes. This is why it makes a good Eng. breakfast tea.

High grade is more floral, sweet, deep aroma that dance with your senses. It's as different as night and day. What makes them both the same tea is the finish or after taste. The Earthy, lightly sweet taste lingers in the background.

The low grade sits in the background and lets you add milk or other ingredients to make it more colorful to the taste buds. The high grade is colorful from the start and then mellows out at the end.

Only thing I don't like is the long wait to get the tea and why the names are not more specific to know the difference. Out of so many sellers and sites, everyone states Kee Mun. Which one is which?

They can state sweet, but there are so many different types of sweet. Some can be a lighter sweet such as the Mao Feng Kee Mun. This Kee Mun is a deeper, more fruity caramel aroma.

Think of the Mao Feng Kee Mun as the white shirt, khakis on a Spring day with light colored flowers scenery. Sweet, but it's a nice, fair weather, Spring day.

This one that has the deep aroma is sitting in a wood decorated lounge on a chilly night with the fireplace and a brandy snifter at hand or a smooth bourbon. It has you smell the rich, deep, sweet aroma over and over. If there is an oil to release the natural tea aroma to fill the room similar to this, it would be popular among tea enthusiasts.

For anyone who enjoys a black tea that's rich, deep, dark and sweet, this is the one.

title: Japanese black tea that smells of green tea with sweetness
text:
Tasting notes: Honeysuckle with a hint of light root (ginseng)

If you had to look at it as a green tea, it doesn't have the same characteristics either.

The aroma of the dry leaves reminds me of green tea. It's not the typical aroma for any black tea from different regions. Neither are the leaves completely black. More dark green. This must be on the less oxidized end of black tea.

Despite the aroma being more green and the taste matches that, it's a black tea due to the sweetness. Green teas usually are not sweet. Many teas do not match in aroma and taste. This is one of those that taste about the same as the dry leaf aroma. It has that green, plant note to it. But not grassy or the heavy, Earthy notes.

If Honeysuckle stems have the lingering taste of the nectar, then that's the green part. Light, green note that's not as pronounced as the sweetness which is very unique. Slightly floral, but more sweet than anything.

The lingering note of root may not sound appealing, but it is not that bad. Hint of it. As if you put some root next to the Honeysuckle for a while to let the aroma fly over.

The sweetness is nice. The green, plant taste that I don't find fitting. I'm used to the Earthy sweetness with a bit more heaviness to my black teas than this brighter, green note. For anyone that like the combo of green tea with sweetness, this is your cup of black tea.

Wonder if every other black tea from Japan taste like this. It's very difficult to find black tea from JP. Yes, it's made in Japan despite all the Chinese characters on the package. Chinese and Japanese characters are used in JP writing. Mainly due to how many characters you need in JP to mean the same as 1 character in Chinese.

title: Harney's Smoked Bourbon Not My Cup of Tea
text:
1st off I like to say that I have tried a good amount of H and S tea over the years. I usually don't have issues with their flavored tea except this one. What ever was in this, a few sips gave me a headache and my stomach wasn't reacting well either. I'm a bit surprised which has me wonder what is in it.

It has a smoky aroma which is typical of a smoked Lap Sang Sou Chong. It does have a savory note to it when you make it more concentrated. The light, sweet aroma is from the flavoring. The sweetness is from the tea. Anyone who had a LSSC by itself knows it gives off the smoky aroma as if you're next to a BBQ or grill. But it has a sweetness to the taste. The unsmoked LSSC is sweet.

Set aside the odd reaction to the tea, taste wise isn't my cup of tea either. It doesn't have a lot of depth since it very much taste of a flavoring with LSSC.

As for the aroma of bourbon, that depends on what type you're smelling. If you like the ones that smell more smoky, then this has it. If you're going with more sweet aroma or other notes that make it rich and complex, this is not the one. It can be done with a variety of teas. Just a matter of taking time to blend and be playful.

Their Earl Grey Supreme is the best out of their Earl Grey line. In terms of a lot of flavored teas, that one, Tower of London, Diamond Jubilee and Tropical Green stand out the most.

title: Trio Sampler - Nilgiri, Darjeeling, Assam - Basic taste
text:
Price isn't bad for the basic taste of the teas. It taste basic compared to others for the same teas. Yes, it's crisp, smooth and clean. But it also lacks a lot of character that makes each tea more distinctive. The one to stand out the most is the Nilgiri.

Nilgiri - Floral, green plant, light sweetness

Darjeeling - Mellow, typical taste that is clearly Darjeeling. It has a very toned down muscatel note. Earthy, light wood, wet leaves pungent. Better to blend another tea to balance out the pungent or sharpness. (Earthy, wood, muscatel are usual notes of 2nd flush Darjeeling)

It has more of a blended taste to me than a single estate. As in taking every other lower grade estate that has similar notes to mix. That's trying over a dozen single estate Darjeeling in which each has a distinctive note. If the Avongrove Estate usually taste like this, then I rather go with another estate.

Assam - Slight tartness in wet leaves and taste of tea. Malty when milk added. Brighter note compared to some Assam that are darker, more bitter and not drinkable without milk. Good for blending.

Over all for anyone new to these teas, this is good to start. It has the generic, classic taste of each. Nice that it is organic. For anyone who has tried a lot of teas and tried different Assam, Darjeeling and Nilgiri, this wouldn't be anything to stand out.

Cold brew is best to cut down the astringency and bring out more natural sweetness of any tea. Make it concentrated and then dilute with hot or cold H20 to your liking. This particular sampler is good for blending in terms of it staying in the background vs. be in front.

Thank you for the quick shipping. Nice to know the company keeps the the products clean.

title: Glendale Nilgiri Black -  Not floral
text:
Tasting notes - Earthy, wood, mild, mellow, hint of sweet -- Does not have the typical Nilgiri floral note. Think of a very very very toned down Darjeeling without the muscatel note.

Lack of aroma in the dry tea and steeped. No surprise the taste is lacking too. This is the famous Glendale Estate and the price is over $100/lb for something that doesn't taste like much. I have single estate Darjeeling that cost less than half the price and stand out better. It doesn't bother me if it has different tasting notes as long as it's distinctive in a good way. It has more of a generic, black tea taste.

For the price, where it's from and being a 2nd flush, it has me wonder how low the grade is. Even with a good grade of tea, the taste and aroma can hold up after a year or 2. I had bought a cheaper Nilgiri and then this hoping there would be a huge difference. Go figure the cheaper one has a stronger aroma.

I was wanting to try the Puttabong, but that is not available. Even if the tea is $3/ounce, it is still pricey for lacking in aroma and taste. This blends with other black teas since the notes stay in the background. Not blend as in it has any notes to compliment another tea.

Bit surprised this time with the single estate teas. Usually they're more distinctive in flavor. I tried a long list of teas that range from cheap to pricey. Never had I paid anything in this price range and think it's not worth it. The taste is more fitting to be under $20/lb. Not $118/lb.

There are so many teas I rather have under $20/lb before I even pick this one for the same price. I wouldn't be so bothered if this cost $2.50 for the 50 grams. $5 max if we have to go higher. $10 would be pushing it. For $25, I'm better off getting a pound of some other tea.

Drinkable, smooth, but not memorable or enjoyable enough for me to want a 2nd cup.
1 star for the reasonable shipping time. 1 star for the tea. I should have looked at what else the seller sells that ranges in a lot of products to get an idea of what the tea would be like.

If the tea was stored properly since last Summer, it would still have a good aroma a year later. This taste as if it was left out in open air vs. sealed well and all the aroma went away. Good tea maintains the aroma for a long time.

title: English Breakfast that is not an English Breakfast - Idulgashinna Ceylon
text:
Tasting notes - Earthy, woody, light sweetness (cooked papaya note of wet leaves), light hint of cacao

For those who want an aromatic single estate Ceylon, I suggest the Pettiagala. If freshness was based on aroma with the Idulgashinna Ceylon, then I wouldn't say it is that fresh. The aroma is lacking. It does have a cooked papaya aroma once it's steeping in room temp. H20. Due to the lack of taste and aroma, it's best to cold brew than hot. You only mute the flavor more with hot.

The original Eng. breakfast tea was a Keemun. It later switched to Assam for lower price. These days, a breakfast tea usually has Keemun or Assam. Ceylon is not considered English breakfast tea usually. It may have a more Earthy and wood taste similar to hold up as a breakfast tea, but that does not make it a breakfast tea any more than most Darjeeling having similar notes.

In terms of making it cold brew and having it concentrated enough, it does have a sturdy, hefty taste and feel which is very different from many Ceylon teas. As for it holding up much flavor with some milk, no. It seems more enjoyable as is. There's not a lingering after taste. It's as if a lot was muted with the aroma so even the taste is held back and the finish is hidden.

The taste is sturdy to make it seem like a breakfast tea, but once you add a splash of milk, it doesn't hold up the same as the other heavy, black teas. Even when the teas is more concentrated, it still doesn't blend well enough to taste a certain way.

I was looking forward to trying another single estate Ceylon. Unfortunately, it doesn't have the distinctive taste or dry tea aroma that has me wanting more. It has me wonder about the grade. If there was a distinctive aroma to stand out in a good way, then the price isn't bad. Since there's nothing memorable, the price doesn't seem worth it. Most Ceylon teas are better to blend with.

If you're wanting a breakfast tea in which you can add milk to it and taste right, this is NOT it. If you're wanting a more aromatic Ceylon, try another. If you want a sturdy, brisk Ceylon, this is it. Something that can blend with a basic Darjeeling or Nilgiri if you want another note or dimension to the tea.

Another way to describe this is if you're walking into a white painted room. Empty, clean and plain. Just in black tea form.

Cold brew any tea and then add hot or cold H20 will make it smoother, not astringent and stay fresh for weeks. If you ever come across a tea that's very astringent or harsher in taste or worry about burning your tea, cold steeping is the way to go. Make it concentrated with less H20 and then dilute to your liking. Always have a 2nd or 3rd rinse to extract everything from the leaves.

title: Pleasant Savory Green Tea
text:
Out of the different green teas to drink as is, this one is more enjoyable as a blend. It blends well with a certain creamy, floral oolong. It does not have the same notes as a Dragon Well, Ti Guan Yin, Mao Feng, Spring Snail and others that you can leave as is.

The "Hay Cheun" ( 熙 春 - splendid / radiant Spring) green tea does have that Spring season note. It is not as light as the sen cha. Not a stronger grass taste as a ban cha. Green tasting, but pleasant and easy to drink. Definitely a savory note that pairs well with chicken and seafood. Due to that, the "sweet" part of the tea is not the tea, but the water. If you start off with a more concentrated tea, it taste sweeter as you dilute it more and more.

Unlike other teas that are naturally sweet and not as sweet as you dilute it, this one has the light sweetness from the water. It's savory enough that adding more water brings the light sweetness forward. The tea itself isn't sweet.

If you enjoy sen or ban cha, this is different. Easier to drink than the ban cha which is what many brands use that are labeled green tea. Not a bad tea. It's a matter of preference.

It doesn't taste have the usual Japanese green tea notes that are usually more Earthy green. Some do share similarities such as the Dragon Well (most prized green tea in China) and Gyokuro (most prized in Japan that is not a mat cha).

Depending if you prefer the astringency in any tea, the best way is to cold brew as a form of gentle extraction and then add hot or cold water to have a more subtle sweetness and lack of astringency. Never go wrong with a concentrated cold extraction after a few hours or over night and then dilute to your liking. Time frame of steeping depends on how concentrated you want it and make most of tea. Best results is over night unless you leave room temp. consistent and cool enough in less time.

title: Wonderful Aroma for a Ceylon
text:
Moment I opened the bag, the aroma was strong, sweet and wine like. It has me think dark plum where you have that sweetness and then tartness at the end. The sweetness is more of a dark syrup than of a fruit. Not quite a brown sugar since it doesn't have the smoky note. But a deep, rich, syrup similar to a molasses without the bitter note of that.

The strong sweetness and plum tartness lingers. I wouldn't say stone fruit since that sweetness is more related to a plum vs. a peach or nectarine. Some teas have that all around stone fruit note. This is a dark plum tartness or wine note that hangs around.

As for the taste of the tea, it's not as strong as the aroma of the dry leaves. The sweetness is very toned down and the tartness is more of an essence. The dry leaves aroma is a lot nicer than the tea to drink as is which is why it's better to blend this with a naturally sweeter, black tea. Then the taste would match the aroma more.

No doubt the taste is a Ceylon. Most Ceylon teas tend to be lighter tasting and better for blending. I would enjoy this tea more blended with certain black, sweet teas vs. having it as is.

It's good for anyone that likes a lighter, brighter tasting tea. The English Breakfast by Elmwood has the brighter note too, but also a more pronounced sweeter taste and this is a bit more bland type of sweetness with the hint of tart finish. If you add anything to Ceylon tea, it would mask the natural notes.

Usually Ceylon doesn't have the more Earthy, bitter notes common in Indian teas. One is grown high up in the Himalaya region and the other is on an island. If you take an Indian tea and diluted it quite a bit, then you have a Ceylon some what. In ways, the Ceylon tea reflects the island with the bright sun and lighten feel. Probably more complimenting to the cuisine that's rich in spices.

Any blending with oils should not be with Ceylon tea. You don't taste the tea and it's too light to hold up to anything. Too often, the flavored teas from many brands use Ceylon. You taste the oil, not the tea. It comes down to the lower cost of Ceylon and knowing what type of teas will hold up to the oils better. Not randomly pick an Indian tea and add an oil or flavoring.

If anyone wants to make a spiced tea, a Ceylon would not hold up well. Any spice or oil would take away from the natural notes if there are any. Depends on the grade and blend. Most times, every other tea is a blend. It's nice to have a single estate tea which usually applies to Indian and Ceylon teas.

title: English breakfast is a nice Keemun
text:
Tasting notes: Bright, light floral sweet, light aroma of peach skin, pleasant, easy on palate.

Enjoyable as is. Sweeter version of a single estate Selim Hill Darjeeling. To blend this with the muscatel notes of Darjeeling would give it a more Earthy, sturdy and bitter notes.
=======
For those into Keemun, this is a brighter note than Davidson teas. It doesn't have a heavier, darker cacao note that I was expecting. Some what sweeter vs. bitter which makes it nice to drink without any milk.

Keemun was the original breakfast tea before Assam came into the pic. For the price, I know it's a lower grade Keemun. Those familiar with the lower and higher would know there's a huge difference on taste and aroma. Lower grade has more cacao notes. Think 100% cacao powder in a tea. Toasty, heavier which is why it would be a breakfast tea with splash of milk. I like this one as is and will order more from Elmwood Inn.

Higher grade is floral, sweeter and the flavor stands out more. But the finishing Earthy note on both are the same which makes it distinctively Keemun. When I made it more concentrated and tasted it cold brew, the brighter note and deeper flavor reminded me of the higher grade. A hint of it.

You have to make 2 - 3x the serving per cup of H20 to taste it well. If you use 1 tsp to a cup then it will have a faint, sweet note. Keep in mind this is cold brew.

You can't ever burn your tea if you cold brew it 1st concentrated and then dilute to your liking in hot or cold H20. Gentle way of extracting even though it takes a few hours room temp. or over night in fridge. Best part is cold brew stays fresh for 2 - 3 weeks or longer. If you use hot water, it changes the taste after a few hours and you don't taste the natural sweetness as much. It will also be astringent.

30-40% tea by volume in container and rest with H20. Sit over night. Pour out tea in container, add enough H20 to cover the leaves, shake for 10 sec and then pour out the 2nd more cloudy tea into the 1st for even taste. You can do a 3rd if it's very concentrated and you want to make the most of it.

Same with coffee. Cold brew is a form of extraction just like hot. It doesn't mean you have to drink it cold. Changes the chemistry which changes the flavor profile. No more astringency and burnt tea/coffee with this method. Make it concentrated to save space and time. Beauty of the cold brew tea is even if it becomes tart after a month, it's still drinkable. Think of it as a raw version of kom bu cha without the SCOBY. It taste the same regardless of which tea you use that's non flavored. Once it's tart, same taste on all teas.

Cold is bold. Hot is muted. If you want to taste your drink of any sort more, cold or room temp. stands out more than hot or warm.

Diamond Jubilee is good too if you like that all around grapefruit peel bitter taste. Tower of London is more sweet aroma of stone fruits and vanilla.

title: An upbeat breakfast tea that offers a different note
text:
The Ntingwe Kwazulu is without a doubt a breakfast tea. It would not be an all day drinking tea in the sense of having it straight. Definitely has the darker color of a breakfast tea. The taste on the other hand is upbeat compared to other breakfast teas. It doesn't have that same bitterness in the background. Bit on the light side to be there much even for a more concentrated brew.

It's more fine than a CTC since there isn't much of a curl. They almost look uniform in cut and a coffee filter would be suggested for this. Not quite the bitterness as the Assam, Ceylon and combination of the two if someone is looking for an alternative to the coffee and cream to start the day.

If the idea is to have an alternative to an espresso or Turkish coffee in terms of that heavier taste, I suggest the Assam, Ceylon or combo. This one would be more of an alternative to that brand everyone is familiar seeing at every other street corner or in a mall. Much of the coffee that brand has are from Africa so this would be similar in the lightness or upbeat characteristic.

I would say that not every Assam and Ceylon are going to be the same. T of H Assam is weak. Assam is known for the maltiness when you add the milk. Ceylon lends more of the bitterness. To have a good combo of the two that makes a good coffee and cream alternative is the royal blend by F&M. I like the royal blend and this one for a breakfast tea. Main difference is that the royal blend is more addictive for me. This one is good in a different way.

For those who enjoy a good breakfast tea, I would recommend this. It does have a twist to it that isn't present in most breakfast teas. It has a tenor note to it at the end. The taste starts off as breakfast and then finishes at the end with a light jump. Many breakfast teas end with a fall vs. a jump. Not fall in a bad way. More of the note being heavier, bitter, characteristics of coffee and a bass note.

Taste wise, it's good. In a way, refreshing for a breakfast tea. Full body, but still some lightness to it. Milk and honey/sugar would be suggested for this the way most breakfast teas are better paired with.

To compare it to coffee, this is more of a medium roast. For those who want that French roast or espresso, I suggest the Assam and Ceylon. Unlike coffee, it does not have that nice aroma to travel around the room when it is hot.

The unique note to the Ntingwe Kwazulu is hard to describe, but it's noticeable in a good way. Can not seem to find any other brand that offers the tea from this region.

Anyone who is not familiar with breakfast teas, do keep in mind it is the tea version of coffee minus the strong aroma. They are usually heavier, stronger and meant to be mixed with milk and sugar/honey. There isn't a set rule of what qualifies as a breakfast tea. Most of them are stronger, heavier, darker and is usually an Assam, Ceylon, Kenyan or a combo of any of them.

If you're looking for a tea that doesn't require milk or anything at all, the breakfast teas are the ones to stay away from. It's not an all day drinking tea. All day or afternoon drinking tea usually means a lighter tea than the breakfast ones. The flavored teas, the more colorful ones, those are all day drinking teas. Those will always stand out a bit more due to the different ingredients added. Where as the breakfast tea is going to be a tad more on the dull side. The caffeine may wake up the senses, but the taste itself isn't going to be as lively as a peach/ginger tea, a Lady Grey, a tisane and such.

For the ones who are experimenting with teas and the different flavors, the breakfast tea is in a whole different category by itself. It's not made to stand out so differently as if you are picking apples, oranges, pears, plums, apricots, berries and such. It's a very subtle type of tea that usually isn't meant to be mixed with anything else that you would find in the afternoon or all day drinking teas.

A breakfast tea with a little more distinction, this is the one. Most breakfast teas just has people go ehh. Similar to having toast with butter and plain corn flakes. It's not to meant to be very exciting. Not that it couldn't be, but the base of most breakfast teas aren't made that way. The minor details or subtle differences varies, but that is what has one choose one breakfast tea over the other.

You will find that some co. make more than one combo of the same teas. It doesn't mean they all taste the same. Sometimes it varies by grade and they won't tell you or they vary by region or something else. Only way to figure out which one you like better than the other is by trying them. Describing can only go so far. What has that je ne sais quoi for one drinker may not for another.

I enjoy the heavier taste of the Assam/Ceylon combo, but then I am one to enjoy espresso and Turkish coffee. This is a 2nd alternative for a breakfast tea if I want something a little brighter. To like something heavier in taste does not necessarily mean that the tea is made more concentrated. A good, heavier tea doesn't require a heavier serving to get a good result. In fact, good teas that are distinctive enough would not require 2-3x the serving to be adequate.

The same goes for coffee as well. If something is made well, the one serving is enough to get that taste, texture and over all experience that is most enjoyable. To double the amount in coffee or tea to make it more enjoyable either says the product isn't made well enough to begin with or the person has a heavier palate.

You can double the serving into one cup for this tea, but it won't be the same as a Ceylon or Assam. That is because it isn't a Ceylon or Assam. That would be similar to saying that one expects a mushroom of any kind to be covered in any sauce and expect it to be the same experience as having steak. It can be cooked in beef fat and it's still not beef. Not the same texture, taste or over all experience.

My advice is if you find a good breakfast tea you like, whether it be an Assam, Ceylon or combo, stick to that. If you want to experiment trying to blend those teas till you find one you like, you will find yourself owning a small tea shop. The combinations are endless. More so than the many combos of Earl Grey.

title: The shy Earl Grey for the timid
text:
This can be either a shy Earl Grey or a shy Darjeeling. Shy in the sense that the distinctive notes that gives the tea their name aren't really there.

For those who are not a fan of Bergamot, but want a black tea that hangs around in the background that doesn't come forward by much, this is the tea for you. The complete opposite of the Earl Grey Roi by M.F. The French brand can definitely make this one seem dainty. The British are not known to be dainty. Not in the teas usually nor in their food. But this one, dainty would be the word.

It's not a bad tea. The color and flavor of black tea is there. The Bergamot on the other hand is quite absent. More of tease to the palate. It's a gentle tea that is smoother than T of H Afternoon Darjeeling. Makes a good tea to get through the day. Can be refreshing with some ice cubes. Easy on the palate and can go with almost any dish.

The nice thing about T of H sachet is that they are all individually wrapped in a sealed bag that is waterproof. Upon opening the bag, the lack of aroma pretty much gave a good idea of how the tea would taste. Either this has been sitting on the shelf too long or this is the usual way it is made. I would not doubt it since it fits the theme of most T of H teas. Their teas tend to be on the weak and lacking side. They make T------- seem more present and prominent in taste.

Even Bradleys has more of an aroma and that would be classified as a nickel tea. Although this is better than that brand in terms of not being able to smell the cheap Bergamot aroma. I would not mind drinking this on any given day if I had nothing else better. But I would not exactly think of it as an Earl Grey since it lacks that scent.

For those who love their Earl Grey, this is not the one. For those who are new to Earl Grey and want a good introduction, this is not the one. For a smooth black tea that you can add citrus to or drink as is both hot or cold that lacks character, this is the one.

Out of the different brands of Earl Grey I have tried, I would recommend the Earl Grey Supreme by H & Sons. The silver tips adds another angle to the tea. It is definitely a Darjeeling base that stands out equally to the Bergamot if not more than the Bergamot. That one makes a sturdy tea that allows citrus to be added and still taste great.

Surprisingly, I did not expect the T of H to be this lacking on such a classic tea. I would go through this more often than cheap Earl Grey mainly for it not having that Bergamot aroma. When you double the tea bags into one cup, what you get is the Darjeeling base. The Bergamot is still hiding some where. It's missing a lot of notes quite similar to their Afternoon Darjeeling.

Think of it this way. Afternoon Darjeeling without the woodsy bitterness and you have this one that they call Earl Grey. This Earl Grey with the woodsy bitterness added and you have their Afternoon Darjeeling that is rough and unrefined in taste.

Most Earl Greys have a Darjeeling base. This one has the color and taste of a Darjeeling. But it lacks so many natural notes that you question what kind of Darjeeling it is other than the bottom of the barrel or something sitting around too long that a lot of flavor has faded away. The flavor is a little more bitter and heavier when you double the amount, but then it seems more Darjeeling than anything else.

It is best to consider this as a black tea or plain Darjeeling and nothing more. Perhaps one can make their own Earl Grey by adding some form of grapefruit into the tea. It lacks the distinctive aroma and taste of Bergamot. This one fades into the background without a stand.

I give it 2 stars for being a decent black tea. 1 star for being an Earl Grey. 4 stars for T of H keeping their teas consistent even if the theme is weak. Aside from their Afternoon Darjeeling, it is the brand to go to if you want something tamed, mild, not distinctive enough in a good way and don't want any surprises. The aroma is lacking too. It's a Darjeeling that lacks a lot of character. How T of H has managed to find a weak Darjeeling to go with a weak Bergamot and sell so much of it is amazing.

I usually give certain brands a try on a variety of different teas so that I would know if they carry a similar theme or if they vary greatly. T of H does not vary much. The box and bag is usually a nicer presentation than the taste of the tea.

For a good Earl Grey tea experience, the H & S does a good job with their supreme since there is more than one. You get the combo of the tea and Bergamot in a good way.

For those who ever wonder if there is a tea that says, "BERGAMOT" more than tea, the M.F. brand is good with that and they have 3 versions with E.G. Roi being the most prominent one. As in it hangs around your taste buds longer than a breath mint can. The bitterness and aroma stays around for a long time. The leaves smell strong when they are dry and when the tea is made, your palate would definitely be knocked over. The brand has been around since the 1800's. They have their fair share in testing what works and what doesn't after a while. Every other brand on the market is quite subtle on the Bergamot.

The M.F. brand is exclusive so it is not that easy to find it in the U.S. and most of the world. Only certain co. carry the brand, but it's very very limited in flavors. It is usually their signature tea that is sold. It is a hit and miss on flavors. High quality, but it is similar to a selection of pastries. Not every kind agrees with every palate. T of H is more predictable which is sort of the theme for many British made teas.

If you want Bergamot that zings and has your senses wake up with a soprano note, the F&M Earl Grey would do that. That is from smelling the unopened tin that has not been opened before. I would not ever call Bergamot lemony since usually the taste is heavier and more similar to a grapefruit. The F&M one has high citrus notes.

Out of all the different citrus to add to an Earl Grey, the pink grapefruit compliments it best. If you add any sweetness to it, the sweet will be in front and the bitter will come from the back as an after taste. Quite enjoyable. You know you have a good Earl Grey when you can add a citrus note to it and it still taste good. When you add that and you don't taste much of anything else then the tea is lacking in something.

A splash of citrus usually compliments an Earl Grey if the Bergamot is present enough. If not, the citrus won't do much. It seems many like the Lady Grey and not realize that is what it is when they add lemon to their Earl Grey.

If you add flowers to a Lady Grey, it is called a Baroness Grey. Different citrus and ingredients equal a different name since it changes the drink.

title: Decent tea.  Lacking in flavor.
text:
I did not have high hopes for the tea to begin with. It is what I classify as a nickel tea meaning it is not something I would want to pay more than a nickel per bag for regardless of how much you pay for it.

On a brighter note, it does taste better than Tazo. I had to double the bag to make a decent cup. This is after trying with different amount of milk and honey. Breakfast teas require that or it would be a bit difficult to drink. This is a tea for those who do not want anything loud, too forward or anything to stand out to make you have a funny face such as the R of T breakfast tea.

I would recommend it to those who want a simple, hang in the background type of breakfast tea. For those who ever had the F&M royal blend, they mix the Assam and Ceylon quite nicely. It has that je ne sais quoi to it. In a way they're both kind of in the background in the sense that this is a breakfast tea, not a wild and exotic flavors that keeps you guessing what the 10 different ingredients are type of tea. But I much prefer the royal blend any day. It is much smoother and has the bitterness in the background to stand out once you have the right amount of milk/honey with it that makes it more enjoyable than Williamson.

For the no surprise, straight forward, breakfast tea that is on the affordable level if you look at every other site, this isn't a bad way to go. Just remember to double the bags to a serving if you're wanting a little more boost in flavor. Breakfast tea is the tea version of coffee with cream and sugar. It is that bitterness in the back of the mouth that makes it enjoyable. It requires the sweetness in front from the sugar/honey in order for that to happen or the bitterness will be all over not in a good way. That's breakfast tea for you if you do not know to mix the milk and sweetness of your choice.

If this tea was on the shelf along with the other usual teas on the store shelf, I would get this or the other well known UK brand that is on every shelf. If it was next to the nicer teas of other brands that you won't find in the stores, I would go with the nicer ones if I want to pay a little more for a nicer experience to start my day. But to each their own. I have tasted many brands and types of tea. Eventually you start categorizing to differentiate them.

Some prefer the grocery store level teas. Some prefer the more exclusive and finer teas. For those who prefer it on a grocery store level, this isn't a bad tea to go with. For those who really get into their finer teas, you know where to go for the finer cup.

I just hope they keep the price down here on Amazon. title: An excellent value in a soy-free mayo
text:
Mayonnaise that is not soy-based is getting hard to find. For those of us who wish to avoid soy, this poses a problem. It used to be that Trader Joe's had a wonderful mayo that was soy-free, had great ingredients and came in a glass jar, but sadly they have discontinued it (and instead brought in an organic, SOY-BASED mayo in a tiny jar for a higher price!)

Since TJ has let us all down, this Whole Foods house-brand mayo is a nice replacement. Tangy and fresh-tasting, with good ingredients, and a much more palatable price than the (very few) alternatives available. It does come in a plastic jar, which to me is less preferable than glass, but many of the alternatives do too.

One annoyance: I started to order this Whole Foods item for curbside pickup outside our local store, then decided I had other shopping to do too, so I canceled my order and went to the store and grabbed a cart. Surprise: their shelf price for this mayo was higher than their online price, and the store management would not match the online deal! Guys, it's the same company! ...but no joy, they would not budge. So, resolute against the principle of allowing them the couple dollars of difference, I ended up ordering online for curbside pickup right then and there and waited for them to bring it to me. So silly.

The kernels are nicely varied and are of the correct size for a typical home grinder. (I've tried other brands that had huge kernels my grinders could not accommodate-- no such trouble with this.)

title: (UPDATED) Great Hearty Couscous!
text:
Love this stuff! By itself it doesn't have much of a taste but then again, you're supposed to season couscous otherwise it's just a bland pasta. A little bit goes a long way and it cooks up fast and easy. My husband and I noticed that it is very hearty, just a small portion feels like a brick, which is awesome. For years we purchased in bulk a well known store bought brand of couscous and we could eat a lot of it in one go because it never seemed to fill us up. We assumed all couscous was like this. Until now. This organic whole wheat couscous just looks and tastes like better quality, and as I said, it's very hearty, you fill up fast on just a small portion!
This is how I prepare it: I use a 2 to 1 ratio, so for a side dish (not the main meal) for just two people, I bring 1 cup of water to a boil with 1 teaspoon of olive oil. I pre-mix the seasonings (1-1/2" teaspoons of garlic powder, 1/4 teaspoon of sea salt, 1/2 teaspoon of curry powder, 1/4 teaspoon of onion powder, and 1 teaspoon of something green like dried basil or dried rosemarry, or dried marjoram). When the water is boiling, I first stir in the seasoning mix, then follow with 1/2 a cup of couscous, giving it all a good stir for about 10 seconds then I cover the pot with a lid and turn the heat completely off, but I leave the pot on the burner. The couscous continues to cook and absorb the water. In about 10 minutes the water is absorbed and I simply fluff the couscous and serve.

UPDATE:
My family and I LOVE this couscous! I had first purchased the 1 lb bag just to try it, but had to come back to buy the 5 lb bag because it just so good. It cooks up beautifully and quick, and so incredibly hearty. But alas, I was so disappointed when upon opening my order, there was a hole in the couscous bag. Oddly enough it was sent inside another clear bag, as if whomever sent it, knew/saw the hole and simply double bagged it. While the clear bag kept the spilled couscous from getting all over everything else in my order, it's still inedible as now I have no idea how long that hole has been there - if there is still 5 lb of product in it, if all the freshness is gone, or if any critters (like grain bugs) have gotten into it. Such a let down, as my family and I really do love this couscous.

title: Priced doubled in 5 months; quality suffered
text: I love this tea!  A breakfast tea that is not too harsh yet brisk enough to start my day.  In July 2022,  I ordered a box of 100 teabags that were individually packaged for $9.96.  December 2022 I tried  to re-order but was surprised to see that the price has doubled to $19.99. In order to get the same July price, I had to order two boxes of 50 bags that are: (1) not individually packaged, (2) two bags are attached to each other so you do have to rip them a part which is no big deal, (3) these bags are missing the string on each to easily remove the teabag from scalding water in tea cup; (4) the box has no inner wax paper lining to keep the tea from drying out.  Disappointing. With what’s going on in the world today with supply chain issues and all, I can understand a price increase but double?! I’ll be putting the new teabags in a jar with a tight fitting lid to keep them fresh.  My photo shows the new box of tea bags with no lining with the previous individually packaged tea bag in front of it.

Also, box is thin paperboard so it was heavily dented when it was shipped in a plastic bag instead of a box.  Not really in shape for a gift.  But that is minor as I got it for myself.  I have to see if this tea company has other flavors.

title: Perfect
text:
I love chai tea and this is really good. I was surprised with the Smokey flavor of the lapsong souchong black tea as I had never had that paired with traditional chai tea before. I also really liked the cherry and pomegranate mixed with the chai spices - it was amazing. I purchased 3 canisters in total, I liked it that much at $25 a canister (canister has 100 grams of tea, in theory about 50 cups of tea I've been told).

How I made it - I boiled my water to 190 degrees, let tea steep with a lid on for 5 minutes, strain and add sugar and French vanilla creamer. I taste the spices better with a warm/room temperature tea so I let my tea sit for another 5 minutes before I drink it. Perfect cup of tea, wish it was available all year long not just Christmas. Sooo good!

title: Just add anise oil, French vanilla creamer...holiday in a cup
text: I love this holiday chai tea.  As the stash tea bags are intended for smaller (8 ounces) cups of tea, I use 2 tea bags for 16 ounces cup and so forth.  I boil the water in a electric tea kettle to 190 degrees and steep for 10 minutes.  Once I remove the tea bags, I add 4 teaspoons of sugar, 3 drops of anise oil, and add a liberal amount of French vanilla creamer (creamer refrigerated from dairy section at grocery store works best).  This concoction paired perfectly with stash holiday chai tea ...It is awesome and has a kick that is like Christmas in a cup.  If you are not that big on anise flavor you might want to scale down to taste as I like the anise strong in my chai.  Love it, hard to find with the covid tea shortage...

title: Love cherry tea infusions flavor
text:
I love this tea. I love cherry flavor tea in general but have found that this is not common to find in herbal tea flavor. I also like the Taylor's of Harrogate Sour Cherry tea too but the predominant flavor is anise and cherry mixed in the tea unlike the Ahmad Rosehip & Cherry tea which does not have anise at all. Both are awesome and are a staple for my tea collection. If you like cherry flavor, I recommend both Ahmad Rosehip & Cherry Infusion and Taylor's of Harrogate Sour Cherry Infusion teas.

Side Note - the rose is not a prominent flavor in this tea. If you are looking for rose flavored tea I recommend Rose Lemonade by Taylor's of Harrigate tea. Another staple in my tea collection when I need rose flavor, however this Ahmad Rosehip & Cherry tea does not have much rose flavor only cherry.

title: Just like thai restaurant
text:
I love this tea. I was sceptical when reading the directions on the package that called for 1 cup (16 tbs) of tea for 4 cups of boiling water, but I did it anyways. Added tea directly to boiled water in a glass pitcher and waited 30 minutes - It was the perfect consistency like the restaurant makes it. The directions called for a strainer and I found a strainer for the Thai tea specifically on amazon by manufacturers named DDPremium under ASIN number B00N48M0OO. It is really important to have the strainer since the tea is not a powder form and needs to be strained before drinking. Other than that, it was easy to make. Will order again, restraunt quality at home.

Advise - If you should stain clothing from this orange colored mixture (i.e. a couple specks/dots on a dish towel), I soaked the cloth in the sink with Tide Original laundry soap mixed in some water and it came right out. Phew!!

title: Love this vegetarian chili - no tofu
text:
I love this vegetarian chili - black bean medium low fat. I especially like that it does not use tofu. The can does not list oven baking directions, but i bake it in the oven under 350 degree for 25 minutes in a casserole dish with tinfoil as the lid covering. Word of the wise? I added water to the casserole dish without reading the can thoroughly the first time around...big mistake...The can says not to mix with water but I mistakenly mixed with water and it made the chili really watery and it will not thicken when cooked and instead stays well runny. Much better when I did not add water to bake. Perfect! Love it! OOh, The spices had just enough heat without your eyes watering.

Side note -
Highly recommend Amy's vegetarian line to any vegetarian, they also have a frozen food line too with Amazing vegetarian pot pies which is so good for us non carnivores. There are two pot pies - Vegetable pot pie (with tofu) and Broccoli pot pie (with no tofu). Love them!

title: Mild chai tea

I do not believe (from tasting this) that it contains cardamom nor even black pepper (but I am no expert here, this is my humble opinion) because it does not have the spicy kick more like a simple, authentic, nostalgic coffee house soothing chai tea.  I read another review that said it was weak and bland but I don't think it should get a bad rap because it is not spicy and bold but instead rather it is soothing when you do not want the spicy kick that sometimes can burn your taste buds.  Also, the tea may have been weak because the package says to only steep for 4-6 minutes however I steep all Chai tea for 10 minutes despite the suggestion on the package.  I will continue to buy this Chai tea, I like it alot.

text: Opening the bag, you are immediately hit with the aroma of..., nothing. At all. Take some of the dried out flowers and putting them up to your nose, you "might" get "dusty cardboard" nuances, but that is all I could get from them. Steeping a heaping tablespoon full in a cup of hot water produced the same dust and cardboard aroma, very faint. But jasmine? None. No scent, dried to the dust point and any flavor these had was gone LONG ago. I think this stuff is left over from an extraction process? They look like jasmine buds (and stems..., lots of stems), but have zero scent left, not even able to coax out a hint steeping a handful (see pic, after 5 mins steep in hot water = ZERO smell of any kind). Waste of the $'s to package them, let alone label, ship, etc.

The EB tea was as-expected, tea leaves, cut and dried, but not pounded to dust. This..., was pounded to dust. Spoon pic looks better than it actually came, the majority of "tea" in the bag is what you'd use for cheap bagged tea. Tea dust, not dried leaves. Not impressed or happy, esp. considering the price of this stuff. At just shy of $10/lb, Ahmed teas are a MUCH better deal.

Bottom line, I like most H&S teas, but this is dried out and broken into dust. I'd avoid unless you want to make expensive iced tea with it...

If more would insist on organic and buy it, it would be cheaper and fresher. But, the pound I bought from Swanson is broken into small bits and is very dusty and "crumbly" dry with very little flavor, regardless of amount of tea used or steep times.

Dried out and broken into mostly fine powder. Tried a cup and it was very bitter and tasted like weeds or mown hay (that smell is how this tea tasted). Really was hoping I'd found a hidden gem, but not this time around. Not this tea.

title: What a lovely tea, and at the price? - updated review
text:
"You're gonna be sorrryyyy...," was the little voice in my head as I made cup number three of this lovely, aromatic tea in the middle of the afternoon. Yes, I'll be awake till next week, but I don't sleep much anyway, so I'll enjoy life in the moment I'm living right now (and regret it later, but that's later, so who cares?)

Came packed in a sealed foil bag inside of the Ahmad box. When I cut the bag open, there was a rich, flowery scent. Took a few long, deep inhales directly from the bag. A rush, for sure.

Brewing it, people say you can let it steep longer than the Barooti, but I'd disagree, after three-mins it was already more powerful than most Assams. 3-4mins using a tablespoon (perhaps my addiction has become out of control, but I like tea to have taste!) per cup and it's already getting a little tannic. 2-3mins seems best. Not the classic Assam flavor I'm used to (and I get my Assams from a tea shop in India where I teach and live part-time), but it's a lovely cup of tea no less. If you're looking for that light, fleeting Assam flowery taste, perhaps use only a teaspoon and brew for less time. Overall, esp. considering price per pound, this tea is a WINNER!

EDIT: After more than a month with this tea, it's my new go-to in the morning (or afternoon when I get really stupid). Not the best tea I've had (the old Rishi China Breakfast Black was that, but even that is different now, changed growers and blend, still good, but not the best), but certainly for the price it's a solid, lovely tea. Sipping a cup now and had forgotten that I'd left a review, so leaving this edit. If you like black teas, you will not regret this purchase at all!

-------------

Update Aug 2019: Bought another pound of this tea, it's again my favorite go-to morning tea. Still a great tea. Fresh and lovely flavor, very rich and malty. For the price it's the best bargain around!

-------------
Update Oct 2020: Another pound, but this one took one star away. Lackluster, dried out tasting, tastes like "tea," but nothing like the classic, flowery Assam flavor this tea has always had. Not sure if maybe I received a pkg that had sat on the shelf too long or what, but this is not worth looking forward to in the morning. Will keep trying, perhaps the next pound will correct what this one lacked.

--------------
Update May 2021: Another pound, still not what it was, but still a good, solid morning tea. Lacking in the classic Assam taste it once had. Thought it might be me, that my taste had changed, but I still have a handful of the older stuff from a few years ago and one cup tells me this is different from what the older stuff was. Again though, it's still a nice morning tea, better than any bagged tea out there...
--------------
Update, Aug 2022: Got another pound, dry and tastes "old" or oxidized. Packing label shows October 2019, foil bag inside is sealed, but I use DOUBLE what I normally used and change steeping times, but still not the flavor and aroma I remember from this tea. It's an "OK" tea, probably good for making iced tea, but far from the rich, flowery taste of classic Assam. Used to drink this every day, now, it's too lackluster of a tea for that, so maybe once a week. Sad...

-----------
UPDATE, Dec 2022: Still a very drinkable tea, for the $9 it sells for a pound, it's hard to complain. Latest batch is again dried out a bit, breaks into dust easily, flavor is OK, but tastes a bit "dusty" and old. All in all though, still my go-to for a bfast tea.

title: Dusty, dry, lackluster flavor - third day taste was better
text:
First opening this tea, there's a dust-orama happening inside the bag. Tried to photo, you can see the dust on sides of bag, but most of it had settled by the time I snapped the shot. Had to use two-tablespoons of tea, steeped for 2-mins, to get any noticeable flavor, after 5-mins there's some strength, but not much (and oddly low-tannins for having steeped so long), just a dark caramel-colored water. Will try again tomorrow and edit this if somehow it comes up with flavor (sometimes I find I taste things differently on different days, so I try to average out my assessment of teas and other necessities of life). Currently I'd suggest passing this up for something else (their -Rishi- China Breakfast Black was an excellent mainstay, it has changed over time, but last order, though quite dried out, was still flavorful enough to drink every day).

*EDIT: tried again and by the third day, there was enough flavor to say this was acceptable. Not worth the price in my opinion, but it's a decent tea. I spend many months of the year traveling in Asia, have tasted some marvelous teas in China, Singapore, Sri Lanka and India, but perhaps I need to set my standards lower for teas bought here in the U.S.?

title: One of the most flavorful black teas I've found. - edited 10/16: not the same tea.
text:
This is the number one most flavorful tea I have found. Started buying it in bulk at the local health store (at $45/pound), so looked online and found on Amazon. Much better deal and the same strong, great taste (but not high tannins). LOVE this stuff, it's an every morning tea and wishing I could drink in the afternoon too (but can't do that much caffeine).

-------------------------

EDIT: 27 Oct 2016: Just received another 1lb bag and..., well..., it just lost Rishi two-stars. This new batch is not only very dry with very little aroma, it tastes like a cheap Pu'er (that horse-dung -not in a bad way- smell/taste, "muddy," flat). Someone else posted on this stuff that the older stuff was worth climbing a mountain over. This..., is not. Certainly not for the price when you can buy a Pu'er for close to nothing around here and mix it with some dirt from a well-managed garden to come up with the same flavor. NOT happy. But in a way, glad that I had a chance to taste it when it was good. Like all pleasures in life, simple and profound, they are fleeting...

EDIT: 01 April 2018: Tried another pound of this, always hoping Rishi will find another matching tea to the outstanding stuff they had some years back. Well, this isn't it. It's nice, has some of the same aroma, but it's like a dried-out tea. Took two tablespoons and a long steeping just to get flavor out of it. So it's more like paying for a pound and getting a half. With a bit of dried-out, dusty taste to it.

Edit addendum: The seller of my last purchase of this tea, Starship Shops, went WAY out of their way and not only called me about the tea, but refunded me, then sent me some samples of other teas they sell. One was an excellent Darjeeling, but I get to India once a year or so and bring back many kilo's of teas I try there, one is another excellent Darjeeling. In the future, I'll seek out this particular tea seller as they know their teas and go out of their way to not only procure the best they can, but also to sell the best they can.

EDIT: 30 June, 2018: Each time I am tempted and try this tea again, hoping for the original taste, I'll make sure I review it. Bought this again, June 2018, after emailing the seller (Tamurai Tea Co) asking how fresh it is and promptly receiving a sincere reply addressing my freshness concerns. They indeed do order small so that it's always recently from Rishi, but this tea is dried-out and very dusty (just pouring from the back whipped-up a Kansas dust-bowl era storm, right in my kitchen! Not the sellers fault, this is a new bag from Rishi, it's an issue with Rishi Tea themselves. Very "brittle," dried out and lots of broken, "dust" in this bag. With that said, the tea is acceptable, a hint of what the old, original CBB tea was like. Definitely worth it and tastes OK, but oddly, tastes like there's almost an "artificial" flavor added to make it taste like the old stuff? Odd. Conclusion: Dried-out and dusty, but still flavorful and worth the price.

EDIT: 6 Dec 2018: Bought another pound. From Tamurai tea. Still not the spectacular tea that it once was, but this is a very lovely, drinkable tea. Used to be I'd look forward to morning tea of the original China Breakfast Black. Now, it's OK, worth the price, for sure, but not "inspiring" as it once was. Overall though, worth the $26/pound.

EDIT: 08 Sept 2019: Not the original, but still an excellent tea, and certainly for the price! Bought another pound and it's a bit dry, dusty, but has good, solid flavor and a bit of that floral that the original had. I think Rishi is doing their best to find alternatives to their original China Breakfast Black.

title: Weak and tasteless. Makes carmal-colored water.
text:
Was hoping this was the same as a perfectly lovely China breakfast bulk tea sold locally. It's not. This has that pu erh tea flavor to it. That light aroma of fresh horse manure. I don't mean that in a bad way at all, I mean that fresh organic smell that is not unpleasant (not to me anyway, having worked as a cowboy at an old-timey ranch back in the day...). Kind of a "dusty" or "woody/earthy" smell and taste to it. Anyway, not what I care for and I bought a pound of it. If anyone wants to try it before buying a pound, email me.

BTW, having lived in various tea-centric countries during the course of mi vida loca, I've come to know and appreciate really aromatic teas; Assam's, Ceylon's, Chinese breakfast (by Rishi - expensive!), etc., so my opinion might be a bit skewed. And having lived with a lovely English lass for a time (who would threaten bodily harm if I was ever caught squeezing out a tea bag or leaves), my patience with unacceptable tea has been all but used up...

--------------------

EDIT 09 Mar 2018: Purchased again after seeing other new reviews stating its resemblance to the old Rishi China Breakfast Black. The reviewer must have gotten a different batch than I. This is pretty much a sticks and stems taste to it. Dark carmal color, but no taste. Brew for three, five, ten minutes, tastes the same. Might be cheaper than the Rishi tea, but not even close for flavor.

title: Carmelina's canned tomatoes
text:
Theses are very good tomatoes from Italy. Not DOP so they are abit more reasonably priced. Nice size cans for a single serving.
It is really great to get a big box delivered to my door so promptly. I don't have to lug bags full of heavy cans from the grocery store. title: Astonished
text:
I am completely astonished that this product garners such high reviews. I bought it as an avid consumer of "Dirty Martinis" in hopes of recreating the excellent ones at my local bars in Frederick MD and as such expected that the addition of this olive juice to Grey Goose, Belvedere or Ketel One, all premium brands, would result in a dirty vodka martini of high quality. Instead I was struck speechless, (briefly), by the insipid and decayed taste of Dirty Sue. Either my taste buds are decaying or the product is. I looked in the mirror and went to my local bar and ordered a dirty martini and discovered that it was not me.
The terms sherry, as in the decline of a wine to an undrinkable beverage, came to mind when I tasted it. I was initially concerned that I had added too much Dry Vermouth to the mix, so I halved the usual proportions from 6 parts vodka to 1 part of vermouth to an extremely dry 12:1 and still felt the problem was the Dirty Socks. For those of you who feel that a true vodka martini is essentially pure vodka plus ????? cold, I can't help you. Try shots. Olives optional.
Perhaps I just got a bad batch, (like the other negative reviewers), but for now I am planning on using the juice from high quality olives from the barrels of olives from my "local" olive emporium, (currently South Street Philly). Sorry Sue, I can't recommend you. I will try to get my local bartenders to reveal their secret sauce, but so far they all profess ignorance of DS.

title: Now has big clumps, overly chewy for amuch poorer texture
text: I had been buying Hodgon's Oat Brand for over 10 years as part of my daily effort to reduce my cholesterol naturally rather than take Rx. When I started, I realized that I actually loved the taste - especially when mixed with honey and cinnamon. Now, I cannot stand the texture. I miss the prior product's creaminess and better texture, and I'll probably not buy it again. Because I also have tinnitus (ringing in the ears), I also have to stay away from certain foods. Their Oat Bran used to be fine but because my tinnitus is food-induced or triggered , especially by certain pesticides, I'm suspecting that the company may have changed the pesticides they used to use to new ones - for I get lots of ringing now. So, as a former heavy user, I'm saying good-bye until they return to their original formulation, manufacturing process and pesticide usage.

title: Really like this tea

I have gotten to the point where I prefer loose tea because it tastes better and is more economical. I noticed some of the posts about health concerns. text: This has a really great coconut taste. I used it to make a protein coffee drink. It works really great for this. I will definitely be a returning customer.

text: I bought these for my mom. She makes homemade chocolate sour dough bread. These chips made the bread incredible. It is moister and has a very clean chocolate taste. I will definitely be a returning customer. Thanks for such a great product!

title: Nice tea, but ''with mint" is a stretch
text: There's a faint mint smell when you open the packet, that doesn't seem to reach the cup. When brewed I get a vanilla flavor, but not mint. The packaging says 'mint'. Did I get an old or dud package? If I hadn't opened and used a package I'd return this in half a heartbeat!

title: Product description should have mentioned very light roast.
text:
I bought this after reading a glowing review; and I thought it might be time to check out new coffee companies and roasters. The George Howell review should have been a tip off.
When I opened the bag, the beans were a dark beige, extremely light, just barely roasted. Even though I've taken an in person tasting course with Howell, I do not like beans roasted to the coffee equivalent of bloody rare meat.

title: Really like all three of these sauces
text: I started with the 'Funky' Sauce, then got the black bean one for Christmas, then ordered the Earthy, Spicy Tingly - plus a pack of all three for a present for my son!  So yes, I guess you can say I love them.  The Earthy one isn't as spicy as I had feared:  just nicely spicy with the cumin giving a lot of flavor.  These sauces count as umami bombs; a lot of flavor for a little sauce.  I've made the best fried rice of my life, and look forward to trying these for dips or hamburger seasonings or whatever.

title: Lovely tea - afraid I may develop an obsession here...
text:
I bought this first in an Amazon promotion - I'm a total cheapy, not as involved with tea as some of my friends. I roast my own coffee, and only think of tea as sort of a break from espresso.....
That said: this is lovely black tea. the flavor is exquisite, cleaner and less muddy than other brands I've tried. The silk tea bags are so luxurious,but the tea inside tastes much better than the gift store silk triangle teas.
It's so good, I think I'll have to pay full price and check out some of the other estate teas!

title: Nice tea
text: The lemon grass gives the tea a little richer flavor, and the mint isn't too strong.  This is one of our favorite green teas, and the automatic delivery means I dont have to hunt for it, or for a sale!

title: It actually tastes good!
text: I was expecting a nasty faux-bacon flavour-type.  But the salt actually does taste of bacon, and is great on eggs.  Nice service from the company too.

title: Love ordering tea in the mail
text: We always have a nice cuppa Good Earth after dinner. I don't have to wait for a supermarket sale to stock up, our very nice mailman brings it up to the porch.  Such a nice deal:  no time, no gasoline, good price.

title: Personal Issues Digesting It
text:
I wanted a citrus tea that was cheaper than Twinnings Lady Grey and found this. However, this tea reliably gives me a stomach ache. This doesn't happen with any other tea or coffee for me and it's happened at least 5 times before I was sure enough to pin it on the tea and write this review. Maybe it's me, maybe it's because it was delivered in 95 degree weather, maybe it's something else.

Other than that major issue, it tastes great and is affordable.

title: Great Value
text: Great value / convenience.  No additional sugar or grape/apple juice added like a lot of "cranberry juice".

title: Flavor Masked by Citrus
text:
The overwhelming flavor of this is the citric acid that they've added to it. It's so overwhelming that you can barely taste the Quinine and herbs.

If you want a high-end traditional tonic, I'd go with Jack Rudy's syrup or Q Tonic water.

title: Somewhat mashed, melted but not maple-e!
text: We really like stroopwaffles and we liked these, however, I thought they were caramel when we were eating some.  I just realized the reason I ordered them in the first place... Because I wanted to try the maple ones!  I asked my husband if he realized they were maple and not caramel and he didn't know they were maple.  So...if you're looking for maple flavor keep looking it's not in these!  Now one other thing...  And its not the product fault.  Amazon shipped these UPS in a padded plastic envelope.  The stroopwaffle box was bashed up a bit and apparently not kept in air conditioning at all, the bottom half of the package was melted and mashed together.  Mind you we ate them anyways.  They still tasted good just no maple flavor.
